items.title: A Borrower Pays €100. Where Does the Money Go?
items.author: Adam Saghy
items.content:
A few years ago, I worked on a problem in Apache Fineract (an open-source platform for building financial services and core banking systems) that sounds simple until you start looking closely at it: when a borrower makes a payment, exactly where should that money go?

To solve this problem, I designed the Advanced Payment Allocation Strategy introduced in Apache Fineract 1.9.0 and implemented core parts of its behavior. The goal was to move away from repayment strategies where allocation rules were largely hard-coded, and make those rules much more configurable.

Advanced Payment Allocation allows financial institutions to define how different transaction types should be applied across past-due, currently due, and future installments; how principal, interest, fees, and penalties should be prioritized; and how payments made in advance should affect future installments. It also introduced chronological reprocessing of transactions and charges and supports different horizontal and vertical approaches to allocation. I later presented the work at Community Over Code Europe 2024 conference, where I discussed both the business requirements behind the strategy and the mechanics used to implement it.

However, building it exposed a much broader financial software design problem, which I found interesting: how do you translate a financial institution’s business policy into precise, deterministic software behavior that remains correct as transactions, schedules, and product rules evolve? Payment allocation is a good example of what happens when a financial institution's business policy has to become precise, deterministic software behavior. A rule that sounds straightforward to a product or finance team can quickly become a combination of priorities, state transitions, chronology, lifecycle events, and exceptions. That is where payment allocation connects to a broader idea, Financial Product Engineering: the discipline of translating financial intent into precise, reliable, and evolvable software behavior.

To see why, let’s start with a (deceptively) simple question: a borrower makes a payment of €100. Where does the money go? At first, this sounds like one of the simpler questions a lending system should be able to answer. Reduce the balance by €100… but which balance? Does the payment cover overdue principal first? Accrued interest? A fee? A penalty? The current installment? A future installment? If some of the money remains after the current obligation is satisfied, does it reduce the next installment? The final installment? Should it be spread across future installments? And should a repayment follow the same rules as a merchant refund, goodwill credit, charge adjustment, or another type of transaction? Once you start answering those questions, payment allocation stops looking like a payment-processing detail - it becomes financial product behavior.

While designing and implementing core parts of Apache Fineract's Advanced Payment Allocation strategy, this was one of the engineering lessons that became clear to me. The difficult problem was not taking an amount and distributing it across balances; it was translating financial policy into software behavior precisely enough that the system could apply it consistently, explainably, and safely as the loan evolved. And that problem goes beyond payment allocation - I think it illustrates a broader discipline that financial software teams increasingly need to treat explicitly: Financial Product Engineering. Payment allocation is a good place to see why that matters.

The €100 Payment Is Really a Policy Decision

Let’s say a borrower has the following obligations:

So the borrower sends €100. There is no universal answer to how those €100 should be applied. One lender might prioritize overdue interest before principal, another might prioritize principal, and another may require fees to be settled first. The priority might also depend on the transaction type. And if the payment exceeds everything currently due, there is another decision to make: what does the remaining amount do to the future schedule? Each answer represents a financial policy, and software has to turn that policy into something deterministic. For example:

    And another product could have a completely different sequence. The important observation is that this ordering is not metadata about the loan. Once the system starts processing transactions, the ordering becomes the product's behavior: it determines balances, it influences the repayment schedule, it affects what becomes overdue, it can influence interest calculations and accounting consequences, and it changes the financial state from which the next event will be processed. A configuration field in a lending platform can therefore carry far more meaning than a typical software setting - it can encode financial policy.

    Hard-Coding Financial Policy Works Until the Product Needs to Change

    Apache Fineract has supported different transaction-processing strategies for many years. The problem with traditional repayment strategies was not that they couldn't allocate payments (they could). The problem was that the allocation behavior was embedded in predefined strategies. If a particular institution needed a different sequence, the usual engineering response was to represent another set of business rules in code. That approach works surprisingly well when the product is stable; it becomes painful when financial products start evolving.

    Fineract's Advanced Payment Allocation model was introduced specifically to allow allocation rules to be configured dynamically by transaction type rather than having those rules fixed inside separate repayment strategies. The model can distinguish past-due, due and future installments; prioritize principal, interest, fees and penalties; define how future installments should be treated; and chronologically reprocess transactions and charges. That change might sound like a normal move from hard-coded logic to configuration, but in financial software, there is a deeper architectural shift underneath it.

    The system is moving from: Financial policy → Developer interpretation → Code

    To: Financial policy → Explicit product rules → Generic execution model → Financial state

    The goal is to make the financial rule itself a first-class concept in the system.

    Configurable Does Not Mean Vague

    There is a trap here. When engineers hear "make it configurable," the instinct can be to expose enough switches and parameters that almost anything becomes possible. In financial systems, that could be dangerous. Configurability does not remove the need for precision - it increases it. If a system allows payment allocation to vary, then it needs an exact vocabulary for expressing that variation. For example, there are at least two different dimensions involved.

    The first is which installment should receive money: Past due / Due now / Future

    The second is which financial component should receive money: Principal / Interest / Fee / Penalty

    Then, future payments introduce another question. If money should be allocated to installments that are not yet due, which ones? Apache Fineract's model supports different approaches, including allocating toward the next installment, the last installment, or re-amortizing an amount across future installments. Those are not cosmetic choices, they produce different financial outcomes. This is why good financial configuration needs strong semantics. A useful financial rule should be flexible enough to represent product policy but constrained enough that its meaning remains clear.

    In other words: The purpose of financial configuration is not unlimited flexibility, it is controlled variation with deterministic financial meaning.

    Payment allocation also taught me that even something as simple as priority can have more than one interpretation. Let’s imagine three overdue installments: each contains principal, interest, and perhaps fees or penalties. Should the system completely satisfy the oldest installment before moving on to the next? Conceptually:

        Or should it prioritize one balance category across the relevant installments? For example:

        • then all applicable interest
        • then all applicable principal

        These different ways of traversing the financial state can lead to different results. They also demonstrate why product specialists and software engineers need a shared model. Saying "penalties come first" is not necessarily sufficient, an engineer still needs to know: Penalties where? Across which installments? Relative to which other dimensions? Under which transaction type? At which point in the loan lifecycle? Many difficult financial-software bugs begin in the space between a sentence that sounds clear to a human and a rule that must be unambiguous to a machine.

        Chronology Is Part of the Financial Model

        There was another aspect of Advanced Payment Allocation that I found particularly important: chronological processing. Imagine this sequence:

        • January 15 - charge created
        • January 20 - another repayment

        Now imagine that something causes the system to reprocess the loan. The January 10 payment should not suddenly behave as though the January 15 charge already existed, as that would rewrite financial history. The system needs to reproduce what the financial state should have been at each point in the sequence. This is why Advanced Payment Allocation processes transactions and charges chronologically. It is not merely a technical implementation preference; it protects the relationship between an event and the financial state that existed when that event occurred. This leads to a broader principle:

        In financial software, the result of an event often depends not only on what happened, but on what the system knew financially at the moment it happened.

        That becomes really important when dealing with reversals, corrections, backdated transactions, restructures, refunds, and other lifecycle events. A loan cannot always be understood by looking only at its current database state, sometimes you need to understand the sequence that created that state.

        A Loan Is a Financial State Machine

        That is why I tend to think about lending systems as financial state machines.

        A payment is not simply: balance = balance - payment

        It is closer to: current financial state + transaction + applicable product rules → new financial state

        And the new financial state becomes the input for whatever happens next. The consequences compound.

        Consider: Disbursement → Repayment → Partial repayment → Fee → Late payment → Charge adjustment → Prepayment → Reversal

        Every step depends on the state produced by the previous steps. This is why the happy path is rarely the hardest part of a lending engine. Creating a loan, generating a schedule, and processing an ordinary repayment might demonstrate that the basic model works. The more revealing questions come later.

        • What happens when the payment arrives early?
        • What happens when it arrives late?
        • What happens when it only covers part of the amount due?
        • What happens when the transaction gets reversed?
        • What happens when a previous charge changes?
        • What happens when the loan is restructured?
        • What happens when multiple financial behaviors interact?

        Those are not secondary scenarios, they are where the product model is actually tested.

        Financial Intent Has to Survive Several Translations

        I find it useful to describe this using what I call the Financial Product Engineering Chain: Financial Intent → Product Rules → Software Behavior → Financial State → Validation → Evolution

        Payment allocation can travel through the entire chain.

        : A lender decides how borrower payments should satisfy obligations.

        : That policy becomes explicit priorities covering installments, balance components, transaction types, and future allocation.

        : The platform executes those rules when transactions occur.

        : Principal, interest, fees, penalties, installments, and schedules change as a result.

        : The team needs to prove that sequences of events produce the expected financial outcome.

        : The financial institution changes its product, requiring different rules without corrupting existing contracts.

        The difficult part is preserving meaning all the way through. A financial policy can be perfectly reasonable at the intent level and still become incorrect software behavior if one of those translations is ambiguous.

        Existing Loans Make Product Evolution Harder

        Changing a rule in financial software introduces another problem that conventional configuration systems do not always face. Existing contracts already have financial history. Let’s say a lender changes its payment-allocation policy today. Should an existing loan that originated six months ago suddenly start following the new behavior? Sometimes, maybe. Sometimes not. Apache Fineract's Advanced Payment Allocation requirements explicitly state that changes made to payment-allocation rules at loan-product level apply to newly created loan accounts, while existing accounts retain the old rules. That is an important architectural idea.

        Financial Products Evolve, but Financial Contracts Persist

        Software has to represent both realities. That means product configuration is not simply about the current settings, it is also about knowing which financial behavior applies to which contract. Once a platform has thousands or millions of live loans, changing product behavior safely becomes a versioning problem, a lifecycle problem, and a data-integrity problem at the same time. This is why I believe the ability to change a financial product is increasingly a technology capability. The question is not only if the system can support this lending product. A better question is: If the product changes next year, can we introduce the new behavior without losing the meaning of everything that already happened?

        Testing Numbers Is Not Enough

        This also changes how financial software should be tested. A test such as: payment allocation result = €100 doesn't tell us much. The interesting tests describe financial behavior. For example, given:

          When: a €100 repayment is made

          Then: allocation follows the configured priority

          And: the correct installments are updated

          And: the remaining balances are correct

          Then introduce another event. Reverse the payment. Add a charge between two historical transactions. Make the next payment early. Change the sequence. Use another transaction type. The unit of correctness increasingly becomes the financial lifecycle, not an isolated calculation. This is one reason financial-domain knowledge matters so much in lending engineering. A technically correct implementation of the wrong financial rule is still wrong.

          Product and Engineering Cannot Live in Separate Worlds

          Payment allocation might sound like an unusually specialized example. I think it reveals something much broader about building financial products. Traditional product development often assumes a sequence:

          Business defines requirements → Product refines them → Engineering implements them

          That separation becomes problematic when the requirement itself contains complex executable behavior. An engineer designing payment allocation needs to understand why allocation order matters; a product specialist needs to understand what must be explicit for the software to execute the policy deterministically; a financial-domain specialist needs to understand the constraints of transaction histories, schedules, reversals, and state. None of those disciplines can safely operate only at the end of the chain, they have to converge much earlier. That convergence is what I mean by Financial Product Engineering - it is the point where all three have to meet.

          The Bigger Lesson From Payment Allocation

          Advanced Payment Allocation was designed to solve a specific lending problem, but the architectural lesson I take from it is much broader.

          • Financial products contain behavior.
          • Interest accrual contains behavior.
          • Repayment schedules contain behavior.
          • Delinquency contains behavior.
          • Prepayment contains behavior.
          • Restructuring contains behavior.
          • Corrections and reversals contain behavior.

          If those rules are buried throughout application code, changing the financial product becomes increasingly risky. If they become configurable without precise semantics, the system becomes flexible but difficult to reason about. The engineering challenge lies between those two extremes. We need financial behavior that is explicit enough to understand, precise enough to execute, constrained enough to trust, testable enough to validate, and evolvable enough to change. That is the deeper reason I find payment allocation interesting. The question was never simply where a €100 payment goes, but how do you take a financial institution's intent about that €100 and turn it into software behavior that remains correct through every event that follows? That is a Financial Product Engineering problem.

          Disclosure: I am a member of the Apache Software Foundation and contributed to Apache Fineract, including work on the Advanced Payment Allocation functionality discussed in this article. This article is written in a personal capacity and is not sponsored.

items.title: How to Shadow-Test an AI Agent Without Letting It Act Twice
items.author: Raju Dandigam
items.content:
You have a new prompt, model, or orchestration policy. Offline tests look good, but the change will see vocabulary, timing, and context combinations that your fixture set never captured.

So you shadow-test it: send production traffic to both the current agent and the candidate, compare their decisions, and keep the current agent in control.

Then the candidate calls too.

Now one user request has produced two real messages. The “safe” experiment has become a duplicate-action incident.

This synthetic failure happens when shadowing is implemented as “run the whole application twice.” For agents that can change the world, shadow testing must duplicate observation and decision—not authority and effects.

The Architecture Boundary That Makes Shadowing Safe

An action-taking agent contains at least four separable stages:

input -> decision proposal -> policy/approval -> tool execution -> outcome

The shadow should stop after the proposal and policy simulation:

                         +--> primary decision --> real policy --> execute
sanitized input/context -|
                         +--> shadow decision  --> dry policy  --> record only

This boundary is useful beyond experiments. It makes approvals testable, prevents a model response from directly becoming an external write, and gives you structured evidence to compare.

Represent Intent Before Execution

Instead of letting the model own an executable tool object, normalize its choice into a proposal:

type ActionProposal = {
  action: string;
  schemaVersion: number;
  args: Record<string, unknown>;
  reasonCode: string;
  confidence?: {
    value: number;
    source: "model" | "calibrator";
  };
};

type PolicyDecision = {
  result: "allow" | "deny" | "require_approval";
  policyVersion: string;
  reasonCodes: string[];
};

Do not collect hidden chain-of-thought. A bounded reason code such as or is reviewable. If you store a short explanation, treat it as untrusted, redact it, and never require private reasoning from a model.

The executor accepts only a proposal that has passed real policy:

async function executeAuthorized(
  proposal: ActionProposal,
  decision: PolicyDecision,
  context: ExecutionContext,
) {
  if (context.mode !== "primary") {
    throw new Error("Effects are disabled outside primary mode");
  }
  if (decision.result !== "allow") {
    throw new Error(`Action is not authorized: ${decision.result}`);
  }

  return toolRegistry.execute(proposal, context);
}

That mode check is defense in depth. The stronger control is that the shadow environment never receives write-capable credentials.

A flag passed into a real tool is fragile. One tool may ignore it, a refactor may omit it, or a newly registered tool may default to execution.

Build a distinct registry:

type ToolDescriptor = {
  name: string;
  inputSchema: object;
  sideEffect: "read" | "write";
};

const shadowTools = realTools.map(({ name, inputSchema, sideEffect }) => ({
  name,
  inputSchema,
  sideEffect,
} satisfies ToolDescriptor));

The candidate sees the same tool names and schemas needed to make a decision, but the objects have no method. If it proposes , the harness records the arguments and predicted policy result.

At the infrastructure layer, use separate identities and network policy:

  • no production write tokens;
  • no direct access to message brokers used for effects;
  • read-only or synthetic dependencies where possible;
  • a separate telemetry namespace;
  • hard spend and concurrency budgets; and
  • a kill switch independent of model behavior.

Application checks can fail. Missing credentials fail closed.

Decide What Context the Shadow Is Allowed to See

Copying an entire production prompt into an experiment can expose personal, contractual, or security-sensitive data. Define a context projection:

type ShadowContext = {
  requestClass: string;
  locale: string;
  accountTier: string;
  recentEventCodes: string[];
  policyFacts: Record<string, boolean | number | string>;
};

function toShadowContext(input: LiveContext): ShadowContext {
  return {
    requestClass: input.requestClass,
    locale: input.locale,
    accountTier: input.accountTier,
    recentEventCodes: input.events.map(event => event.code).slice(-10),
    policyFacts: selectApprovedPolicyFacts(input),
  };
}

Run this projection through privacy and threat review. The candidate often needs less context than the primary runtime accumulated.

Two good agents can explain the same decision differently. Text similarity therefore creates noisy promotion gates.

Compare structured behavior:

type DecisionDiff = {
  sameAction: boolean;
  changedArgumentPaths: string[];
  primaryPolicy: PolicyDecision["result"];
  shadowPolicy: PolicyDecision["result"];
  riskClass: "equivalent" | "benign_change" | "review" | "unsafe";
};

The highest-signal mismatches are usually:

  • primary says “stay silent,” candidate proposes a write;
  • primary requests approval, candidate predicts allow;
  • both choose the same tool but differ on amount, recipient, or scope;
  • candidate calls a forbidden or nonexistent tool;
  • candidate exceeds latency, token, or tool-call budgets; or
  • candidate makes a user-facing claim unsupported by the proposed evidence.

Google's Agents CLI evaluation guide reflects this broader view of agent quality: it separates tool-use quality, trajectory quality, task success, final-response quality, hallucination, grounding, and safety. A shadow score should likewise be a vector, not a single “similarity” percentage.

Use Policy Simulation Carefully

The shadow can run the current policy engine in a non-authoritative mode. That reveals whether the candidate's proposal be allowed.

const simulated = await policy.evaluate({
  proposal: shadowProposal,
  principal: redactedPrincipalFacts,
  mode: "simulate",
  policyVersion: productionPolicyVersion,
});

Simulation must not mint approval tokens, reserve inventory, mutate rate-limit counters, or write audit decisions into the authoritative ledger. If the policy system cannot evaluate without side effects, build a pure policy core and keep recording outside it.

Also record the policy version. A candidate comparison is uninterpretable if primary and shadow were evaluated under different rules without saying so.

It is easy to shadow only the simple requests that survive a convenient filter. The resulting dashboard says the candidate is safe because risky traffic never entered the experiment.

Define inclusion explicitly:

type ShadowEligibility = {
  eligible: boolean;
  reason:
    | "selected"
    | "privacy_excluded"
    | "unsupported_tool"
    | "budget_excluded"
    | "control_group";
};

Report both the evaluated population and exclusions. Stratify results by action type, risk level, language, account segment, workflow length, and whether the primary required recovery. Otherwise a large aggregate can hide the exact slice that matters.

One primary output versus one candidate output does not tell you the candidate's variance. For a bounded sample, run multiple candidate trials with fixed configuration and preserve the random seed where the provider supports it.

Do not mistake a seed for full determinism. Provider updates, retrieval changes, timestamps, tool data, and concurrency can still change behavior.

Useful summaries include:

action agreement distribution
forbidden-action proposal rate
approval-bypass proposal rate
argument-diff severity
p50/p95 decision latency
token and cost distribution
variance across repeated candidate runs
coverage and exclusion rate

Never invent thresholds because they sound mature. Set them from product risk and baseline behavior, then document the decision.

Shadowing is one stage, not a release strategy by itself.

  1. schemas, tool allowlists, secret scanning, policy tests.
  2. sanitized, versioned fixtures with known expected behavior.
  3. Repeated model evaluation: measure variance and grader stability.
  4. real context projection, no effect authority.
  5. Internal or consented canary: narrow population, real effects, rollback controls.
  6. risk-aware expansion with outcome monitoring.

Promotion should consider downstream outcomes, not only proposal agreement. The current agent may be consistently wrong. A candidate that disagrees could be an improvement, so route meaningful disagreements to labeled review rather than automatically treating the primary as truth.

What a Shadow Record Should Contain

A reviewable record needs enough context to reproduce the comparison without becoming a privacy archive:

type ShadowRecord = {
  experimentId: string;
  requestFingerprint: string;
  cohort: string;
  primary: { proposal: ActionProposal; policy: PolicyDecision };
  candidate: { proposal: ActionProposal; policy: PolicyDecision };
  diff: DecisionDiff;
  primaryVersion: string;
  candidateVersion: string;
  policyVersion: string;
  evaluatedAt: string;
};

Store raw prompts and outputs only when authorized and necessary. Prefer schema-approved fields, stable fingerprints, and short retention. Observability should reduce uncertainty without expanding the blast radius of sensitive data.

The Non-Negotiable Invariant

I would encode this as an automated contract:

For every shadow run:
  external_write_count == 0
  authoritative_approval_count == 0
  production_message_publish_count == 0

If the telemetry needed to verify those invariants is missing, the experiment should fail closed or pause. “We did not see a write” is weaker than “the shadow identity could not write.”

The point of shadow testing is to learn from realistic inputs before granting realistic authority. Duplicate the decision surface. Keep the effect surface singular.

items.title: A Second Brain Is Not a Memory Store
items.author: Hanul Lee (이하늘)
items.content:
The term second brain is not new. For years, people have used it to describe the habit of collecting notes in an app, tagging them, and searching for them when needed.

That is how I began, too.

These approaches have one thing in common: a person puts things in, and a person looks for them. Even after AI was added, only the last step changed. A person saves a record, a person searches for it, and AI reads the result. What I had not put in did not exist. What I had not searched for never came to mind.

However large a filing cabinet becomes, it is still a filing cabinet.

English key to the original diagram. Top, the filing-cabinet second brain: a person stores → a person searches → AI reads. What I do not enter is absent; what I do not search for never comes to mind. Bottom, the reflecting second brain: reality comes in → memories accumulate → they reorganize themselves → retrieve the past → connect it to new events. Sentences nobody entered are formed within memory.

Figure 4. Above is the second brain we knew; below is the kind of second brain now emerging.

When the filing cabinet starts organizing itself

My thinking changed when I began looking into agent memory architectures such as Hindsight.

I will keep the technical explanation brief. What systems of this kind do can be reduced to three words: retain, recall, and reflect. They store incoming information as facts, experiences, and beliefs that change over time; retrieve memories relevant to the present situation; and reread accumulated memories to develop new understanding.

Here, “reflection” is a broad description of memory consolidation and reasoning over memory. In Hindsight’s documentation, retain extracts and stores facts and relationships; recall retrieves relevant memories; and reflect searches memory and synthesizes an answer. Consolidating several facts into observations is a separate process triggered after retain. The meeting-and-email passage below illustrates the kind of inference being discussed. It does not report a measured result. A generated observation still needs evidence; these operations alone do not establish human-like experience.

It was the third operation that caught my attention.

Memory that reflects does not sit still. Minutes from a meeting three months ago connect with yesterday’s email, and that connection becomes an observation: “This person uses these expressions when postponing a commitment.” Nobody ever entered that sentence. Memory produced it by reading memory.

Human memory works that way, too. We rewrite the past a little each time we retrieve it. That is why the same event can mean something different at twenty and at forty. Memory is less like an object in a warehouse than a manuscript we keep revising.

AI memory has begun to acquire that quality.

Architectures have emerged in which AI does more than store the past: it keeps reworking the past and using it in present judgment.

When one agent became dozens

With only one agent, I did not need to worry about this. I simply had to manage the context that particular agent needed to remember.

With dozens, the situation changed. It was the problem I described in the prologue. The version of me known to the assistant differed from the version known to the business agent, and each new agent started from a blank page. A company in which every employee understands the CEO differently will not last long.

What I needed was one long-term memory shared by all the agents. And that memory could not be a filing cabinet. I could not personally organize all the records that dozens of agents generated every day. It had to be a memory that could make connections, organize itself, and revise itself.

From then on, what I was building was no longer an extension of a notebook.

The second brain is evolving from a place that stores memories for me into a brain that keeps reconstructing me.

What decisions would you delegate to an AI that can reinterpret its memories of you?

This article is an English translation of Chapter 1 of my whitepaper, Super Second Brain, with an added technical note. The whitepaper series is also being serialized in Korean on Substack; read the Korean prologue here. Generative AI assisted with translation and editing. The diagram is reproduced from my original whitepaper; its English key appears directly below it.
