items.title: The Hidden Cost of Real-Time Data: Why Faster Pipelines Don't Always Deliver Better Decisions
items.author: FNU Aditya Ranjan
items.content:
Latency is only one dimension of real-time data engineering. Correctness, freshness, recoverability, and operational cost determine whether a streaming architecture delivers useful business value.

Real-Time Is Easy to Promise. Reliable Real-Time Is Harder to Deliver.

The appeal of real-time data is obvious. Organizations want to react to transactions as they happen, detect anomalies before they become incidents, and make operational decisions using the most current information available.

Modern technologies such as Apache Kafka, Apache Flink, AWS Kinesis, and change data capture (CDC) frameworks make continuous data movement increasingly accessible.

But there is a difference between moving events quickly and delivering trustworthy information quickly.

A streaming pipeline may process an event in milliseconds while a downstream dashboard displays information that is several minutes old. An event may arrive on time but be processed twice. A late correction may change an aggregate that consumers have already acted upon.

These are not simply implementation bugs. They are consequences of distributed systems operating across independently failing components.

The more useful architectural question is not, "How low can we make latency?"

It is, "How quickly can we deliver information that is sufficiently complete, correct, and recoverable for the decision being made?"

The Four Dimensions of Streaming Reliability

I find it useful to evaluate streaming systems along four dimensions.

How long does an event take to reach the consumer?

Are duplicates, missing events, and out-of-order events handled?

How current is the information available for decisions?

Can the system replay and repair data after failure?

These dimensions are related, but optimizing one does not guarantee improvement in the others.

For example, reducing event-time waiting may lower output latency while increasing the number of late corrections. Increasing checkpoint frequency may reduce recovery work but increase storage and coordination overhead.

The correct balance depends on the business operation.

A fraud-detection system may need an immediate preliminary signal. A financial reconciliation process may require completeness and consistency, even if that introduces additional delay.

1. Event Time and Processing Time Are Not the Same

Consider a retail transaction created at 10:00:00.

The point-of-sale system may publish the transaction at 10:00:02. A streaming processor may consume it at 10:00:05, while a downstream data product becomes available at 10:00:08.

There are several clocks in this architecture:

  • Event time: when the business activity occurred.
  • Ingestion time: when the platform received the event.
  • Processing time: when a processor handled the event.
  • Availability time: when the result became usable by its consumer.

A pipeline that measures only processing duration can overlook substantial upstream and downstream delay.

For this reason, end-to-end freshness should be measured at the point where information is actually consumed.

2. Exactly-Once Processing Has Boundaries

Exactly-once semantics are frequently discussed as though they eliminate duplication everywhere.

In practice, guarantees depend on the processing framework, source, state backend, sink, and transaction boundaries.

Kafka supports transactional capabilities and exactly-once processing patterns within supported configurations. Flink provides state-consistency mechanisms through checkpointing and compatible connectors.

Neither automatically guarantees that every external API call, database write, notification, or business action occurs exactly once.

Consider a pipeline that processes a payment event and calls an external service. If the service accepts the request but the processor fails before recording completion, replay can trigger another request.

A robust design may require:

  • Stable event identifiers.
  • Transactional sinks where supported.
  • Explicit reconciliation procedures.

Exactly-once behavior is therefore an end-to-end property to establish, not a label to assume.

3. Late Events Create a Correctness Problem

Suppose a streaming application calculates sales totals in five-minute windows.

A transaction occurring at 10:03 might not arrive until 10:12 because an upstream system was temporarily disconnected.

Should the 10:00–10:05 aggregate change?

That depends on the windowing strategy, watermark configuration, allowed lateness, and downstream requirements.

Ignoring late events improves apparent stability but can produce incomplete results. Accepting late corrections improves completeness but requires consumers to handle revisions.

For analytical systems, I recommend explicitly distinguishing preliminary results from finalized results.

This makes the data contract clearer than presenting every streaming output as immediately authoritative.

Stateful processing enables joins, aggregations, deduplication, and event-time windows.

It also introduces storage, checkpointing, recovery, and operational complexity.

A deduplication mechanism that retains every event identifier indefinitely will eventually encounter scaling problems. A stream-stream join with unbounded state can accumulate information that is no longer useful.

State-retention policies should reflect business correctness requirements rather than arbitrary technical defaults.

The key design questions include how long late events remain valid, how much state must survive failures, and what happens when recovery exceeds the freshness SLA.

A Practical Freshness SLA Framework

Instead of defining a single latency objective, I propose a four-part freshness contract.

A defined percentage of events becomes queryable within the target delay.

The consumer receives the expected proportion of eligible events within a defined time window.

Late-arriving updates and reversals are reflected within a separate correction window.

After a recoverable failure, the pipeline restores processing and catches up within an agreed interval.

These objectives should be measured independently.

For example, an illustrative design might target 99% event availability within 30 seconds while allowing up to 15 minutes for late corrections. These are example requirements, not benchmark findings or universal recommendations.

A useful freshness measure is:

Freshness lag = consumer availability timestamp − event timestamp

The timestamps must have clearly defined semantics, synchronized clocks where appropriate, and instrumentation that accounts for missing or invalid event times.

Percentiles such as p95 and p99 are often more informative than averages because they reveal the slow tail.

How I Would Evaluate Two Streaming Designs

Consider two candidate architectures:

Kafka → stream processor → operational database.

Kafka → stream processor → durable analytical table → serving layer.

Architecture A may provide a shorter serving path. Architecture B may provide stronger historical replay and analytical flexibility.

Neither is universally superior.

I would compare them using the same event generator, event-time distribution, payload sizes, throughput profiles, and failure scenarios.

The evaluation would record end-to-end freshness, p95/p99 latency, duplicate output rate, correction behavior, checkpoint overhead, recovery time, and total infrastructure cost.

It should also include intentionally delayed events, repeated events, processor failures, and downstream unavailability.

Without these tests, a streaming benchmark mostly measures the happy path.

Real-Time Architecture Is a Business Contract

The next stage of real-time engineering should focus less on minimizing isolated processing latency and more on delivering dependable information under imperfect conditions.

That means treating event-time correctness, recovery, freshness, and cost as first-class architecture decisions.

A streaming system is not successful merely because events move quickly.

It is successful when consumers understand how current the information is, what guarantees apply, and how the platform behaves when something goes wrong.

Author: FNU Aditya Ranjan is a senior data engineering professional with more than 16 years of experience in enterprise data platforms, distributed processing, cloud architectures, and data integration.

items.title: Immutable Architecture: Why the Future of AI Models Demands Permanent Storage
items.author: vishwa vimukthi gammuduwaththage
items.content:
I ship software that depends on model weights. When I pin a version of a library, I expect the same bytes tomorrow. I want the same from a model, because a perception model that behaves a little differently next month is a different product.

This article is about who holds the files, and what happens when the holder changes its mind.

The single shelf problem.

The open-model ecosystem has one main shelf. Hugging Face reports about 18 million users, and for most open models it is the default and sometimes the only public download location.

On September 3, 2026, NVIDIA announced an agreement to buy Hugging Face for about $12.9 billion. Jensen Huang said it "will remain an open platform." I have no evidence that this promise will be broken. But the main distribution point for open weights is now set to belong to the company that sells most of the chips those weights run on. That is a lot of trust in one place.

Models do disappear, and not always for bad reasons:

  • In August 2024, Runway removed its Stable Diffusion 1.5 repository from Hugging Face. The most widely used open image model of its time lost its official home, and the community carried on from mirrors.
  • In September 2026, Hugging Face disabled a modified GLM-5.3 repository that was labeled as built for offensive cyber work, citing its content policy. The publisher said it did not know which rule it had broken. A renamed version stayed up.

You can agree with one of those decisions, both, or neither. The structural point is the same. As one recent analysis put it, permission to use a model and dependable access to it are separate properties. A license covers the first. Nothing covers the second.

The second problem is quieter. A model can stay available under the same name and stop being the same model.

The best-known measurement is from Chen, Zaharia, and Zou at Stanford and Berkeley. They ran the same prompts against GPT-4 in March and June 2023. On a task asking whether a number is prime, accuracy fell from 84 percent to 51 percent. The model name was unchanged. People debated why the numbers moved, but nobody disputed that behavior shifted under a stable label.

It keeps happening in different forms. In August 2025, OpenAI removed GPT-4o from ChatGPT when it launched GPT-5, then brought it back after users objected. In September 2025, Anthropic published a postmortem saying that infrastructure bugs, not deliberate changes, had degraded some Claude responses for weeks.

That last case is worth noting. Drift is not always a decision. Sometimes it is a routing bug or a hardware change. From the user's side, it looks identical: yesterday's output is gone, and nobody told you.

Open weights should be immune to this, and mostly they are. But a repository is mutable. Its owner can push new files to the same branch, and anyone who downloads by name instead of by commit gets whatever is there today.

Content Addressing: The idea that does the work.

A URL tells you where a file is. It says nothing about what the file is. Whoever controls the server controls the answer.

Content addressing reverses this. The address is a cryptographic hash of the file. Change one byte and the address changes. You can fetch the file from anyone, including someone you do not trust, and check it yourself.

You can get the core of this today with no blockchain at all:

import hashlib

def sha256_of(path, chunk=1 << 20):
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        while block := f.read(chunk):
            h.update(block)
    return h.hexdigest()

EXPECTED = "paste the published hash here"
assert sha256_of("model.safetensors") == EXPECTED, "weights do not match"

And pin the exact revision when you download, never a branch name:

from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download

snapshot_download(
    repo_id="org/model",
    revision="full 40-character commit hash",
)

These two habits remove most silent-update risk for weights you run yourself. What they do not solve is availability. A hash is useless if no one still has the file.

Three storage models, three different promises.

This is where decentralized storage comes in, and the three names in the usual pitch are not interchangeable.

is a protocol for content addressing and peer-to-peer transfer. It is not a storage guarantee. A file stays available only while at least one node chooses to keep it. If everyone stops, the address still exists and points to nothing.

adds a market on top. You pay storage providers for a fixed term, and they must post cryptographic proofs that they still hold your data. This is verifiable, paid storage with an end date. Deals have to be renewed. Its newer Onchain Cloud launched on mainnet in January 2026, with early usage reported at around 49 terabytes. That source is promotional, so treat the figure as a claim.

makes the boldest promise. You pay once, and part of the fee goes into an endowment meant to fund storage for at least 200 years, on the assumption that storage keeps getting cheaper. "Permanent" here is an economic forecast. It depends on that cost trend and on miners staying interested for centuries.

Size is a practical issue. A 70-billion-parameter model at 16-bit precision is about 140 GB. Paying a one-time permanence fee per gigabyte for every checkpoint, quantization, and fine-tune gets expensive fast. Prices move with the token, so check a live calculator before you plan around any number.

Version control for weights.

Git solved this for code. Each commit is a hash that includes its parent's hash, so history cannot be rewritten without everyone noticing. Model hubs borrow the idea, but the history lives on the hub's servers.

A decentralized version needs two small pieces:

  1. Each set of weights is stored under its content hash.
  2. A public record that says "version 1.2 of this model is hash X, signed by this publisher, on this date."

The log is tiny, a few hundred bytes per release. It can live on Arweave or any public chain for almost nothing. The blobs are large and can live anywhere: Filecoin, a torrent swarm, a university mirror, your own disk.

This split is the main thing I took from the research. The record of what a model is can be permanent and cheap. The copies only need to be numerous.

I think the arguments against this idea are stronger than its supporters usually admit.

It does not touch closed models. The worst silent updates happen behind APIs from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. You cannot hash weights you cannot download. Permanent storage only helps with open models, which are already the easier case.

It cannot verify remote inference. Most people do not run open models themselves. They call a hosted endpoint. A hash on Arweave says nothing about which weights that server loaded, or whether it quietly swapped in a cheaper quantization. Proving that needs hardware attestation or verifiable inference, and neither is mature at large-model scale.

Immutable means you cannot take it back. In December 2023, the LAION-5B dataset was pulled after researchers found links to child abuse material in it. That removal was right, and it was possible because the data sat on servers someone controlled. The same applies to a model with a planted backdoor, leaked proprietary weights, or a model trained on personal data that a court orders deleted. A network that cannot delete also cannot fix mistakes.

Arweave's endowment rests on assumptions about hardware costs across two centuries. Filecoin deals lapse if nobody renews them. IPFS content vanishes when the last node drops it. Each one is a different kind of promise from an economic system that is under ten years old.

The simpler tools mostly work. Pin your revisions, verify hashes, keep your own copies, and seed a torrent. Community projects already index Hugging Face models with their hashes and magnet links. That gets a careful team most of the benefit with no token involved.

A matching hash is not safety. It proves the file is the one that was published. It does not prove the published file is harmless. Old pickle-based checkpoints can run arbitrary code when loaded.

I do not think every checkpoint should be written to a permanent ledger. That would be expensive, and it would preserve our mistakes along with our work.

A narrower version holds up. Foundational open models are becoming shared infrastructure, like compilers and kernels. For those, three things seem worth doing:

  • Publish a signed content hash with every release, in a public append-only record that no single company can edit.
  • Keep copies in several independent places, with at least one outside any commercial platform.
  • Treat model names as labels and hashes as identity, in your own code and in your papers.

Permanent storage is one way to get the second point. It is not the only way, and it is not the most important of the three. The hash is.

items.title: Tic Tac Toe in SwiftUI, Done Properly: Value-Type State, Win Detection and Minimax AI
items.author: Alok Singh
items.content:
The smallest game worth architecting: an immutable board, testable rules, a view that just renders state, and the classic AI you can bolt on in 40 lines

Tic tac toe is the "hello world" of game development, which is exactly why it's worth doing properly. It's small enough to hold in your head, but it still has every piece a real game needs: state, rules, turns, an end condition, a UI that reflects state, and, if you want it, an opponent that thinks.

One of my earliest App Store apps is , published in April 2020. Its listing is as short as the game: "Put away your pencil and paper", with one-player and two-player modes, so you can play against another person or against yourself.

This article uses tic tac toe to show an architecture I'd use for any turn-based game: a that owns all the rules, a that only renders state and forwards taps, for the rules, and a as an optional extension. To be clear: the listing doesn't say the app has a computer opponent. The minimax section is the approach I'd add, not a description of the app. API names are checked against Apple's documentation.

1. Why architecture matters even here.

The quick version of tic tac toe puts nine strings in a view and checks for a winner inside the button action. It works for an afternoon. Then you want an undo button, a computer player, a "new game" animation, a stats screen and tests, and every one of those features has to reach into the view.

Instead, split it like this:

Game (struct)      ← all rules: whose turn, legal moves, winner, draw
   ▲     │
   │     ▼
GameViewModel      ← owns a Game, applies moves, triggers AI, publishes state
   ▲     │
   │     ▼
GameView (SwiftUI) ← renders state, sends taps; no rules at all

The model is a plain struct with no UIKit, SwiftUI, or timers, which means you can test it, copy it (undo is free), and hand a copy to an AI to explore future moves without touching the real game.

2. The Model: A board that can't be wrong.

enum Player: String, CaseIterable {
    case x = "X", o = "O"
    var opponent: Player { self == .x ? .o : .x }
}

enum Outcome: Equatable {
    case inProgress
    case win(Player, line: [Int])
    case draw
}

struct Game: Equatable {
    private(set) var cells: [Player?] = Array(repeating: nil, count: 9)
    private(set) var current: Player = .x
    private(set) var moves: [Int] = []          // history, for undo and replays

    static let lines: [[Int]] = [
        [0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5], [6, 7, 8],         // rows
        [0, 3, 6], [1, 4, 7], [2, 5, 8],         // columns
        [0, 4, 8], [2, 4, 6]                     // diagonals
    ]

    var outcome: Outcome {
        for line in Self.lines {
            if let p = cells[line[0]], cells[line[1]] == p, cells[line[2]] == p {
                return .win(p, line: line)
            }
        }
        return cells.allSatisfy { $0 != nil } ? .draw : .inProgress
    }

    var legalMoves: [Int] {
        guard outcome == .inProgress else { return [] }
        return cells.indices.filter { cells[$0] == nil }
    }

    /// Returns a new game with the move applied, or nil if the move is illegal.
    func playing(_ index: Int) -> Game? {
        guard legalMoves.contains(index) else { return nil }
        var next = self
        next.cells[index] = current
        next.moves.append(index)
        next.current = current.opponent
        return next
    }

    func undoing() -> Game {
        guard let last = moves.last else { return self }
        var previous = self
        previous.cells[last] = nil
        previous.moves.removeLast()
        previous.current = current.opponent
        return previous
    }
}

A few deliberate choices:

  • Nothing outside the model can put an X in an occupied square or skip a turn. The only way to change the game is , and it validates.
  • returns a new value instead of mutating. That makes the AI trivial, because it explores copies, and it makes "what if?" previews free.
  • Eight hard-coded lines beat a clever loop. For a 3×3 board, a literal table is the most readable rules engine possible. (For an N×N variant, you'd generate the lines instead.)

Because the model is pure, the tests read like the rules of the game:

import XCTest

final class GameTests: XCTestCase {

    private func play(_ moves: [Int]) -> Game {
        moves.reduce(Game()) { game, move in
            guard let next = game.playing(move) else {
                XCTFail("Illegal move \(move)"); return game
            }
            return next
        }
    }

    func testRowWin() {
        // X: 0, 1, 2   O: 3, 4
        XCTAssertEqual(play([0, 3, 1, 4, 2]).outcome, .win(.x, line: [0, 1, 2]))
    }

    func testDiagonalWinForO() {
        // X: 0, 1, 5   O: 2, 4, 6
        XCTAssertEqual(play([0, 2, 1, 4, 5, 6]).outcome, .win(.o, line: [2, 4, 6]))
    }

    func testDraw() {
        // X O X / X O O / O X X
        XCTAssertEqual(play([0, 1, 2, 4, 3, 5, 7, 6, 8]).outcome, .draw)
    }

    func testCannotPlayOccupiedSquareOrAfterWin() {
        let game = play([0, 3, 1, 4, 2])          // X has won
        XCTAssertNil(Game().playing(0)?.playing(0))
        XCTAssertNil(game.playing(8))
    }

    func testUndoRestoresTurn() {
        let game = play([4]).undoing()
        XCTAssertEqual(game, Game())
    }
}

These run in milliseconds, with no simulator UI. When you later add an AI or a new mode, they're your safety net.

4. The View: Render state, forward taps.

The view model holds the game and the mode. The view is a grid:

import SwiftUI

@MainActor
final class GameViewModel: ObservableObject {
    enum Mode { case twoPlayer, onePlayer(computer: Player) }

    @Published private(set) var game = Game()
    @Published var mode: Mode = .twoPlayer
    @Published private(set) var isThinking = false

    func tap(_ index: Int) {
        if case .onePlayer(let computer) = mode, game.current == computer { return }
        guard let next = game.playing(index) else { return }
        game = next
        computerMoveIfNeeded()
    }

    func undo() { game = game.undoing() }
    func reset() { game = Game(); computerMoveIfNeeded() }

    private func computerMoveIfNeeded() {
        guard case .onePlayer(let computer) = mode,
              game.current == computer, game.outcome == .inProgress else { return }
        isThinking = true
        let snapshot = game
        Task {
            try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(350))   // feels less robotic
            let move = Minimax.bestMove(in: snapshot)
            if let move, let next = game.playing(move) { game = next }
            isThinking = false
        }
    }
}

struct GameView: View {
    @StateObject private var model = GameViewModel()
    private let columns = Array(repeating: GridItem(.flexible(), spacing: 8), count: 3)

    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 20) {
            Text(status).font(.title2.bold())

            LazyVGrid(columns: columns, spacing: 8) {
                ForEach(0..<9, id: \.self) { index in
                    let mark = model.game.cells[index]
                    Button { model.tap(index) } label: {
                        Text(mark?.rawValue ?? " ")
                            .font(.system(size: 56, weight: .heavy, design: .rounded))
                            .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, minHeight: 96)
                            .background(background(for: index),
                                        in: RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12))
                    }
                    .buttonStyle(.plain)
                    .disabled(mark != nil || model.game.outcome != .inProgress)
                    .accessibilityLabel(label(for: index, mark: mark))
                }
            }
            .padding(.horizontal)

            HStack {
                Button("Undo", action: model.undo).disabled(model.game.moves.isEmpty)
                Spacer()
                Button("New Game", action: model.reset)
            }
            .padding(.horizontal)
        }
        .animation(.easeOut(duration: 0.2), value: model.game)
        .sensoryFeedback(.selection, trigger: model.game.moves.count)   // iOS 17+
    }

    private var status: String {
        switch model.game.outcome {
        case .inProgress: return model.isThinking ? "Thinking…" : "\(model.game.current.rawValue) to play"
        case .win(let p, _): return "\(p.rawValue) wins!"
        case .draw: return "It's a draw"
        }
    }

    private func background(for index: Int) -> Color {
        if case .win(_, let line) = model.game.outcome, line.contains(index) {
            return .green.opacity(0.3)
        }
        return Color(.secondarySystemBackground)
    }

    private func label(for index: Int, mark: Player?) -> String {
        let row = index / 3 + 1, column = index % 3 + 1
        return "Row \(row), column \(column), \(mark.map { $0.rawValue } ?? "empty")"
    }
}

Notice what the view do: it never decides who won or whether a move is legal. Even the disabled state just reads the model.

Version notes, since the app supports iOS 12: is iOS 14+, is iOS 17+, and is iOS 16+.

On an older target, use nested s, UIImpactFeedbackGenerator and , or build the same view model behind a UIKit grid. SwiftUI itself starts at iOS 13, so a genuinely iOS 12-compatible app is UIKit. The architecture doesn't change; only the view layer does.

Tic tac toe is small enough to search . Minimax explores every possible continuation and assumes both players play perfectly: the computer picks the move with the best guaranteed outcome, and assumes you'll pick the one that's worst for it.

enum Minimax {
    /// Best move for `game.current`, or nil if the game is over.
    static func bestMove(in game: Game) -> Int? {
        let me = game.current
        var best: (move: Int, score: Int)?
        for move in game.legalMoves {
            guard let next = game.playing(move) else { continue }
            let score = minimax(next, maximizing: false, me: me, depth: 1,
                                alpha: Int.min, beta: Int.max)
            if best == nil || score > best!.score { best = (move, score) }
        }
        return best?.move
    }

    private static func minimax(_ game: Game, maximizing: Bool, me: Player,
                                depth: Int, alpha: Int, beta: Int) -> Int {
        switch game.outcome {
        case .win(let p, _): return p == me ? 10 - depth : depth - 10   // win sooner, lose later
        case .draw: return 0
        case .inProgress: break
        }
        var alpha = alpha, beta = beta
        var best = maximizing ? Int.min : Int.max
        for move in game.legalMoves {
            guard let next = game.playing(move) else { continue }
            let score = minimax(next, maximizing: !maximizing, me: me,
                                depth: depth + 1, alpha: alpha, beta: beta)
            if maximizing {
                best = max(best, score); alpha = max(alpha, best)
            } else {
                best = min(best, score); beta = min(beta, best)
            }
            if beta <= alpha { break }      // alpha-beta pruning: this branch can't matter
        }
        return best
    }
}

Two details make this feel right:

  • makes the AI prefer winning over winning later, and losing later over losing now. Without it, a perfect AI sometimes "plays with its food" and looks broken.
  • skips branches that can't change the result. The full game tree is only a few hundred thousand positions, so the AI is instant either way, but pruning is a habit worth building for bigger games.

A perfect tic tac toe opponent never loses, which makes it boring quickly. A simple difficulty dial:

extension Minimax {
    /// skill 0.0 = random, 1.0 = perfect
    static func move(in game: Game, skill: Double) -> Int? {
        if Double.random(in: 0..<1) > skill { return game.legalMoves.randomElement() }
        return bestMove(in: game)
    }
}

"Easy" around 0.3, "medium" around 0.7, and "hard" at 1.0 gives three genuinely different games from one function.

6. Real-world example: Tic Tac Toe : Time Pass

At the time of writing, its App Store listing shows:

  • , in (Strategy, Casual) and
  • First released in
  • in the US store, averaging about
  • Supports

The listing says: "Tic Tac Toe supports one player and two player gameplay, so you can play against another human or against yourself."

"Put away your pencil and paper"A value-type model that enforces the rules (section 2)
"Two player gameplay… against another human" mode: one device, alternating turns (section 4)
"One player… against yourself" mode; minimax is the extension I'd add for a computer opponent (section 5)
UIKit is required below iOS 13; the model is identical either way (section 4)

A 3.9 average on a game this simple tells me something too. Casual players expect polish even from "time pass" games: clear win highlighting, a satisfying tap, an easy rematch. The architecture above is what makes that polish cheap to add.

7. Before you ship a small game: A Checklist

  1. Rules live in one pure model, with no UI framework imports.
  2. Illegal states are impossible: state, and validated moves that return new values.
  3. : each kind of win, a draw, illegal moves, moves after a win, and undo.
  4. The view only renders and forwards. If a view contains logic, move it.
  5. and never on the live game. It's tested too: it should never lose from any position where a draw is possible.
  6. Difficulty is a dial, not three AIs.
  7. every cell has a spoken label with row, column and contents, and the result is announced.
  8. The fastest way to a better rating in a casual game.

Tic tac toe is small, but the lessons scale. Put the rules in a value type that can't be put into an illegal state, test it like a spec, keep the view dumb, and treat the AI as just another consumer of the model, one that explores copies. The same shape works for chess, card games and anything else turn-based.

Play it, or explore my other apps:

What's your favourite "tiny game, big lesson" project? Tell me in the comments.

items.title: Before You Blame the Model, Check the Stack
items.author: Spurthi Tallam
items.content:
On September 3, 2026, OpenAI began rolling out GPT-6 Astra. Within days, some developers were reporting what one of them called a "post-launch lobotomy." An open issue in OpenAI's Codex repository, filed by one developer, described turns ending after about 30 seconds and completion reports for work that had never been done.

Others said they had gone back to the previous model, GPT-5.6 Sol. These were reports, not a diagnosis. As of mid-October, OpenAI had not publicly explained those reports, and nobody outside the company could say what, if anything, had changed.

Two months earlier, users had made the same complaint about Sol, and that time there was an answer of sorts. A widely circulated post attributed to OpenAI's Thibault Sottiaux denied Sol had been weakened but said the team had run and reverted experiments that changed its reasoning effort: roughly how much computation the model spends before it answers.

Stories like these get filed under "the model got dumber," which is true from the user's chair and not very useful. A router picks which model runs, an inference stack executes it, a system prompt constrains it, an SDK fills in the parameters you left out, and your application decides what the model gets to see. Any of those can move while the weights sit still.

When an office feels cold, someone checks the thermostat before blaming the furnace. A deployed model has many thermostats, and most are set by defaults nobody inspects.

The name is not the model.

The best-documented case came from Anthropic. On March 4, 2026, it moved Claude Code's default reasoning effort from high to medium to stop pauses that made the interface look frozen. A March 26 caching bug then made sessions that sat idle for more than an hour keep discarding their earlier reasoning on every later turn, and an April 16 system-prompt line capped text between tool calls at 25 words. Users noticed. AMD AI senior director Stella Laurenzo analyzed 6,852 sessions and found shallower reasoning and more premature stopping. Anthropic's April 23 postmortem said the API and inference layer were unaffected. It called the effort change "the wrong tradeoff."

Routers and names fail the same way. When GPT-5's model router broke on launch day in August 2025, Sam Altman said that "the result was GPT-5 seemed way dumber." Earlier that year, Google repointed a dated Gemini endpoint to a newer model, which developers on its forum called a breach of trust. OpenAI's documentation draws the line cleanly: a snapshot locks a model version, while an alias can be repointed. Pinning a dated name protects you only if the provider keeps that name attached to the same model.

Even when the model name stays the same, its defaults can change. When Claude Code's default moved to medium, most users stayed there, even after Anthropic added notices and a selector. A default isn't a suggestion. For most users, it is the product. Defaults move for reasons that look sensible on a dashboard: lower latency, lower token spend, a faster-feeling agent. The cost shows up as a vague sense that the product got less intelligent, and users rarely have a way to connect that feeling to a setting.

The serving stack has opinions.

Below the product settings is the machinery, and it can fail without anyone deciding anything. Anthropic's September 2025 postmortem described three overlapping infrastructure bugs. One bug misrouted Claude Sonnet 4 requests to servers configured for a longer context window, starting at about 0.8% of traffic and reaching 16% at the worst hour after a routine load-balancing change. Another, a compiler bug, could drop the most likely next token from consideration. Anthropic's evaluations missed the degradation, partly because models often recover from a single bad token. The company also said it doesn't reduce quality in response to load. Customers can't audit that claim, but the incident didn't require a conspiracy. Bugs were enough.

Open-weight models make the problem easier to see, because many companies serve the same weights. vLLM's official results for OpenAI's gpt-oss-120b on the AIME 2025 math benchmark show 93.0 at high reasoning effort and 79.6 at medium. That gap matters when a provider mishandles the setting. When Artificial Analysis benchmarked the providers hosting the model at high effort, six scored a median of 93.3%, and Azure scored 80%, a gap of 13.3 points.

In Simon Willison's write-up, Microsoft's Lucas Pickup explained that older vLLM commits "didn't respect reasoning_effort, so all requests defaulted to medium." In that case, the gap came from a serving configuration that ignored the requested setting, not from the weights.

None of this is new, only easier to notice. In 2023, Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia, and James Zou compared the March and June versions of GPT-4. In the revised paper, its accuracy on their prime-number task fell from 84.0% to 51.1%. Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor pointed out that the test contained only primes, so a shift in which answer the model leaned toward could look like a change in math ability. That's a fair correction, though a product built on those prompts would still have behaved differently in June.

So far the story has been "they changed it," which is comfortable because it puts the fault somewhere we can't reach. The less comfortable version is that the same failures live one layer up, in the code we own.

Start with sampling. For years, the standard advice was to use a low temperature for reliable output. Google's Gemini 3 guide now reverses that. It recommends leaving temperature at its default of 1.0 and warns that lower values may cause looping or degraded performance on complex reasoning. A temperature setting that suited one model family can hurt the next, with no change in your code.

Output budgets changed meaning when reasoning models arrived. For newer models, OpenAI deprecated max_tokens in favor of max_completion_tokens, which counts hidden reasoning tokens as well as the visible answer. A tight limit can be spent largely or entirely on thinking. The result can be an empty or cut-off answer from a model that was still working on the problem.

Context limits can change the input without raising an error. Since Ollama 0.15.5, its default context length depends on how much video memory the machine has, from 4,096 tokens on smaller GPUs to 262,144 on the largest. When a conversation overflows, Ollama prunes older messages from the front while trying to keep the system prompt and the latest message. Move the same application to a smaller cloud instance, and the model reads a different conversation. To the user, the model forgot an instruction. To the system, the instruction was never in the prompt.

Retrieval has quiet defaults too. Halve the chunk size without retrieving more chunks, and the model may get much less of the relevant evidence. Change the embedding model without rebuilding the index, and retrieval can break outright. It may also keep working while quietly becoming less accurate. Either way, the model is answering with different evidence from the evidence you thought you gave it.

And the evaluation set usually doesn't notice. Anthropic's April system-prompt change passed several weeks of internal testing. Only broader line-by-line ablations later found a 3% drop on one evaluation. That's a reason not to treat a small smoke test as evidence that a configuration change is harmless.

What Anthropic did afterwards is the useful part. After September 2025, it committed to running quality evaluations continuously against production systems. After April, it added line-by-line ablations for system-prompt changes, review tooling, and gradual rollouts for anything that might trade away intelligence. None of it required retraining the model.

The same discipline works outside the labs, and most of it is record-keeping. Pin dated snapshots rather than aliases, and store the model identifier returned with every response, where the provider exposes one, not just the name you requested. A commenter on that Astra bug report pointed out that their client logged only the requested model, so there was no way to tell what had actually answered. Log the parameters that actually reached the provider after your framework filled in its defaults.

Log the prompt, tool definitions and retrieval settings that were active, the reasoning and output token counts, and the reason each response stopped. Version the SDK, the inference engine, the embedding model, and the index like your own code. These records won't reveal a provider's internal routing error or an undisclosed experiment. They will tell you whether your application sent the same request with the same recorded configuration.

Then test against those records. Keep a golden evaluation set drawn from real traffic, long conversations and awkward edge cases included, and run it repeatedly. One good or bad answer proves little. What matters is whether the difference holds across the test set. At ICLR 2026, Jonas Kübler and colleagues showed that comparing two model versions sample by sample, with a classic paired test called McNemar's, can separate real degradation from noise.

In their case study, it caught an accuracy drop as small as 0.3%. How small a drop you can catch depends on the size of your test set. The test itself is cheap, though generating enough paired outputs may not be. Shadow a new snapshot against the old one before switching, and diff configuration the way you diff code. For open-weight models, run the checks their creators publish, such as OpenAI's compatibility test for gpt-oss and Moonshot's vendor verifier for Kimi K2.

The idea is a decade old. In 2015, D. Sculley and colleagues at Google described configuration debt in "Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems." Their warning still holds: "Hidden debt is dangerous because it compounds silently." The only update is that the configuration now includes someone else's router.

This argument has a boundary, and leaving it out would be selling something.

Sometimes the model really did change. Drift between versions of a service that carries the same name is documented, and logging on the customer's side can't prevent it. It can only catch it. Provider-side faults are harder still: Anthropic's own engineers didn't immediately connect user complaints to the load-balancing change, and customer-side logs are unlikely to find that kind of fault first.

That's where Astra sits as of this writing. The cause is unknown, and from the outside, a quieter default, a fallback route, and post-launch disappointment look the same. What bookkeeping buys is narrower than an answer, and still worth having. It turns "the model got dumber" from a feeling into a short list of things that did or didn't change on your side. If the list comes back clean, you have a stronger case for asking the provider to investigate, and the evidence to support it.

When quality drops, skip the question of whether the model got dumber and ask for the diff. Which snapshot answered, which provider served it, which parameters reached the API, what context survived truncation, which library versions were running, and why did the response stop? If your records can answer, you can rule out the usual suspects quickly and hand the provider a report it can reproduce. If they can't, the first failure isn't the model. Nobody wrote the decisions down, and a default is a decision nobody remembers making.

items.title: Betting on Movement: Options, Futures, and the Art of Risk
items.author: Tobechi
items.content:
Say you run a small airline. Fuel is your biggest expense, and you have very little control over what it costs. A war disrupts oil supplies, a refinery shuts down, or the dollar takes another hit. Any of these could push jet fuel prices up by 30% in a single quarter. The problem is that you have already sold the tickets. Your revenue is largely set, but your costs can still change. And if fuel prices rise sharply enough, the difference comes straight out of your margins. You could take your chances with the market, and hope prices come down. Or you could agree on a price today for fuel you will need six months from now.

This is what the futures market allows businesses to do, and when a company uses a financial contract to protect itself against a risk it already faces, that is . The goal is to make future costs more predictable and protect the business from price movements that could eat into its margins. But locking in a price is only one way to manage that risk. What if the airline wants protection against rising fuel prices while still benefiting if they fall? A futures contract cannot offer that flexibility; an can.

An gives you a right, not an obligation. A lets you buy an asset at a fixed price, known as the , on or before a set date, while a lets you sell at that price. You pay a premium upfront for that right, and that premium is the most you can lose as the buyer, regardless of how far the market moves against you.

Take a stock trading at $100. You buy a call with a strike price of $100 and pay a $4 premium. If the stock falls to $60, you can let the option expire. You lose the $4, but you avoid buying a stock at $100 when it is worth only $60. If the stock rises to $130, your right to buy at $100 is worth $30 per share at expiration.

After deducting the $4 premium, your profit is $26 per share. The seller, known as the , takes the other side of that trade. They collect your $4 upfront, but in return, they take on an obligation. If you exercise your right to buy, they must honor the contract. That obligation can become expensive.

A seller who writes a call without owning the underlying shares, for instance, faces potentially unlimited losses as the share price rises. This is why option sellers may be required to maintain margin. The buyer pays upfront for the right; the seller collects that payment and assumes the obligation.

A contract works differently. Both parties are obligated to fulfil the contract. The buyer and seller agree on a price today for a transaction at a future date. Neither pays an option premium, but both must post , which is collateral held to cover potential losses.

The exchange does not wait until the contract expires to settle those losses. Futures are , meaning gains and losses are credited to or deducted from each party's account as prices change. If your balance falls below the required level, you may have to deposit more money. Margin helps ensure both parties can meet their obligations.

For the airline, the choice comes down to the kind of protection it wants. Futures allow it to lock in a price, but it also gives up the benefit of favorable price movements on the hedged position. Options offer more flexibility. The airline pays a premium for protection against rising prices while retaining the benefit if prices fall. The real flexibility comes from combining these instruments. You can build positions around a particular view of the market, with a defined cost and a specific set of possible outcomes.

Example: A stock is trading at $100, the day before it reports earnings. You buy a call struck at $100 for $4 and a put struck at $100 for another $4. You have spent $8 in total, and that $8 is the hurdle. The stock has to move far enough to cover that cost before you make a profit.

At expiration, only one of the two options can have intrinsic value. If the stock finishes above $100, the call has value, and the put expires worthless. If it finishes below $100, the put has value, and the call expires worthless. Whichever side pays out has to recover the cost of both options.

That puts your break-even points at $108 and $92. Above $108, you make a profit. Below $92, you also make a profit. Between those prices, you lose some or all of the premium. If the stock closes at exactly $100, both options expire worthless, and the full $8 is gone. Outside the break-even points, the two sides behave differently.

The call has no upper limit to its potential profit, because the stock price can keep rising. The put, on the other hand, can only gain as much as the stock falls towards zero. If the stock reaches $115, the call is worth $15, and you are up $7 after the $8 you paid. If it drops to $85, the put is worth $15, and you are up the same $7.

There is another complication with earnings trades. The $8 premium reflects the market's expectations about volatility ahead of the announcement. Options tend to become more expensive when traders expect a large move, and the combined cost of the straddle can give you a rough sense of the move being priced in. Here, the $8 premium is 8% of the stock price, although that is only a rough guide to the expected move, not a precise forecast.

Once the announcement is out, much of that uncertainty disappears. Implied volatility can fall sharply, reducing the value of the options. Traders call this . The stock can move in the direction you expected, and the trade can still lose money if the move is too small or the fall in implied volatility outweighs the gains from the price movement. What matters is whether the stock moves enough to justify what you paid for the position.

A follows the same principle, but the strikes are further apart. Instead of buying a call and a put both struck at $100, you buy a call at $105 and a put at $95. Both options are out of the money when the stock is trading at $100, which generally makes them cheaper. Suppose the pair costs $5, compared with $8 for the straddle; The lower cost comes with a wider distance to profitability. The call starts to have intrinsic value above $105, and the put below $95.

But those are the points where the options start paying out, not where the position breaks even. You still have to recover the $5 premium. That puts the break-even points at $110 and $90. If the stock closes at $107, the call is worth $2, leaving you $3 down on the position. The stock has moved in the right direction, but not far enough to cover what you paid.

The maximum loss on this strangle is $5, compared with $8 for the straddle. But the strangle loses its full premium whenever the stock finishes between $95 and $105, whereas the straddle loses its full premium only when the stock finishes at exactly $100. The strangle costs less to enter, but it needs a larger move to become profitable.

Beyond the break-even points, both positions gain an additional dollar for every dollar the stock moves further in the profitable direction, assuming expiration and ignoring transaction costs. The difference lies in the cost of entry and how far the stock has to move before those gains begin to outweigh it.

Here are the two side by side at expiration, per share:

With these numbers, the strangle only comes out ahead if the stock finishes close to where it started, within about 3 dollars of 100. Anywhere else, the straddle does the same or better. You saved 3 dollars on the ticket, but the options start paying 5 dollars away from the price, so you give back 2 dollars on every big move. A strangle is cheaper to buy and has a smaller worst case. In return, it asks for a bigger move and gives you a wider range where you lose everything you paid.

Trading the stock you already hold.

Not every option strategy starts with a view on how much a stock will move. Sometimes, the shares are already in your portfolio, and the question is what you can do with them.

Take the : you own shares trading at $100 and are in no hurry to sell. You write a call with a strike price of $110 and collect a $3 premium per share. If the stock finishes below $110 at expiration, the option expires worthless. You keep the premium and your shares. If the stock rises above $110, your shares can be called away at that price. Including the premium, you receive $113 per share, even if the stock climbs to $130.

You have collected income today in exchange for giving up any gains above $110, apart from the premium. That can make sense if you are comfortable selling at that price. But the premium offers only limited protection if the stock falls. It cushions the first $3 of losses per share; beyond that, you continue to bear the downside.

A takes the opposite approach. You still own shares trading at $100, but this time you want to protect yourself against a sharp fall without selling them. You buy a put with a strike price of $95 for a $2 premium per share. If the stock falls to $70, your shares lose $30 in value, but the put is worth $25.

Together, those losses leave you $7 down per share: the $5 between the share price and the strike, plus the $2 premium. That is the maximum loss on the combined position at expiration, regardless of how far the stock falls. The protection comes at a cost.

You have spent $2 per share on the put, so the stock needs to rise above $102 for the combined position to show a profit, assuming you measure it against the original $100 share price and ignore other costs. If the stock holds up or rises only slightly, the put may expire worthless, and the premium is gone. Much like insurance, you pay for protection whether or not you end up needing it.

Spreads narrow the bet, and narrow the cost with it

A bull call spread borrows the covered call's trick of giving up upside, but applies it to a brand new position instead of shares you already hold. You buy a call struck at 100 for 6 dollars and sell a call struck at 110 for 2 dollars, so you are out of pocket 4. Compared with buying the 100 call on its own, you have cut your cost by a third, and in return you give up any profit above 110. Your best case is 6 dollars: the 10-dollar gap between the strikes, minus the 4 you paid.

Your worst case is losing the 4, which happens if the stock finishes at 100 or lower. The break-even sits at 104. A bear put spread is the same structure turned over for a bearish view. You buy a put at the higher strike and sell one at a lower strike, so you pay less and cap your gain.

Go one step further, and you reach the iron condor. It is a bear call spread and a bull put spread on the same stock, opened together, so you collect premium on both sides. Take a stock at 100. You sell a 105 call and buy a 110 call to cap it, then sell a 95 put and buy a 90 put for the same reason. Say the whole thing pays you 2 dollars. If the stock stays between 95 and 105 at expiration, everything expires worthless, and you keep the 2.

Outside that range you start losing, up to a worst case of 3 dollars, which is the 5 dollar width of either spread minus the 2 you took in. Only one side can be breached at a time, so you never lose on both. Your break-evens are 93 and 107. You can think of it as a straddle or strangle turned inside out. Instead of paying to bet that something big happens, you get paid to bet that it does not, with a hard limit on what going wrong can cost.

Knowing what a strategy pays at expiration is useful, but someone holding a live position wants to know how its value is moving today. That is what the Greeks measure. Each one isolates how an option's price responds when a single input changes and everything else stays put.

Delta is how much the option's price moves for a 1 dollar move in the stock. A call with a delta of 0.60 gains about 60 cents for each dollar the stock rises. It is also a rough read on the odds of finishing in the money. Traders lean on it most for hedging. A call on 100 shares with a delta of 0.60 is offset by selling 60 shares, and as delta shifts, you adjust that hedge. This is the same replication argument the Black-Scholes model was built on.

Gamma is how quickly delta itself changes as the stock moves. A high gamma position needs its hedge adjusted often, because its sensitivity keeps shifting under you. It is highest for options near the strike that are close to expiry. A low gamma position stays hedged for longer.

Theta is the value an option loses just from time passing, with everything else held still. If you own options, it is a steady drag, and it accelerates as expiry gets close. If you sell them, the same number is income. That is a big part of why a covered call makes money simply by sitting there.

Vega is sensitivity to volatility. The straddle and strangle from earlier are, at heart, long vega positions. They gain when the market expects bigger moves ahead, whichever way the stock ends up going.

Rho is sensitivity to interest rates. It is usually the smallest of the five for short-dated options. It matters more for long-dated ones, or when rates are moving sharply.

Here is a small piece of code that calculates all five for a European option, building directly on the Black-Scholes pricing function.

import math
from statistics import NormalDist


def option_greeks(S0, K, r, T, sigma, option_type="call"):
    """Calculate the five main Greeks for a European option under Black-Scholes.

    S0 : current price of the underlying asset
    K : strike price
    r : risk free interest rate, annualized, as a decimal
    T : time to expiration, in years
    sigma : volatility of the underlying, annualized, as a decimal
    option_type : "call" or "put"
    """
    d1 = (math.log(S0 / K) + (r + 0.5 * sigma ** 2) * T) / (sigma * math.sqrt(T))
    d2 = d1 - sigma * math.sqrt(T)

    N = NormalDist().cdf
    n = NormalDist().pdf

    gamma = n(d1) / (S0 * sigma * math.sqrt(T))
    vega = S0 * n(d1) * math.sqrt(T) / 100  # per 1% change in volatility

    if option_type == "call":
        delta = N(d1)
        theta = (
            -(S0 * n(d1) * sigma) / (2 * math.sqrt(T))
            - r * K * math.exp(-r * T) * N(d2)
        ) / 365  # per calendar day
        rho = (K * T * math.exp(-r * T) * N(d2)) / 100  # per 1% change in rates
    else:
        delta = N(d1) - 1
        theta = (
            -(S0 * n(d1) * sigma) / (2 * math.sqrt(T))
            + r * K * math.exp(-r * T) * N(-d2)
        ) / 365
        rho = (-K * T * math.exp(-r * T) * N(-d2)) / 100

    return {"delta": delta, "gamma": gamma, "theta": theta, "vega": vega, "rho": rho}

Then run it on the same call, a stock at 100, struck at 100, six months out, 20 percent volatility and a 5 percent risk free rate:

greeks = option_greeks(S0=100, K=100, r=0.05, T=0.5, sigma=0.20, option_type="call")

for name, value in greeks.items():
    print(f"{name}: {value:.4f}")

delta: 0.5977
gamma: 0.0274
theta: -0.0222
vega: 0.2736
rho: 0.2644

A delta of about 0.60 means that, for each dollar the stock moves, this option moves roughly 60 cents. Options are quoted per share, but one standard contract covers 100 shares, so a single contract behaves a lot like holding about 60 shares. A theta of about negative 0.022 means the option loses roughly 2.2 cents a day just from time passing, with the stock price and everything else held still. On a full contract, that is about 2 dollars and 22 cents every calendar day.

Managing risk when the position is real money.

Understanding how a strategy works is one thing. Deciding how much of your capital to put behind it is another. Position sizing is where risk management becomes practical, because even a strategy with favorable odds will experience losing streaks. If you take on too much exposure, a run of ordinary losses can do serious damage to your account before the strategy has a chance to recover.

Futures add another layer to this problem because gains and losses are settled daily through marking to market. Your account is credited or debited as the futures price moves, and you must maintain the required margin balance. If your account falls below the maintenance requirement, your broker may issue a margin call, requiring you to deposit more funds. If you cannot meet it, your position may be closed, even if you still believe the trade will eventually work in your favor.

Consider a crude oil futures contract covering 1,000 barrels. A $1 fall in the futures price translates into a $1,000 loss on a long position. That is the effect of leverage: you control a large position with a comparatively small deposit, so relatively small price movements can produce substantial gains or losses against the margin you posted.

The same mechanism can create a cash-flow problem for a hedger. An airline that has taken a futures position to protect itself against rising fuel prices may face margin calls when futures prices fall. The position loses money, but the airline may benefit from lower prices when it buys physical fuel later. Those two effects can offset each other economically, yet the timing may not match. The margin payment is due now; the cheaper fuel may be purchased weeks or months later.

Position size is one part of the picture; you also need to understand what risks your positions share. The Greeks help make those exposures visible. Imagine a portfolio holding straddles across several companies, sectors, and earnings announcements. On paper, the positions appear diversified. But if they are all long vega, they are all exposed to changes in implied volatility. A broad fall in volatility could hurt several positions at once, regardless of how different the underlying companies are.

This is why risk management has to account for the portfolio as a whole. The number of positions you hold tells you very little if those positions respond to the same market event in the same way.

Return to the airline. Its problem was exposure to fuel prices, and the instruments we've covered offer different ways to manage that exposure or shape other market risks.

A futures contract can lock in a price, subject to the details of the hedge. A protective put establishes a floor for shares you own, in exchange for a premium. A covered call generates premium income but caps the gains you can make above the strike price. Spreads can define a narrower range of potential outcomes. A straddle or strangle gives you exposure to a sufficiently large move in either direction, while an iron condor takes the opposite view, earning a premium when the underlying asset stays within a range, but accepting losses if it moves too far.

Each position has a different payoff, cost and set of risks. Choosing between them means understanding which exposure you want and which trade-offs you are prepared to accept.

The Greeks help you track how that exposure changes as prices, time and implied volatility move. Delta measures sensitivity to the underlying price, gamma measures how delta changes, theta captures the effect of time passing, vega measures sensitivity to implied volatility, and rho measures sensitivity to interest rates. A payoff diagram shows the possible outcomes at expiration; the Greeks help explain how the position behaves before then.

But knowing what you hold is only half the job. You also need to know how much you can afford to lose, how much liquidity you need to maintain the position, and whether several apparently different trades are exposing you to the same underlying risk. A sound strategy can still lose money, and leverage or insufficient margin can force you out of a position before your original thesis plays out.

Pricing tells you what a contract is worth. Strategy determines the exposure you take on. Risk management determines how much of that exposure your capital can support.

The aim is to understand the risk before you take it, size the position accordingly, and avoid carrying exposures you never intended to hold.

items.title: Singapore Boffins Weave a GUI Into Fabric
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Researchers at the National University of Singapore have developed a machine-washable electronic fabric that can turn clothing into an interactive graphical user interface. The prototype reportedly survived 50 gentle machine washes and 1,000 bending cycles, though it still relies on external batteries and controllers. The Register reports: The development could lead - at some point - to a "future in which clothing functions as a pervasive, multimodal human-computer interface," according to the study published in peer-reviewed science journal Nature this week. The paper shows someone interacting with computing devices using the sleeve of a wool sweater (no jokes about the Windows ugly sweater please, this is serious). The researchers, led by Singapore National University research engineer Fu Heng, claim this is a big leap forward.
 
"This fiber-centric approach shifts wearable electronics from flexible panels toward truly textile-native architectures, laying the groundwork for fabrics that visualize, sense, communicate and compute as naturally as the garments they inhabit," the paper says. The researchers claim to have developed a scalable process to make millimeter-thick fibers. Using lasers to strip the insulation from specific spots on the thin copper wires, they attached light-emitting chips to the exposed sections, creating electrical connections to the chips. Thousands of chips were connected to the wires with extreme precision using this process.
 
The fibers were then fed into a transparent plastic tube, and made pressure-sensitive by adding two strips of a compressible, conductive polymer into a second longitudinal channel in the tube. The paper says they could make fibers 10 meters long using this method, and that they are thin and flexible enough to be woven into or attached to fabrics. The researchers were also able to add "peripherals" such as a microphone, a speaker, a temperature sensor and a light sensor.

items.title: Your Client Is Borrowing From You: The Cash Exposure Math of a Freelance Project
items.author: azizfromgroundwork
items.content:
Most freelancers think about payment terms as a question of trust. Will this client pay? Do I seem difficult if I ask for a deposit?

There is a more useful way to look at it. Every hour you work before you are paid for it is money you have lent to your client, interest-free, with no security. The amount you are owed at any moment is your : the value of work you have delivered minus the cash you have received. It rises as you work, falls when a payment lands, and it is exactly what you lose if the client disappears tomorrow.

Payment terms decide how big that number gets and how long it stays there. The difference between a good structure and a bad one is not a few percent. On the same project, it is four times as much money at risk.

Take one project and run it three ways.

A $12,000 build, ten weeks long, with the work spread evenly: $1,200 of work delivered each week. Exposure at the end of any week is:

exposure = work delivered so far - cash received so far

A negative number means the client has paid ahead of the work. A positive number is your loan to them.

The most common default. You invoice $12,000 when the project ends at week 10, and the client pays 30 days later, around the end of week 14.

Peak exposure: $12,000, held for four weeks. For fourteen weeks, you have been financing the client's project, and for the last four the entire fee is outstanding. If they go quiet in week 12, you have lost three months of work, not one invoice.

The usual "fair" split. $6,000 arrives before you start; the other $6,000 is invoiced at week 10, net 30.

Half of Structure A, which is why the deposit feels like the fix. But notice the shape: for the first five weeks the client is carrying the risk, and for the last nine it is all on you. The deposit protects the start of the project, and the start is the part that rarely goes wrong.

Structure C: Four Milestones

Same $12,000, split into four payments of $3,000: a deposit before work starts, then one payment at the end of week 4, one at the end of week 7, and the last at handover in week 10. Milestone invoices are due in 7 days, the final one in 14.

Peak exposure: $3,000, and the project is fully paid two weeks earlier. Same client, same work, same total fee. A quarter of the risk of Structure A.

Put the three side by side, and a pattern falls out:

peak exposure ≈ the largest payment you are waiting for

In Structure A, the only payment is $12,000, so that is what you can lose. In Structure C, no single payment is bigger than $3,000, so no moment in the project has more than about $3,000 at stake.

You can design for this directly. Decide the most you are willing to lose if a client vanishes, then size the payments so none of them is bigger than that. If your answer is $3,000 and the project is $12,000, you need at least four payments. The negotiation stops being about trust and becomes arithmetic.

Late Payment Is Worse Than a Low Rate

Exposure has two dimensions: how much, and for how long. Freelancers negotiate hard on the first and accept whatever they get on the second.

Suppose the Structure A client pays 30 days late, in week 18 instead of week 14. Your $12,000 of exposure now lasts eight weeks after handover instead of four. If you would otherwise cover your own bills on a credit card at, say, 24% a year, carrying $12,000 for an extra four weeks costs about $220:

$12,000 × 24% × 4/52 ≈ $222

That is roughly the cost of knocking 2% off your fee, except nobody asked you to agree to it.

Now, run the same 30-day delay on Structure C. The late payment is the final $3,000, so the cost is about $55. Milestones do not just cap the risk; they shrink the damage of the most common thing that goes wrong.

What Makes a Milestone Actually Work

Splitting the invoice is the easy part. Three details decide whether the structure holds when a project goes sideways.

Tie each payment to something the client can see. "Phase 2 complete" invites an argument about what complete means. "Staging site live with checkout working" does not. A milestone the client can verify by clicking a link is a milestone they cannot dispute.

Do not start the next phase until the last payment lands. This is the clause that turns a schedule into protection. Without it, a client who is two weeks late on milestone 2 is also two weeks into milestone 3, and your exposure is quietly back to Structure A levels. Put it in the contract in one sentence so pausing work is following the agreement, not making a threat.

Shorten the terms on everything but the last invoice. Net 30 on a milestone mid-project means you keep working while you wait, which adds a full phase of unpaid work to your exposure. Seven days on milestones is normal and rarely questioned.

Before you send your next proposal, take five minutes:

  1. Write down the project fee and how many weeks it will take.
  2. Divide the fee by the weeks to get your weekly work value.
  3. Sketch when each payment would actually arrive, terms included.
  4. Find the week where work delivered minus cash received is highest.
  5. Ask yourself whether you could lose that number and still pay your rent.

If the answer is no, the fix is not a better client. It is a different payment structure, and it costs nothing to propose.

AI disclosure: this article was written with the help of AI.

items.title: Can You Build an Agent Entirely in SQL? Almost
items.author: Nicholas Lisac
items.content:
When you think of an agent, you think of the LLM - the back-and-forth with the model - but for it to be an agent, it has to . It has to have what is called a 'ReAct loop' in which the agent itself interacts with its environment, calls tools, and decides when its turn is done.

That seems very complicated - you have to create the conditions for the loop, you have to provide tools, you have to interpret the responses and route the messages with logic.

In addition to the ReAct loop, you need other things. You need chat history, the live working transcript, sessions, tool definitions, an environment in which to execute code, a way to compact the conversation, a place to store retrieved information. I wanted to see if I could build all of this in SQL. And I basically did. Its name is Tables.

Tables is tables. Tables runs in a web app, but they don't have to. When you export from the web app, you get a single .sqlite file - a cartridge - and inside that file is the Python code that boots it: python3 your-agent.sqlite3 "What tables do I have?" and they talk back to you.

Tables is built on SQLite. SQLite does need a small amount of external piping to come to life - in my case a bit of JavaScript for the web app, or a little Python for the CLI. To be honest about what "almost" means: what lives outside the file is one HTTPS call out to a model, the ferry that carries it, the thing that draws the results on screen, and your API keys. The agent's entire state and control flow are the file. Everything else is the HTTPS transportation layer.

The loop is just a trigger.

The core loop is a trigger. When a new row is written to the `messages` table, the trigger fires and the cascade starts: it hands the active context to the model, writes the model's answer back into `messages` as a new row, and that insert fires the same trigger again.

If the answer contained a tool call, a second trigger runs the tool and its result lands in `messages` too, which continues the cascade. It repeats until the model stops asking for tools. That's the whole loop, and it needs one flag to exist at all: SQLite doesn't fire triggers from inside triggers by default, so the file sets `PRAGMA recursive_triggers = ON` and calls itself to life.

The model's main tool is `execute_sql` - it thinks and acts inside a SQLite database, which is its whole environment. I did build out the rest of the tool set because I wanted something I could actually use: `search_web` and `fetch_url` because those are table stakes, `materialize` to turn raw JSON from a tool result into a real table with `json_each()` so the data doesn't have to be retyped through the model, and `search_documents` / `ingest_document` backed by an FTS5 table for recall.

Messages are a table. Sessions are a table. The list of tools - a table. Approval rules? Table. The active context is a view that handles compaction. And as mentioned before, the loop is a trigger.

There are some cool things that fall out of this when compared to other agent harnesses. Tables is literally one file. You can take your .sqlite3, send it to another computer, open tables.nicholaslisac.com, load the cartridge, and your agent is good to go - same conversation, same data, same identity - or run the Python that's sitting in the file and never open a browser. The API key never travels in the file; it gets paired once per machine for security.

The chat history is native and easily explorable. Everything the agent has ever done or seen is in the SQLite database it operates from, and nothing is more than a SQL query away. Every write is journaled with who made it - the agent, you at the keyboard, or the interface on your behalf - so a turn can be undone without undoing your own work.

Everything the agent learns ends up in the same place as everything you give it. Drop a CSV on the window, and it becomes a typed table; have it fetch a page and materialize the results, and that becomes a table too. After that they all swim the same way, because for the agent there is no difference between its own history and your data - it's all just rows and columns.

Tables is naturally sandboxed to their database file, with the exception of their web capabilities. The agent can't touch your filesystem, can't install anything, can't notify you. It can't even break its own harness - the internal tables are protected from DDL and DML, on the agent's path and yours.

You also get a scratchpad so Tables acts as your own SQL workbench: runs your query and shares the result with the agent, runs it privately and the agent never sees it. And if you pin a query you like, it becomes an artifact.

Is this the future of Agent harnesses?!

Absolutely not. I wondered if I could build an AI agent loop with SQL as the engine and set out to see if it worked. I got a little carried away and made an entire web app to prove a point. It's part research project, part portfolio piece. And I like it.

Tables is not a coding agent. It doesn't have access to other files on your computer. It can't do most things people want out of their AI in 2026. Tables is just tables. But those tables can talk back to you, do real work in a database, do analysis and gather information from around the internet, and prove that SQL is (almost) as powerful as languages like Python or TypeScript.

The code is open - you can see it on GitHub, and you can check out the explainer here or go right to the app here: tables.nicholaslisac.com. You can use Tables, but you will need to BYOK, whether that is local or cloud.

No guarantee of performance or success - but it will probably be fun to talk to Tables.

items.title: People Are Vibe Coding Their Way to Better TVs
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Frustrated by intrusive ads, sluggish interfaces, and data tracking, smart TV owners are using AI coding tools and open-source projects to strip unwanted software from their televisions and build customized home screens. The Verge reports: Several vibe-coded TV-debloating projects exploded in popularity over the weekend. Cleanyourtv (known as tv-vibehack until the 19th), tv-detox, and dumbtv all claim to accomplish similar things -- remove sponsored ads, debloat the TV so it runs faster, and block unwanted data collection that tracks what you're watching -- without hacking, or rooting, the TV. By default, they all also replace the TV's built-in app launcher with simpler ones. Many users are going a step further and vibe-coding their own replacement launchers, like the Pokemon one below.
 
Most of the projects we've seen so far focus on TVs that run on Android and Google TV operating systems (such as TCL, Hisense, Sony, and older Amazon Fire products), using existing developer modes and the Android Debug Bridge (ADB) to tweak settings and apply (and remove) packages. According to the GitHub pages, they can also work with some Fire TV products that use a custom fork of Android (although likely not on the new Vega-based Fire TV Sticks). Because they use built-in developer tools, they don't require root access or firmware hacking, and they're reversible. Even projects that totally change the look of the interface just use Android's ability to install custom launchers -- in many cases with an assist from Claude Code or a similar tool to create the new launcher, too.
