items.title: Five SEO “Errors” on My Static Site That Weren’t Errors
items.author: Alex
items.content:
I run a small bilingual tutoring site, Intellix Tutoring. It is static HTML built with Jekyll on GitHub Pages: 68 pages, half in English and half in Italian, on a domain registered at the end of May.

This week, I went through Google Search Console and a third-party SEO audit, which between them reported dozens of problems. Almost none of them needed fixing. One "fix" would have made things worse, and the only real issue took a one-line regex.

Here are the five, and how I checked each one.

1. "Page with redirect: Validation failed"

Search Console listed four URLs under "Page with redirect", and the validation I had started in September said :

http://www.intellixtutoring.com/
http://intellixtutoring.com/
https://www.intellixtutoring.com/
https://intellixtutoring.com/it

First check: does each one go straight to the final URL?

for u in http://www.intellixtutoring.com/ http://intellixtutoring.com/ \
         https://www.intellixtutoring.com/ https://intellixtutoring.com/it; do
  echo "== $u"
  curl -sIL "$u" | grep -iE '^(HTTP/|location:)'
done

Each returned a single 301 to the canonical address (HTTPS, no www, trailing slash) and then a 200. That is exactly what you want.

The validation fails because "Validate fix" asks Google to confirm that these URLs no longer redirect. They are supposed to redirect, so it will fail every time. This report is a list of URLs Google won't index because they point somewhere else, not a to-do list.

2. "Discovered – currently not indexed" (39 pages)

This one looked serious: 39 of 68 pages known to Google but never fetched. Before blaming Google, I crawled the site myself with a Googlebot user agent, starting from the home page and the sitemap:

  • all 68 sitemap URLs return 200
  • no in meta tags or headers
  • every page has a self-referencing canonical
  • every sitemap URL is linked from at least three other pages, and the deepest is four clicks from the home page
  • no internal link points at a redirect or a 404

Nothing technical was blocking those pages. The domain is about four months old and has very few links from other sites, so Google crawls it slowly. "Discovered" means the URL is in Google's queue and hasn't been worth a fetch yet.

The crawl did find one thing worth changing: the home page linked to none of the 26 blog posts. They were reachable only through the blog index. That is a signal problem, not an indexing bug, and it's the kind of thing a crawl shows you and a dashboard doesn't.

What actually helps here: request indexing by hand for the most important URLs (Search Console gives you a small daily quota), link important pages from the pages Google already visits, and earn links from other sites.

3. Rich Results: "Invalid datetime value"

Google's Rich Results Test passed every post: valid Article, Breadcrumb, and Organization items, no errors. It did flag four optional warnings on the article markup:

Invalid datetime value for "datePublished" (optional)
Datetime property "datePublished" is missing a timezone (optional)

and the same two for . The JSON-LD had plain dates:

"datePublished": "2026-06-04",
"dateModified": "2026-10-12",

Schema.org accepts a plain date there, but Google wants a full datetime with an offset. The fix across all 26 posts was one substitution:

perl -pi -e 's/("date(?:Published|Modified)": ")(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2})(")/$1$2T12:00:00+02:00$3/g' \
  blog/*.html it/blog/*.html

Two choices in there are deliberate:

  • , because every date on the site falls in Central European Summer Time. Posts dated after the clocks change on 25 October need +01:00.
  • , because I had no record of the actual publishing time, and a midnight timestamp converted to UTC lands on the previous day. Noon keeps the calendar date the same wherever it's read.

Before pushing, I parsed every JSON-LD block on those pages again: 78 blocks, none broken. After the deploy, I fetched a live post to confirm it served the new values.

4. "Person is missing the required property name" (28 errors)

The audit tool reported 28 structured-data errors, one on each blog post and author page. The articles reference the author by ID:

{
  "@type": "BlogPosting",
  "author": { "@id": "https://intellixtutoring.com/#alex" }
}

and a second JSON-LD block on the same page defines that node in full:

{
  "@type": "Person",
  "@id": "https://intellixtutoring.com/#alex",
  "name": "Alex Ćetojević",
  "url": "https://intellixtutoring.com/about/"
}

The tool didn't follow the reference, so it saw an author without a name. Google's documentation uses the same pattern for authors, and the Rich Results Test reported the article as valid, with no errors.

Every post uses identical markup, so a single test settled it for all 26. An audit tool's error is a prediction of what Google will do. The Rich Results Test is the closest thing to asking Google directly.

5. Sitemap "doesn't match" the page date

The audit's most convincing finding: on 12 blog pages, the sitemap said , while the page's said September. The whole sitemap held only two dates, 34 pages each, which looked like build timestamps.

It wasn't. I maintain the sitemap by hand, so I compared each with the last commit that touched the page's source file:

git log -1 --format=%ad --date=short -- blog/ib-math-ia-criteria.html

64 of 68 matched exactly. There are only two dates because the whole site was redesigned on 7 October and half the pages changed again on 12 October.

Then I diffed the article text of the flagged posts from before and after 7 October. On the posts I checked, the text was 98 to 99.8 per cent identical: punctuation and one reworded call to action. But the structured data had changed on every one of them, and Google's sitemap documentation says that "an update to the main content, the structured data, or links on the page is generally considered significant."

So a of 7 October is correct, and a in September is also correct. One tells crawlers when the page changed. The other tells readers when the article text changed.

The four values that didn't match git belonged to posts whose only change on 12 October was the teaser line of a related-post card. That's not significant, so 7 October stands.

"Fixing" this would have meant moving 12 values back to September, which tells Google that 12 redesigned pages hadn't changed, while 39 pages were already waiting to be crawled. That was the one fix that would have made things worse.

What I'd tell myself a week ago

  • Read what a Search Console status means before trying to clear it. Some reports are lists, not to-dos.
  • Reproduce every audit error with Google's own tool before fixing it.
  • On a static site, git history is a good source of truth for .
  • On a new domain, the bottleneck is crawl demand, not markup. The work that matters is links: internal links from the pages Google already visits, and links from other sites.

items.title: Event-Driven CI at Enterprise Scale: Decoupling Webhook Ingestion with Kafka
items.author: Vidhi Shah
items.content:
• Synchronous webhook to runner systems do present some issues but we see that they are at risk for certain problems. The solution isn't to add more runners, instead what we do is we separate input functions from processing via the partitioned event bus.
  • Partitioning effected on the basis of organization, type of repository, type and name of reference preserves arrangement of references while avoiding the creation of hot partitions for big repositories. Because there is a lack of needs of the execution process, the stateless receiver only needs to verify and publish. 
  • When queuing arises, the protocol takes a new form. As it happens, the messages can be delayed, restored, and reverted which implies that some verification must happen before the process of publishing, deduplications on the basis of delivery ID must occur at the moment of delivery and processing should also be checked once again.
  • One must consider that there can be at least one delivery failure. In this case, the idempotent nature of keys allows for eliminating duplicates; the usage of the dead lamb queue allows for processing of bad messages without interruptions; the occurrence of the consumer lag allows for realization of the potential delivery backlogs.

In a typical situation we see a report of a dependency update which in turn affects hundreds of repos in 10 minutes. The code may still do its job fine but what we see is all the repos at once putting out push and pull request events. In our case we have a sync design that is -- for auth, routing, and delivery also sync. Thus the CI receiver is hit by a lot more traffic then is usual, also with no buffer. Some requests will go over the delivery time out, some will get caught up in busy runners, and some will just disappear. Our CI receiver doesn\'t handle redelivery of broken webhooks so these lost requests may reappear in a few hours as pull requests which didn\'t get their status check.

CI traffic is atypical of the fact that we are the source of our own spikes. We see mass dependency updates, a company wide rebase or a nightly job at the same cron tick for each repo which produces a trend that is perfectly in sync across a wide range of sources. AI has made this issue bigger. We are going for a 3x in developer productivity through AI support and also our agents are opening pull requests in some cases across many repos at once. Also, industry research reports that as we adopt AI more into our work flow we see better delivery throughput [2].

This article discusses the workflow, which we created for the CI platform with the goal of achieving 99.99% availability. It also provides details about implementation features making it possible to achieve this level of availability and tells what mistakes we made while working on this project.

Why the Synchronous Webhook Design Breaks

In the synchronous design, the source-control system sends a signed HTTP POST for each push, pull-request update, or tag [3], and the receiver validates it, selects a pipeline, and dispatches to a runner in the same request. Its response time becomes the sum of every downstream call, while GitHub expects a response within ten seconds [4]. Being able to send and receive events is not the issue that we struggle with. Our platform can process almost ten million events in a week; and traffic flow is anything but balanced: peaks are around thirty times higher than the average and happen instantaneously. Kafka can deal with such loads easily. What fails, though, is the connection between receiving and responding to an event, which results in the following four responsibilities.

  • Burst absorption. In the lack of a buffer the receiver has to at once deal with the peak as it happens, also auto scalers do not respond fast enough to 30x peaks. 
  • Partial failures as the new normal. When working at this scale, one component is always down, which creates a bottleneck.
  • Ordering vs throughput. Events for a particular branch or pull request have to be processed in the right order to ensure that an old event does not overwrite a new one. Global ordering is not required and cannot be achieved.
  • Untrusted and replay-worthy input. Queued events go through delay, redelivery, or replay which present a very different set of issues as compared to a verified request at the time of issue.

Adding runners does not resolve any of those problems.

Figure 1 shows the pipeline: A stateless receiver which does validation and publication of events, a partitioned Kafka topic, a consumer group scheduler which uses a database of branch and pull request state, an autoscaled execution layer, a rate limited status write back path to the GitHub API, a dead letter queue and a reconciliation job.

The receiver does three things: Accept requests, check their signatures, and report to Kafka. Also this does not have any other requirements in the request path which means it scales out without coordination and performs well within the platform’s timeout. We only acknowledge the webhook once Kafka has durably recorded the write; by returning success before that we actually reintroduce event loss.

The partition key is the most consequential design choice. We key every event as org/repo/refType/refName, where refType is branch or pr. Events with the same key are consumed in order, while different keys are processed in parallel [5][6]. Concurrently running which is what an event's record and the builds it triggers has gone into. We found out that how the queued builds behave is a per customer configuration. In that which comes to pull requests and feature branches teams tend to batch which means a new commit may leave out older queued builds or may in fact cancel them out of the queue also it allows for the possibility of the older builds to run at the same time. On the main branch we by default run a build for every commit as teams usually want a report for each and every release or audit they do.

The topic has a replication factor of 3 and holds events for a period of 60 days. Long term retention of events means that which have gone into dead letter queues may be replayed once a fix is in place, also in the time of which new consumer groups can catch up with the full history and deduplication window will equal the retention window.

The scheduler is a Kafka consumer group: each instance owns a subset of partitions and the group rebalances as instances join, leave, or fail [7]. Rebalance suspends usage on the partitions that have been transferred from one place to another. Although cooperative rebalance [8] and static membership [9] minimize this process, the automatic scaling agent remains very active, as it is demonstrated in the section of the study referring to experience gained. 

Verifying and publishing at the edge

GitHub webhooks carry an HMAC-SHA256 digest of the raw request body in a header [10]. The receiver recomputes it over the unparsed bytes and compares in constant time [11], because a non-constant-time comparison leaks timing information an attacker can use to forge a signature.

async function verifyAndPublish(rawBody, headers, secret) {
 // Header format is "sha256=<hex digest of raw body>"
 const expected = 'sha256=' + hmacSha256Hex(secret, rawBody);
 if (!constantTimeEquals(expected, headers['x-hub-signature-256'])) {
   return reject(401);
 }
 const event = normalize(parse(rawBody));
 event.deliveryId = headers['x-github-delivery'];   // dedup key for replays
 // refType is "branch" or "pr"; ordering is preserved per key
 const key = [event.org, event.repo, event.refType, event.refName].join('/');
 await publish('ci.build.events', key, event);      // wait for durable ack
 return accept(202);                                // queued, not processed
}

The await on publish matters most: the producer waits for acknowledgment from the in-sync replicas and if Kafka is unavailable the receiver returns an error rather than accept an event it cannot store.

The offset is what Kafka uses for “to date all has been processed. Post processing commit provides at least once delivery [12]. Exactly once semantics break at the first external call [13] which is when the scheduler puts together a deterministic idempotent key for each processing job out of repo, commit SHA, pipeline, and trigger, also the execution layer which we put in to play for duplicate prevention.

Commit time goes up as we see unexpected order of events due to debounce (which is explained later). By default at the end of the process the Spring Kafka does a commit. But in our case the debounce listener goes off before the processing does which means that in the off chance of a crash during that delay the event may be lost. This can be fixed if we do the acknowledgment manually which in turn allows the code to do the commit only after we are really done with the processing.

Manual backs alone still allow out-of-order commits. If offset 100 is still waiting while 101 and 102 finish, committing 102 and then crashing loses event 100. Spring Kafka's asyncAcks prevents this by deferring each commit until every earlier offset has been acknowledged [14]. A simplified version:

factory.getContainerProperties().setAckMode(AckMode.MANUAL);
factory.getContainerProperties().setAsyncAcks(true);
@KafkaListener(topics = "ci.build.events")
void onEvent(BuildEvent event, Acknowledgment ack) {
   if (event.isBranch() && !event.isDefaultBranch()) {
       // Debounce off the listener thread; the partition keeps flowing
       delayed.schedule(() -> {
           resolve(event);
           ack.acknowledge();
       }, 2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
   } else {
       handle(event);
       ack.acknowledge();
   }
}

Deduplicating branch and pull-request builds

A push to the head branch of a pull request generates an event for the branch and a separate event for the pull request, meaning that they can get delivered in any order. It would be wasteful to build two separate events for each pull request. 

Upon getting a branch event for any branch that is not the default one the scheduler puts it on hold for a 2 second period and then checks its db for any present pull request which has the same branch name at its head. When it identifies a proper pull request it goes forward without the need to build out the branch, instead just the head commit SHA is updated, which is handled by the pull-request pipeline for the actual build. Also if the pull request’s status is not known at that point the scheduler does a slower but more accurate query to the GitHub API to determine if there is in fact an open pull request. This also helps to avoid duplicate builds, a thing that does not play out at all when using the default branch which in turn can be put forth as the most active branch in the monorepo.

In the resolution of out-of-order events, timestamps prove to be very useful at keeping events in chronological order and at the same time assuring present moment information is reliable. This system helps assign timestamps to each event transformation, depending on the timing of the event itself determined by the type of event, such as the branch event timestamp or timestamp of the last update in case of a PR event. In instances when an event falls under the out-of-order event category due to being older than the event state preserved so far, it is rejected. Delivery time cannot be utilized in this scenario, as in such cases the event while being delayed or undelivered may seem to occur after, while commit dates cannot be used either, as newly created commit timestamps may contradict the actual timestamp of zero commit.

Sizing the Partition Count

In the issue of out-of-order events timestamps play a key role in maintaining chronological accuracy of events at the same time they see to it that we receive reliable info in the present moment. This system helps assign timestamps to each event transformation, depending on the timing of the event itself determined by the type of event, such as the branch event timestamp or timestamp of the last update in case of a PR event. 

In instances when an event falls under the out-of-order event category due to being older than the event state preserved so far, it is rejected. Delivery time cannot be utilized in this scenario, as in such cases the event while being delayed or undelivered may seem to occur after, while commit dates cannot be used either, as newly created commit timestamps may contradict the actual timestamp of zero commit.

  • Baseline: divide observed peak load by 20 events/second to get the minimum partition count.
  • Skew allowance (1.5x) for busy organizations and refs.
  • Growth headroom (3x), matching the AI productivity target. Partitions cannot be removed, and adding them later changes the key-to-partition mapping.
  • Round up to a power of two. We use 128 partitions, which gives roughly 2,500 events per second of scheduling capacity and allows up to 128 scheduler instances, though far fewer normally run.

Partition out count, consumer parallelism, execution layer autoscale and tenant isolation. These have to be tuned in tandem. Four elements which determine if this architecture scales are partition count, consumer parallelism, execution layer autoscaling and tenant isolation.

  • Partition count caps consumer parallelism, because a consumer group can have no more active members than the topic has partitions [6]. Choose it with headroom. By adding partitions later on, keys will be remapped and the ordering per-reference will be briefly disrupted, plus the number of partitions cannot be minimized. Consumer batching which processes multiple events per poll instead of one at a time increases the throughput per consumer but at the same time causes higher latency per event in lightly loaded conditions. This should be made a variable instead of a hard code. 
  • Autoscaling should follow leading signals. Consumers should be scaled based on the lag of the consumers and the runners based on the depth of the pending builds queue, instead of measured CPU or memory usage. 
  • At that point, the resource metrics will show saturation, with an upstream request backlog already in place.
  • In terms of the isolation of tenants, it is important to note that hash partitioning involves a lot of tenants in each partition meaning that the burst of one of the enterprises might delay all the rest.

In durable queues, whatever reaches the bus remains for a time of 60 days and can be retried or replayed:

  • Only confirmed events can enter the bus. The receiver checks the signature of each one before sending it to publish [10][11] and it is the only entity that can write to the build-event topic. A consumer should not be the first checker of an event.
  • However signatures do not protect against replay. The HMAC does not have a timestamp, which means that a request can be obtained in determination for an unlimited time. We deduplicate according to the delivery ID for the entire retention window.
  • Authorize again at the moment of execution. Minutes may pass between acceptance and execution which is why the scheduler checks that the actor has access, that the ref is to the commit, and that the fork policy allows the build.
  • Take care of not disclosing secrets in events. Credentials are received from the secrets manager at the moment of execution because events can be replayed or exposed.

The first sign which appears is consumer lag. Kafka, in this case, directly reflects it [15] and before the errors and latency. The correlation ID, which is passed from the webhook to the status write-back [16], presents the answer to the question "why didn't this build get a status?"

The dead letter queue must come before that one and the problem with the first poison-pill event arises. A message which has a status issue can block everything that is in the partition line for the queue. After a number of retries it is moved to the dead letter queue meaning that there must be its own monitoring and a checking process in the dead letter queue. It means that if the retention period is over sixty days then it is possible for us to repeat the events once we have the fix.

Back pressure. When the execution layer is overloaded or the debounce pool is full then consumers are forced to yellow their partitions and let Kafka take care of the backlog and avoid memory use from consumers.

Limits on service requests. GitHub has set limits on the number of service requests made by a particular organization [17], but both the callback and pull requests can be counted as service requests dependent on those limits. In the case of our particular GitHub application, it can be installed to each organization separately so the requests made by one organization can never affect the limit of another organization. 

Data validation. There are some events that are never delivered by GitHub [1], which means the system never receives them. In this way, there is a special job that compares current pushes with the requests already recorded in the system and generates the missing requests.

Trade-offs and Limitations

After a webhook comes in the status check may take a bit to show. Also the event bus becomes a primary dependency. If it goes out the whole pipeline grinds to a halt, not just a single request.

In an organization that runs through a few hundred builds a day this architecture is overkill. At that scale the simple, easy to debug and economical nature of a synchronous design is what is required and a partitioned bus with a consumer group scheduler just adds to the cost and issues without bettering the product. The crossover point is not a set number. It is when you see burst absorption issues, partial failures which aren’t isolated, or order at scale becoming a regular ops issue instead of a what if scenario.

Production Lessons Learned

Rebalance storms are not a theory—they are a real problem. Every time a scaling event happens the consumer group rebalances and consumption stops on the affected partitions until the reassignment finishes [7]. If a scheduler scales frequently it spends most of its time rebalancing instead of actually processing messages. From the outside it looks like the system is stuck even though every consumer is running fine. Tuning the rebalance protocol didn’t help much. What really made a difference was changing how we autoscale—scale up, scale down slowly and make sure there’s a cooldown period between each scaling event.

Migrate customers out in batches, at once we did not do a full scale move of all at once. The old system did not have an event bus; it was the sync design which went before and was the only go to live option for all teams, which also did not allow for down time. Instead of a full scale switch over we put customers into the new pipeline in batches:.

Dependency analysis was done to see what the old service did which documentation didn't report. 

We started with a small set of what we thought to be low risk organizations for the batch migration and only grew each batch once the previous one went through without issue.

Also we had a pre determined roll back plan for any batch which may have to be moved back to the old system without having to improvise.

Batching kept the blast radius small. A problem in the new pipeline affected only the organizations already moved and issues from monorepos and high-volume organizations surfaced before they could reach everyone.

Rehearse failures before production. Hot partitions, rebalance storms and poison-pill events are far cheaper to find on purpose than in an incident. Two forms of validation are worth building in. First we will run through a set of anonymized production webhooks which includes bursts on the staging environment because synthetic uniform load does not present the issue at hand which it should. Second we will introduce the failures which the design is intended to weather out[18]:

Kill a consumer in the middle of a batch to see that no event is lost and that redelivered duplicates are rejected by idempotency keys. 

Put forth a malformed event to have it land in the dead letter queue instead of causing its partition to stall. 

Scale the consumer group up and down to see what amount of lag a rebalance at the current partition count adds.

The design of the synchronous webhook is appropriate for the workload that most companies run. However, the trouble starts when groups believe they can scale the webhook by increasing the number of runners. Long before the execution capability becomes a limiting factor, changes need to be made at the ingestion level: before the execution capacity is reached the structure should change: there should be *stateless receivers for verification and publication*, partitioned announcement tool, horizontally scalable groups of consumers for planning the workload, and the collection of undelivered events to control the processing of batched tasks. All of these components are well-known. The trick lies in bringing them together in a way appropriate for the requirements generated by the work of the software (including the requirements for putting the records in their proper order, authorizing access to the information, and isolating failures).

That which we see is coming faster for more teams. We see in industry research a greater distance growing between what organizations do with CI/CD as a core infrastructure as opposed to a utility issue [2] also in play is AI in development which is increasing build volume still. We will put the bus forward as a source of operational signal as we do for a scheduling issue. We will add a structured failure classification field at publish time which will turn each build failure event into a data point for the auto diagnostician, we do away with a separate log scraping pipeline. As more organizations make this transition we expect to see shared and proven tooling for CI ingestion to come out rather than each team having to piece together from general purpose messaging we did.

items.title: Greece Enacts Social Media Ban For Kids Under 15
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Greece has passed a law banning children under 15 from social media platforms beginning January 1, 2027. The legislation requires platforms to implement reliable age verification and parents to use government-backed apps to restrict access, with penalties for noncompliance under the EU's Digital Services Act. Engadget reports: "It would have been very easy to do absolutely nothing today and wait for the perfect European law. But the challenge is here. Children are sinking into the internet every day, and I believe a responsible government must do what it is obliged to do," said Greece's digital governance and AI minister, Dimitris Papastergiou.
 
The legislation was opposed by Greece's minority parties, so Mitsotakis used his majority government to pass the bill. The nation previously barred mobile phones in schools in 2024, and opinion polls show that the new social media ban for children is widely supported by Greece's adult population. Mitsotakis previously said that his government's "goal is to push the European Union in this direction as well."

items.title: Hunting Replication Lag: A Queue-by-Queue Method for Diagnosing Oracle GoldenGate
items.author: Zalak Shrof
items.content:
• GoldenGate lag is not one number but the sum of waits in a chain of queues, and the fix depends entirely on which queue is growing.
  • Heartbeat tables measure true end-to-end lag at the target, while process-level LAG output only says how stale the record a process is touching is.
  • Apply parallelism helps only when the apply stage is the bottleneck and the workload is not serialized by dependencies, barriers or hot rows.
  • A missing or unusable index on the target turns replicated updates into scans, and on hot tables extra appliers stop helping once each hot-row chain is saturated.
  • Once an upstream bottleneck clears, the backlog moves downstream, so drain time is set by the next-slowest stage rather than by the original fault.

When replication falls behind, the reflex is to raise Replicat parallelism, which works only when apply is the binding constraint. This article treats an Oracle GoldenGate pipeline as a series of queues, from redo generation through Extract, trail, distribution and Replicat to target commit, and shows how to find the queue that is actually growing. A small model injects three faults: a burst of large transactions, an unusable index on a hot target table, and a network throttle. Adding appliers leaves peak lag unchanged for the barrier and network faults, and on hot rows it stops helping once each per-key chain is saturated. The method: measure every hop, fix the growing queue, and expect the backlog to move downstream.

At a hospitality software company, I build GoldenGate Integrated Extract/Replicat and Microservices pipelines for CDB-to-PDB and CDB-to-CDB replication on Oracle 19c, including bi-directional active-active topologies. I tune GoldenGate parameter files to reduce replication lag and troubleshoot trail-file corruption, checkpoint, and network issues. The common reflex to lag is adding appliers; often lag stays put.

"Lag" names a symptom, not a component. By Little's law, the number of items in a stable system equals arrival rate times time spent in it [1], so a lag figure only tells you how much work is queued somewhere. Kingman's heavy-traffic result adds that waiting explodes as a stage nears full utilization [2]. Lag is dominated by whichever stage is closest to saturation; the job is to find it.

Work piles up in six places: source redo generation, Extract capture, trail write, the distribution path from the Distribution Service to the Receiver Service [3], Replicat apply, and target commit. Oracle recommends Parallel Replicat unless a feature requires another mode [4]: mappers read the trail, a master calculates dependencies from primary, unique and foreign key columns, and appliers execute batches of independent transactions [5], [6]. That is why parallelism has a ceiling: transactions touching the same row apply in order, whatever the applicant count.

Process lag is not end-to-end lag

Replicat lag from LAG or SEND ... GETLAG is the processing time minus the record's trail timestamp; INFO is less precise because it uses the last checkpointed record [7], [8]. A Replicat sitting at end-of-file has nothing new to measure, so its figure can look healthy while a congested path holds fresh data upstream.

Heartbeat tables measure the target's real position. ADD HEARTBEAT TABLE creates heartbeat and history tables, the GG_LAG and GG_LAG_HISTORY views, and a job writing a heartbeat every 60 seconds by default [9]. Each heartbeat is stamped by Extract, the routing path and Replicat, so lag decomposes hop by hop; with several pumps in series, though, the single routing timestamp is overwritten and becomes an aggregate [10].

-- End-to-end lag per path, run on the target as the GoldenGate admin user
SELECT remote_database,
       incoming_path,
       incoming_lag,
       incoming_heartbeat_age,
       outgoing_lag
FROM   ggadmin.gg_lag
ORDER  BY incoming_lag DESC;

Read INCOMING_HEARTBEAT_AGE alongside INCOMING_LAG [7]. If the age keeps climbing while lag looks stable, heartbeats have stopped arriving, and the real lag is at least the age.

Lag in active-active topologies

With bi-directional replication and conflict detection and resolution, each direction is its own pipeline, so read OUTGOING_LAG alongside INCOMING_LAG at every site [7]. Lag sets the width of the window in which both sites can update the same row before either sees the other's change. A wider window means more conflicts for the resolution logic to settle. A backlog that moves downstream does not close that window; it shifts it, so conflict volume can stay high through the drain, after the original fault is fixed. Here lag is a correctness signal, not just a freshness metric.

Three common causes sit outside the appliers' reach:

  • Large transactions. Parallel Replicat serializes transactions larger than CHUNK_SIZE, unless SPLIT_TRANS_RECS breaks them into pieces [5].
  • Dependencies and hot rows. If a fifth of the workload updates a handful of status rows, those transactions form a chain; Oracle's own experiment shows a dependent workload leaving appliers idle [6].
  • Missing keys or indexes on the target. Without a primary key, unique key or unique index, Replicat builds its WHERE clause from all columns, essentially a full table scan [11]. Parallel Replicat also requires foreign key columns to be indexed [5].

Starting from heartbeat lag and age, this is the map I use:

For tables without a usable key, KEYCOLS tells Replicat which columns identify a row, with those columns supplementally logged at the source [11], [20]. The part people skip: KEYCOLS defines identity, not an access path. Without a target index on those columns, the scan remains. When a root-level Integrated Extract captures from a PDB, the source side of each MAP needs a three-part name or SOURCECATALOG, while the target stays two-part because Replicat connects to one PDB [21].

REPLICAT rpar
USERIDALIAS tgt_ogg
MAP_PARALLELISM 3
MIN_APPLY_PARALLELISM 2
MAX_APPLY_PARALLELISM 10
CHUNK_SIZE 50000
SPLIT_TRANS_RECS 10000
MAP pdb_pms.pms.rate_status, TARGET pms.rate_status, KEYCOLS (property_id, rate_code);

Object names are hypothetical [5], [21].

A small discrete-time model (z3_exp.py) makes this concrete; it models the mechanism, not Oracle. Assumptions: 200 five-row transactions per second; capture 1,800 rows/s; network 2,500 rows/s; 400 row-units/s per applier; per-key ordering with a 10,000-transaction lookahead; transactions over 50,000 rows serialized unless split into 10,000-row pieces. Faults run from t=300 s to 900 s: three 100,000-row batch transactions committing at 600 s; an index left unusable by maintenance (or a plan regression) making apply ten times costlier for 20% of transactions, spread over four hot keys; a network throttled to 600 rows/s. A control run keeps the hot keys at normal cost. Lag is the age of the oldest unapplied transaction. Absolute rates are deliberately low; the ratios drive the results: demand to capacity at each stage, and work per second on each hot-key chain.

† Upper bound: the model gives split pieces unique keys.

With large transactions, quadrupling appliers leaves peak lag at 823 s because the barrier runs on one applier while busy time falls to 10%, though 16 appliers do shorten the post-barrier drain (back under 5 s at 1,574 s versus beyond 2,400 s). Splitting cuts peak lag to 178 s, but the model gives pieces unique keys, while Oracle still honors dependencies between them [5], so it overstates that benefit. Capture backlog peaked at 60,000 rows as the redo spike hit Extract first. The same hot keys cause no lag with a healthy index. Without it, 16 appliers beat 4 because aggregate capacity was also short, but 64 match 16 exactly: each hot key's chain needs more than one second of work per second. Under the network throttle, peak lag is identical for 4 and 16 appliers; after recovery, the burst floods a 4-applier Replicat, so more appliers shorten the drain, not the incident.

Integrated Extract interoperates with TDE [22], but TDE-protected data captured by Extract is written to the trail unencrypted unless trail encryption is enabled; NOENCRYPTTRAIL is the default [23]. Distribution paths can also encrypt trail data in transit [3]; that costs CPU, so capacity tests without it understate production load.

Trail-file corruption deserves a runbook. INFO EXTRACT ... SHOWCH displays checkpoints, including the recovery checkpoint at the oldest open transaction [24]. A primary Integrated Extract is repositioned by SCN (ALTER EXTRACT ... SCN) plus a trail rollover, not by EXTSEQNO; EXTSEQNO and EXTRBA reposition trail readers such as pumps and Replicat [24]. In Microservices, the distribution path plays the pump's role and the Distribution Service repositions it [3]. Repositioning skips or replays data, so confirm the target tolerates it first.

Trade-offs and Limitations

The model ignores contention between appliers: sixteen sessions scanning the same table compete for I/O and CPU, so it flatters parallelism. Fixed rates understate the variability effect Kingman describes [2]. Integrated Replicat's serial fallback for DDL and SQLEXEC is not modeled [25]. Heartbeat frequency trades resolution for overhead [9].

  • Low DB time on the target during a lag window is the fastest way to rule out apply [17].
  • Hot-row chains and unusable indexes compound, because the slowest rows are also the most serialized.
  • An unusable index after a maintenance window looks like a GoldenGate problem; check index status on replicated targets first.
  • Deploy heartbeat tables on every path before go-live and alert on heartbeat age as well as lag.
  • Audit target tables for primary keys and indexed KEYCOLS before the initial load, not during an incident.
  • Budget Streams pool memory for root-level Extracts and Integrated Replicats when sizing the SGA.
  • Benchmark the distribution path with encryption enabled.

Auto-tuning between MIN_APPLY_PARALLELISM and MAX_APPLY_PARALLELISM [5] chooses the applier count within bounds you set, but it cannot remove barriers, hot-row chains or upstream throttles.

Measure every hop before touching a knob, and act only on the queue that is growing. Fix that queue, then plan for the backlog, and in active-active the conflict window, to move to the next stage. If added appliers leave lag unchanged, treat that as evidence that the constraint is elsewhere.

[1]J. D. C. Little, "A proof for the queuing formula: L = λW," Operations Research, vol. 9, no. 3, pp. 383-387, 1961, doi: 10.1287/opre.9.3.383. [Online]. Available: https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383

[2]J. F. C. Kingman, "The single server queue in heavy traffic," Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society, vol. 57, no. 4, pp. 902-904, 1961, doi: 10.1017/S0305004100036094. [Online]. Available: https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305004100036094

Zalak Shroff is a database engineer and IT manager with more than ten years of experience running Oracle databases from 10g through 19c, including RAC, Data Guard, ASM, RMAN, and GoldenGate. She currently works on Oracle 19c multitenant platforms on OCI and AWS for hospitality software, where she migrates standalone databases into pluggable databases and builds GoldenGate replication, including bi-directional active-active topologies with conflict detection and resolution. Earlier, in telecom, she automated RMAN backup and recovery, tuned performance with AWR and ASH, and implemented TDE, VPD and role-based access controls for SOX and GDPR compliance. She holds an M.S. in Computer Science and is a named inventor on a patent for a network application that notifies users of an impending coverage lapse.

items.title: Type a Formula, Render Art: Build an Interactive Fractal Generator in 2026
items.author: Joe bou khalil
items.content:
For this project I wanted something new. Something that involves art. A new type of art. I wanted to combine mathematics visuals with formulas so you can experiment and create your own art.

You change the numbers and exponents, add z or c, and create your own art. Your imagination is the limit. What I created is a fractal laboratory.

  • Download it as a PNG or SVG.

In simple terms, fractal art is digital art created using mathematical formulas and repeated patterns rather than drawing every shape manually.

In another way, fractal art is a form of art that uses mathematics to display perfect geometric shapes. That could not be created manually.

The fun part of the code:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>Responsive Mathematical Fractal Generator</title>
  <script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/mathjs/11.8.0/math.js"></script>
  <style>
    :root {
      --bg-color: #0f111a;
      --panel-bg: #1e2230;
      --accent-color: #6366f1;
      --accent-hover: #4f46e5;
      --text-color: #f3f4f6;
      --text-muted: #9ca3af;
      --border-color: #374151;
    }

    * {
      box-sizing: border-box;
      margin: 0;
      padding: 0;
      font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif;
    }

    body {
      background-color: var(--bg-color);
      color: var(--text-color);
      display: flex;
      flex-direction: column;
      min-height: 100vh;
      min-height: 100dvh; /* Dynamic viewport height for mobile browsers */
      overflow: x-hidden;
    }

    /* Responsive Main Layout (Column on Mobile, Row on Desktop) */
    .app-container {
      display: flex;
      flex-direction: column;
      flex: 1;
      width: 100%;
      height: 100%;
    }

    @media (min-width: 850px) {
      .app-container {
        flex-direction: row;
        height: 100vh;
        overflow: hidden;
      }
    }

    /* Sidebar controls */
    .sidebar {
      width: 100%;
      background-color: var(--panel-bg);
      border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border-color);
      padding: 16px;
      display: flex;
      flex-direction: column;
      gap: 14px;
    }

    @media (min-width: 850px) {
      .sidebar {
        width: 340px;
        min-width: 340px;
        border-bottom: none;
        border-right: 1px solid var(--border-color);
        padding: 20px;
        overflow-y: auto;
      }
    }

    h1 {
      font-size: 1.2rem;
      font-weight: 600;
      color: #fff;
    }

    .input-group {
      display: flex;
      flex-direction: column;
      gap: 6px;
    }

    label {
      font-size: 0.85rem;

      background: #11131f;
      border: 1px solid var(--border-color);
      color: var(--text-color);
      padding: 10px;
      border-radius: 6px;

      outline: none;
      width: 100%;
    }

    input[type="text"]:focus, input[type="number"]:focus, select:focus {
      border-color: var(--accent-color);
    }

    .btn {
      background-color: var(--accent-color);
      color: white;
      border: none;
      padding: 12px;
      border-radius: 6px;
      font-weight: 600;
      cursor: pointer;
      transition: background 0.2s;
      width: 100%;
      touch-action: manipulation;
    }

    .btn:hover {
      background-color: var(--accent-hover);
    }

    .btn-secondary {
      background-color: transparent;
      border: 1px solid var(--border-color);
      color: var(--text-color);
    }

    .btn-secondary:hover {
      background-color: #2a2f45;
    }

    .button-row {
      display: flex;
      gap: 8px;
    }

    .download-section {
      display: flex;
      gap: 10px;
      margin-top: 6px;
    }

    @media (min-width: 850px) {
      .download-section {
        margin-top: auto;
      }
    }

    /* Canvas Viewport */
    .main-viewport {
      flex: 1;
      display: flex;
      justify-content: center;
      align-items: center;
      position: relative;
      background: #090a0f;
      padding: 12px;
      min-height: 350px;
    }

    .canvas-container {
      position: relative;
      width: 100%;
      max-width: 600px;
      aspect-ratio: 1 / 1;
      display: flex;
      justify-content: center;
      align-items: center;
    }

    canvas {
      width: 100% !important;
      height: 100% !important;
      box-shadow: 0 10px 30px rgba(0,0,0,0.5);
      border-radius: 6px;
      touch-action: none;
    }

    .status-overlay {
      position: absolute;
      top: 10px;
      right: 10px;
      background: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.75);
      padding: 6px 12px;
      border-radius: 16px;
      font-size: 0.75rem;
      color: var(--text-muted);
      pointer-events: none;
    }
  </style>
</head>
<body>

  <div class="app-container">
    <div class="sidebar">
      <h1>Fractal Generator</h1>
      
      <div class="input-group">
        <label for="formula">Formula f(z, c):</label>
        <input type="text" id="formula" value="z^2 + c" placeholder="e.g. z^2 + c">
      </div>

      <div class="input-group">
        <label for="type">Fractal Type:</label>
        <select id="type">
          <option value="mandelbrot">Mandelbrot Style (Vary c)</option>
          <option value="julia">Julia Set (Fixed c, Vary z)</option>
        </select>
      </div>

      <div class="input-group" id="julia-params" style="display: none;">
        <label>Constant c (Real, Imaginary):</label>
        <div style="display: flex; gap: 8px;">
          <input type="number" id="c_real" value="-0.7" step="0.05" placeholder="Real">
          <input type="number" id="c_imag" value="0.27015" step="0.05" placeholder="Imag">
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="input-group">
        <label for="maxIter">Resolution / Iterations:</label>
        <input type="number" id="maxIter" value="50" min="10" max="250">
      </div>

      <div class="input-group">
        <label for="colorPalette">Color Palette:</label>
        <select id="colorPalette">
          <option value="electric">Electric Neon</option>
          <option value="fire">Fire & Gold</option>
          <option value="ocean">Deep Ocean</option>
          <option value="grayscale">Monochrome</option>
        </select>
      </div>

      <div class="button-row">
        <button class="btn" id="renderBtn">Render</button>
        <button class="btn btn-secondary" id="resetBtn">Reset</button>
      </div>

      <div class="download-section">
        <button class="btn btn-secondary" id="downloadPNG">PNG</button>
        <button class="btn btn-secondary" id="downloadSVG">SVG</button>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="main-viewport">
      <div class="canvas-container">
        <div class="status-overlay" id="status">Ready</div>
        <canvas id="fractalCanvas" width="500" height="500"></canvas>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <script>
    const canvas = document.getElementById('fractalCanvas');
    const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
    const statusEl = document.getElementById('status');

    let zoom = 1;
    let centerX = 0;
    let centerY = 0;

    // Toggle Julia controls
    document.getElementById('type').addEventListener('change', (e) => {
      document.getElementById('julia-params').style.display = 
        e.target.value === 'julia' ? 'flex' : 'none';
    });

    // Color Palettes
    function getColor(iter, maxIter, palette) {
      if (iter === maxIter) return [0, 0, 0];
      
      let t = iter / maxIter;
      
      if (palette === 'electric') {
        return [
          Math.sin(t * 10) * 127 + 128,
          Math.cos(t * 15) * 127 + 128,
          Math.sin(t * 25) * 127 + 128
        ];
      } else if (palette === 'fire') {
        return [
          Math.min(255, iter * 8),
          Math.min(255, iter * 3),
          Math.min(255, iter * 0.5)
        ];
      } else if (palette === 'ocean') {
        return [
          Math.sin(t * 5) * 50,
          Math.sin(t * 10) * 100 + 100,
          Math.sin(t * 20) * 127 + 128
        ];
      } else {
        let val = Math.floor((iter / maxIter) * 255);
        return [val, val, val];
      }
    }

    // Main Render Loop
    function renderFractal() {
      statusEl.innerText = "Rendering...";
      
      setTimeout(() => {
        const formulaStr = document.getElementById('formula').value;
        const fractalType = document.getElementById('type').value;
        const maxIter = parseInt(document.getElementById('maxIter').value);
        const palette = document.getElementById('colorPalette').value;
        
        const cRealFixed = parseFloat(document.getElementById('c_real').value);
        const cImagFixed = parseFloat(document.getElementById('c_imag').value);

        let compiledExpr;
        try {
          compiledExpr = math.compile(formulaStr);
        } catch (err) {
          alert("Invalid Formula: " + err.message);
          statusEl.innerText = "Error";
          return;
        }

        const width = canvas.width;
        const height = canvas.height;
        const imgData = ctx.createImageData(width, height);
        const data = imgData.data;

        const scale = 3.0 / (zoom * Math.min(width, height));

        for (let py = 0; py < height; py++) {
          for (let px = 0; px < width; px++) {
            
            let x0 = (px - width / 2) * scale + centerX;
            let y0 = (py - height / 2) * scale + centerY;

            let z, c;
            if (fractalType === 'mandelbrot') {
              z = math.complex(0, 0);
              c = math.complex(x0, y0);
            } else {
              z = math.complex(x0, y0);
              c = math.complex(cRealFixed, cImagFixed);
            }

            let iter = 0;
            let escaped = false;

            while (iter < maxIter) {
              try {
                z = compiledExpr.evaluate({ z: z, c: c });
                if ((z.re * z.re + z.im * z.im) > 4.0) {
                  escaped = true;
                  break;
                }
              } catch (e) {
                escaped = true;
                break;
              }
              iter++;
            }

            const [r, g, b] = getColor(iter, maxIter, palette);
            const pixelIdx = (py * width + px) * 4;
            data[pixelIdx] = r;
            data[pixelIdx + 1] = g;
            data[pixelIdx + 2] = b;
            data[pixelIdx + 3] = 255;
          }
        }

        ctx.putImageData(imgData, 0, 0);
        statusEl.innerText = "Done";
      }, 20);
    }

    // Export Handlers
    document.getElementById('downloadPNG').addEventListener('click', () => {
      const link = document.createElement('a');
      link.download = 'fractal.png';
      link.href = canvas.toDataURL('image/png');
      link.click();
    });

    document.getElementById('downloadSVG').addEventListener('click', () => {
      const dataURL = canvas.toDataURL('image/png');
      const svgString = 
`<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="${canvas.width}" height="${canvas.height}">
  <image href="${dataURL}" width="${canvas.width}" height="${canvas.height}" />
</svg>`;
      
      const blob = new Blob([svgString], { type: 'image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8' });
      const link = document.createElement('a');
      link.download = 'fractal.svg';
      link.href = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
      link.click();
    });

    // Control Listeners
    document.getElementById('renderBtn').addEventListener('click', renderFractal);
    
    document.getElementById('resetBtn').addEventListener('click', () => {
      zoom = 1;
      centerX = 0;
      centerY = 0;
      renderFractal();
    });

    // Zoom on Click / Tap
    canvas.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
      const rect = canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
      const clickX = (e.clientX - rect.left) * (canvas.width / rect.width);
      const clickY = (e.clientY - rect.top) * (canvas.height / rect.height);

      const scale = 3.0 / (zoom * Math.min(canvas.width, canvas.height));
      centerX += (clickX - canvas.width / 2) * scale;
      centerY += (clickY - canvas.height / 2) * scale;
      zoom *= 2;

      renderFractal();
    });

    // Initial render
    renderFractal();
  </script>
</body>
</html>

items.title: SpaceX In Talks to Access 80,000 Cell Sites For New Network
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
SpaceX is reportedly seeking access to at least 80,000 cellular tower sites across the U.S. as it prepares to launch Starlink Mobile as a fourth nationwide wireless carrier. "We will be building out our terrestrial networks so there's broad-based connectivity anywhere that SpaceX and Starlink are allowed to operate," Musk said during SpaceX's earnings call this week. Satellite launches plus spectrum acquisition "will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US," he said. Bloomberg reports: One of the companies they're in talks with is Crown Castle, which, along with American Tower and Vertical Bridge Holdings, are among the largest owners of cellular towers. When asked on a Wednesday earnings conference call whether Crown Castle is discussing leases with SpaceX, Amazon.com or other satellite-based telecom providers, Chief Executive Officer Chris Hillabrant said, "You can assume that we're talking to all parties." He declined to discuss specific customer details.
 
Mobile networks rely on antennas placed on towers across the country to transmit wireless signals. Carriers such as AT&T Inc., Verizon Communications Inc. and T-Mobile US Inc. typically lease room for their equipment at the tower sites because it's more cost effective than owning and maintaining them, in part because the facilities can be shared. The value of the deals with SpaceX could reach into the billions.

items.title: Stop Leaving Quality to QA Alone: Shipping Features Customers Actually Adopt in 2026
items.author: Susan Isaac
items.content:
A few years ago, software development was linear – every team had a well scoped role. Product Managers decided requirements, engineers wrote code, QA tested and gave the green signal. Agile started to blur the boundaries, we started thinking of building products as a team and not in silos. Concepts such as ‘fail fast and learn’ needed all teams involved right from the beginning. Now with AI, features are being shipped faster and faster, but customer adoption remains low and in many cases is trending down. It’s become painfully obvious that end to end quality assurance cannot be treated as the final checkpoint before a release – it needs to be incorporated into every iteration.

We’ve all had the experience of shipping a feature with no major defects, but customers still complain that the feature is not intuitive and easy to use. QA ensured the requirements were met, found defects and ensured that technically, the feature behaves exactly as designed, but the customer’s experience still ending up being disappointing. This is the biggest drawback of the traditional QA process.

The big question that is being asked currently is whether testing is just the job of QA or should it be more inclusive? This sounds controversial, because isn’t QA what QA does? But in this world of weekly releases and vibe coding, is it fair to expect QA to be the only function that validates features being released? QA will always be accountable and responsible for quality, however ensuring that the product delivers the required value to the customer is not something that QA can do alone.

Product Manager talk to customers, analyze workflows and processes to identity problems, prioritize these problems and design features to solve these problems. However, all of this knowledge is rarely passed onto the QA teams. Requirements, use case scenarios, stories and acceptance criteria – these are all necessary, but unfortunately, they are not sufficient.  These do not help answer questions like:

·       Does this workflow solve the customer’s problem?

·       Is the feature intuitive to use?

·       Does the feature align with the customer’s business metrics?

·       Can a customer naturally discover and use this capability?

The answers to these questions rarely can be found in a test plan, yet they often determine whether a feature succeeds or fails after shipping.

So what does this mean – should Product Managers execute test plans and regressions? Absolutely not. The answer is

To make UAT effective, teams need to establish a clear testing environment that closely mirrors the customer experience. Test data should represent real-world conditions and processes, along with the necessary hardware and software interfaces set up and functional. This helps in testing all scenarios including edge cases, workarounds, and dependencies that may not appear in requirements documents.

An important call out here: if possible, this test environment should always be reserved for UAT. I’ve been part of UATs where I’ve spent 30 mins executing a full workflow process and the feature breaks suddenly because a developer deployed a piece of code to conduct some quick tests of their own.

In many organizations that create software for industries such as healthcare, defense, etc. many employees are also former customers. These employees have experience in your customers’ workflows with all the problems and workarounds. Identifying a sub-set of these employees as your Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) group and asking them to participate in UAT can be very beneficial. These SMEs know and have lived the edge cases and the 1% situations, and in many cases also have experience with your competition’s products. Hence, their feedback can truly help make your product better. SMEs cannot be expected to participate in every sprint, but a dedicated UAT environment can enable them to test on their own time.

In traditional development models, UAT often happens just before release when most of the features have been developed, and we are in the bug fixing stage. Unfortunately, by this stage feedback can be expensive, time consuming to incorporate, leading to feature releases that does not delight customers. Modern project teams should instead incorporate quick UATs in every sprint. When a sprint is completed, the product team must be expected and allowed to test the product. This helps identify design and implementation flaws early, when improvements and changes are still possible.

The primary goal of UAT is not to find bugs. Yes, read that again – this is not a bug finding exercise. Bugs finding is still very much the purview of QA. UAT’s north star is to validate if the feature solves the identified customer problem in an intuitive and usable way. Before testing begins, Product Managers and QA should agree on the goals of each UAT cycle - especially the critical customer workflows that need to be evaluated. This includes defining realistic user scenarios, expected outcomes, and key questions that the team wants answered. They should focus on executing common workflows without relying on implementation knowledge and ask simple but important questions, as these observations uncover improvements that can never appear in a bug report.

Example, rather than focusing on whether a particular button works, the focus should be on asking the following questions:

·       Is the button placement intuitive?

·       Does the customer understand the purpose of the button easily?

·       Would the customer know when to use the button?

·       Are the inputs accepted relevant to that particular use case?

The results of the UAT must be discussed as a team. All bugs identified are owned by the QA team, whereas it’s the Product Manager who must decide when the various improvements or design changes must be incorporated into the development process. In a truly agile environment, these tests will allow incremental improvements that lead to the delivery of a product that delivers value to customers.

Successful teams set up UAT as a necessary partnership between Product Management and QA. Together, they ensure that teams are not only building products that work correctly, but products that delight their customers. In an AI-driven world where speed of delivery continues to increase, this partnership is becoming less of a nice-to-have and more of a must-have.
