items.title: Knicks Sent Employees Fake Offer of Championship Rings In Phishing Test
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
The New York Knicks reportedly sent employees a fake offer of complimentary NBA championship rings as part of an internal phishing test, requiring anyone who clicked the link to attend mandatory cybersecurity training. "Congratulations, your Employee Championship Ring is here," the email said. According to The New York Times, Madison Square Garden employees who clicked that link "were forced to attend a mandatory cybersecurity class to help satisfy some of [owner James] Dolan's growing cybersecurity concerns." Ars Technica reports: The offer wasn't implausible, either. "Typically, most employees for NBA teams receive rings, even if they are not as fancy and expensive as the ones the players receive," wrote Joe Vardon, senior NBA writer for The Athletic, which was bought by The New York Times in 2022 and then merged into the parent news organization. Vardon's article was primarily about how Knicks assistant coaches did not get rings on Tuesday when the team raised its first league championship banner since 1973. The assistant coaches were handed boxes without rings inside, though they are expected to receive rings later on.
 
"Ring orders, designs, and measurements can take time, and not every coaching staff for every defending champion gets its rings on ring night... The Knicks assistants were told they would receive championship rings eventually, but many longtime employees at Madison Square Garden, including some who work in the Knicks' business operations, will not receive rings at all, team sources told The Athletic," Vardon wrote. MSG employee hopes were raised "at the end of September when the Knicks sent an email to a long list of employees, which gave recipients a first glimpse at their would-be championship rings," Vardon wrote. The email included "a graphic of two differently styled rings" that the lucky employees could supposedly choose from, the article said.
 
"(Employee name), this one is on the house. MSG is issuing a complimentary employee championship ring. The same jeweler, the same craftsmanship, personalized with your name. No cost to you," the email said. "There are two designs to choose from: Championship Gold and Garden Classic. Reserve the one you want below." Vardon wrote that "multiple team sources" confirmed the email was a phishing test. It's not clear how many employees clicked the link or whether any of the employees who received the email will eventually get some type of championship ring. We contacted the Madison Square Garden Sports organization with these questions and will update this article if we get a response.

items.title: The AI Model That Promised to Crush GPT-6 Has a Surprising Weakness
items.author: Bruce Li
items.content:
We test Inception's Mercury 3 against the fastest autoregressive models from Anthropic, Google Gemini, OpenAI, and Cerebras to find out

On October 19, 2026, Inception Labs launched Mercury 3 with a bold pitch: a diffusion language model that beats GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on benchmarks while running 4 to 8 times faster, at more than 1,000 tokens per second (Inception blog, "Diffusion at Scale: Introducing Mercury 3", Oct 19, 2026).

Faster  smarter than the big labs' speed models. That is the kind of sentence that makes a benchmark nerd reach for a credit card. So I did. About $34 of API spend and more than 48,000 model calls later, here is what I found.

 Mercury 3 is genuinely fast and genuinely good. It is not the fastest thing on the menu, it is not the cheapest per right answer, and it has one very odd habit.

Diffusion LLMs in one paragraph

Normal (autoregressive) LLMs write like a typist: one token at a time, left to right. A diffusion LLM writes like a sculptor: it starts with a rough block of placeholder text and refines many tokens in parallel over a few passes, until the answer "comes into focus." In theory that means far fewer sequential steps, and so much more speed. If you want the longer explainer, I wrote one back when Mercury first launched: What is Diffusion LLM and why it matters (Feb 2025).

Here is the 2026 version doing its thing, on the same kind of prompt I used in 2025 ("write a Python function that splits an image into left and right halves"):

Across 30 such captures, answers resolved in 5–11 visible steps, in well under a second at the median. One detail the marketing animations skip: refinement is not a smooth fade-in. In every one of the 30 calls, at least one step moved  from the final text before coming back. The sculptor occasionally un-chisels.

The two tests, in plain English

I picked two jobs where speed actually matters to a person waiting on a screen.

Test 1: "Write me this function" (code generation). Each model gets a programming task, for example "write a Python function that checks whether any two numbers in a list are closer to each other than a given threshold." We run its code against hidden tests. Pass or fail, no partial credit. That's 637 problems from three well-known sets (HumanEval+, MBPP+, and LiveCodeBench), 5 tries each, for every model. This is the coding-assistant use case: you ask, you wait, you hope.

Test 2: "Answer this question from our database" (a SQL agent). The model gets a real database and a question like "What is the total amount of money spent on food?" (from BIRD, a standard text-to-SQL benchmark). It can't see the data upfront. It has to look around: list tables, peek at columns, run a few test queries, then submit the query that answers the question. Up to 8 turns. We check whether its query returns the same rows as the official answer. 150 questions, 3 tries each.

Why an agent? Because agents are where speed compounds. If one call takes a second and the agent needs six of them, you're waiting six seconds. A model that is fast per call but needs more calls can lose the race. More on that in a moment.

, each the "fast" tier of its maker:

  •  (Inception, diffusion), at four reasoning settings from  to 
  •  (Anthropic),  (OpenAI),  (Google)
  • : an ordinary autoregressive open model running on very fast specialised chips. This one is my control. If Mercury is fast because of , it should beat a normal model on fast hardware. If it's fast because of , it won't.

Same prompts, same settings, randomised order, everything measured end-to-end over the public APIs from one machine. Full code, configs and raw results: github.com/zbruceli/mercury3.

Finding 1: Speed is real, but it is not unique

On code generation, Mercury 3 at its best setting () passes  of problems with a median response time of . That ties Claude Haiku with thinking off (86.1% at 0.97 s) and edges out GPT-6 Luna with reasoning off (83.2% at 1.28 s).

Then the control walks in. gpt-oss-120b on Cerebras passes 84.9% at 0.34 seconds. Within about a point of Mercury, at well under half the wait.

Raw generation speed tells the same story. Measured as visible text streamed after the first token, Mercury 3 writes about 850–900 tokens per second. That's roughly 2× Gemini Flash-Lite, 2.8× Claude Haiku and 6× GPT-6 Luna, which lands neatly inside Inception's "4–8× faster" for Luna, and short of it for Haiku. But gpt-oss on Cerebras writes about 2,400–2,500 tokens per second, ~2.7× Mercury, at every output length we tried. Diffusion's advantage is a constant factor, and it doesn't grow on longer outputs.

One nice touch you can feel: short Mercury answers arrive in a single block. Total time (0.30 s) is basically the time to first token (0.29 s). The answer doesn't stream in; it just appears.

Finding 2: In agents, the number of turns matters as much as speed per turn

In the SQL agent, Mercury 3 () finishes a whole task in  at the median. Claude Haiku takes , Gemini , GPT-6 Luna . That's 1.9–2.9× faster than the frontier labs' fast models per task. Diffusion, or at least this product, delivers in the agent loop.

But look at how it gets there:

Claude Haiku is 3.2× slower than Mercury per call, but only 1.9× slower per task, because it solves the problem in about 3.2 turns where Mercury takes 5.1. Haiku thinks less often and better. Meanwhile gpt-oss on Cerebras is 1.7×  than Mercury per call, but takes 6.3 turns, and ends up only slightly faster per task (1.82 s). At its  setting it's actually slower than Mercury per task.

Lesson for agent builders: task latency ≈ call latency × number of turns, and the number of turns is a property of the model, not something your speed chart will tell you.

On accuracy, everyone lands within a few points (47.6% to 59.1% correct). Claude Haiku is the most accurate, about 5 points ahead of Mercury 3 when compared on the same questions, but that lead is borderline: its confidence interval reaches down to zero. With 150 questions, the per-model error bars are ±7–8 points, so I wouldn't crown anyone here.

Finding 3: Cheap per token is not cheap per answer

Mercury 3 is priced at $0.10 / $0.35 per million input / output tokens, a 50% launch promo off the regular $0.20 / $0.70. Low per-token prices, but what matters is cost per  answer:

  •  Mercury 3  costs $0.59 per 1,000 passing answers at the promo price ($1.19 regular). GPT-6 Luna with reasoning off costs . Claude Haiku (thinking off) costs $0.14.
  •  Mercury 3  costs $1.31 per 1,000 correct tasks ($2.62 regular). Luna costs . gpt-oss on Cerebras and Gemini are the priciest here ($4.83–$6.56), because more turns mean re-sending more context.

Mercury isn't expensive, but it's also not the bargain the per-token sticker suggests, and the promo price won't last.

Finding 4: Mercury 3 sometimes thinks forever

Here's the odd habit. Mercury 3 has reasoning settings, and you'd expect more reasoning to mean better answers. It's the opposite. On code, accuracy  from 86.0% at  to 82.3% at  and 81.4% at .

The reason: at higher settings, Mercury 3 sometimes reasons silently until it hits the 32,768-token output cap and returns nothing at all. That happened on  and 8.6% at . Those runaway calls burned 61% of all the output tokens Mercury 3 used in the code test, and pushed its slowest-5% response times past 50 seconds. Giving it 4× more room barely helped: in a small 12-call probe, only one extra call finished. No other model in the code test ran away even once.

My favourite example: an easy-looking problem asking for the "directrix of a parabola," whose single worked example doesn't match the textbook formula. The autoregressive models shrug, write the standard formula, and fail. Mercury 3 at  and  tries to reconcile the math with the example on all 10 attempts, and thinks until it runs out of budget. Same score as a wrong guess, but at ~32,000 tokens and close to a minute per attempt. Autoregressive models fail by committing; this one fails by not stopping.

Practical advice:  or . At  it is also 9 points better than its predecessor Mercury 2.5 at the same setting (86.0% vs 76.9%), and faster (0.83 s vs 1.36 s). Real progress in 20 months.

Surprises that have nothing to do with diffusion

Benchmarking five vendors side by side turns up some gossip.

  • OpenAI has a slow front door. Even a free "list models" request took about 0.8–1.2 s of server-side processing at OpenAI, where the same call to the other providers came back in about 15–225 ms. On real requests, OpenAI spent ~0.6 s server-side before doing anything visible. It's not your account tier: paying 2× for OpenAI's Fast mode trimmed only ~0.15 s at the median (it mostly fixes the worst cases).
  • The cheapest right answer comes from GPT-6 Luna with reasoning off. Slowest decoder in the test (about 130–160 tokens/s), cheapest per solved problem in both tests.
  • Some models really like to talk. Asked for an ~800-line program, Claude Haiku and GPT-6 Luna wrote about 15,000 tokens; gpt-oss wrote about 6,000. Compare speeds in tokens per second, not total seconds.
  • Haiku stops exploring when you ask for JSON. With a strict JSON output format switched on, Claude Haiku answered all 150 database questions in one shot, without looking at the database once. It still scored 53.3%.
  • Mercury 3 sometimes leaks its own plumbing. In that same strict-JSON mode, it broke the format on 6 of 150 tasks, mostly by appending fragments of its internal tool-call markup after valid JSON. Every other model: zero.
  • Cerebras throttled us below its published limit. We kept under its documented 1,000 requests per minute and still collected 765 rate-limit errors in the code test.

So, is it the speed demon as promised?

Back to Inception's claim:

  • "More than 1,000 tokens per second": close. We measured ~850–900 visible tokens/s from the client side, over the network, so it includes streaming and network overhead that a server-side number doesn't.
  • "4–8× faster than Luna and Haiku": on raw generation speed, about 3× Haiku and 6× Luna. On what you actually wait for, smaller: 1.2–1.5× per coding answer at matched quality, and 1.9–2.9× per agent task.
  • "Outperforms Luna and Haiku": ties them when their reasoning is off, trails them when it's on (88.4% and 87.9% vs 86.0% on code). In the SQL agent, all three are within the error bars.
  •  this is where the claim needs a caveat. An ordinary autoregressive model on Cerebras hardware was faster than Mercury 3 in both tests. What we measured is a  (model plus serving stack), not an architecture. Diffusion may well be why Mercury beats the big labs' fast models, but it isn't the only road to speed.

Verdict: Mercury 3 is faster than the big labs' fast models, about as accurate as them with reasoning off, and especially good in agent loops. It's a speed demon, just not the only one in town.

  • Products, not architectures. Every comparison includes each vendor's hardware, network and API overhead.
  • LiveCodeBench is not contamination-free. All public problems predate the models' training cutoffs, so it serves as a "harder set," equal for everyone, not a fresh one.
  • The SQL accuracy numbers are noisy. ±7–8 points per model; only paired differences are worth quoting.
  •  Mercury's numbers double at the regular price. Both are shown.
  • One machine, one region, one day. Single client host in the US West, standard (non-priority) API tiers, measured October 2026. Your latency will vary.
  •  (all ~500 scorable BIRD questions) to shrink those error bars.
  • , if Inception ever serves it on Cerebras- or Groq-class chips. That's the clean "diffusion vs. hardware" experiment.
  • : Inception's separate Mercury Edit model does fill-in-the-middle and next-edit prediction, which this study didn't touch.
  • Real-time and voice-style workloads, where Mercury's  flag might matter (it made no difference for code).
  • : early research suggested diffusion models handle "reverse this" tasks that trip up left-to-right models. Worth a proper probe.

All code, configs, run data summaries, and the scripts that generate every chart here are on GitHub: github.com/zbruceli/mercury3. If you find a bug in my numbers, I'd genuinely like to hear about it.

items.title: Left Alone With Nothing To Do, AI Agents Started Playing
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: AI agents left to explore a virtual island without a specific task began inventing challenges of their own. MIT researchers say the behavior bears the hallmarks of play. The researchers put 13 AI agents called Eko, each running on Claude Opus 4.7, alone on a simulated desert island for 30 hours. They describe the experiment in a paper posted on arXiv, a site where researchers share studies before peer review. Afterward, they gave the agents specific challenges, like getting as many objects as possible onto the island's tallest rock spire. The Eko agents that had spent those 30 hours playing generally beat identical agents that had never set foot on the island.
 
Today, developers decide in advance what AI should practice and what counts as success. The researchers see this technique -- exploring without a goal -- as a different way for AI agents to learn skills, especially skills that could one day be used to control robots. "We normally develop artificial agents by deciding in advance what they should practice, what they should optimize, and what counts as progress," the researchers write in their report. "Play suggests another regime: give an agent a sufficiently rich and safe world, let it choose what is interesting, and allow useful knowledge to accumulate from the history that follows." UC Berkeley cognitive scientist Eunice Yiu told MIT Technology Review she was impressed with the findings but that more evidence is needed to determine whether AI models are genuinely playing. "It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don't know based on the paper," says Yiu. "If you only have the behavioral piece, it could be the case that they're just trying to abide by the prompt, trying to imitate humans."
 
MIT professor and coauthor of the paper, Phillip Isola, added: "It's not like this is a system that just suddenly magically decided to play. It's an artifact that learned from our culture, was trained by engineers at Anthropic, and was then placed on an island by us. It does things that surprise us and that are causally related to its future skillful behavior."

items.title: Microsoft Announces Per-Hour Cost for Xbox Cloud Gaming Service
items.author: BeauHD
items.content: Microsoft has revealed pay-as-you-go pricing for Xbox Cloud Gaming, with introductory packages costing $3.99 for 10 hours, $7.99 for 25 hours, or $11.99 for 50 hours. Starting in November, Game Pass subscribers will receive only 5 to 15 included cloud-gaming hours depending on their tier and will have to buy additional time -- even to stream games they've already purchased. Gizmodo reports: Back in September, before these changes were announced, you paid full purchase price for a game that isn't in the Game Pass library on the assumption that you'd be able to play it via cloud streaming. Maybe your hardware doesn't meet the specs for this fancy new game. Maybe your gaming PC exploded/got stuck on a ship/had a component fail. Maybe you just want to be able to play it in bed on your laptop. Whatever. Now you find that in addition to the cost of the game you bought, you're going to be paying by the hour to play it once your monthly allotment of hours is up. If this is you, I expect you're not particularly amused. Thankfully, Microsoft notes that the playtime you purchase "remains available until it's used," so you won't have to worry about losing any unused time between gaming sessions.

items.title: The High-Stakes Paddock: Why Enterprise Giants Are Gathering in Austin to Tame Agentic AI
items.author: Stewart Rogers
items.content:
Trustwise GENESIS 2026 is GO, GO, GO!

Every October, Austin transforms into something far grander than Texas's idiosyncratic tech capital. When the Formula 1 circus rolls into town for the United States Grand Prix at Circuit of the Americas, the city becomes the temporary crossroads of the global elite. Billionaires, sovereign wealth funds, automotive titans, and tech luminaries descend on the Hill Country. The paddock club, corporate villas, and downtown rooftops morph into an unannounced global boardroom where high-velocity capital meets the ruthless reality of engineering.

Yet this year, nestled alongside the ear-splitting roar of turbocharged V6 engines, a distinctly different kind of high-stakes gathering is taking place behind closed doors.

Today, an invitation-only cohort of enterprise heavyweights, institutional investors, and governance architects gathered in Austin for GENESIS 2026. Convened by AI control plane pioneer Trustwise, the summit was not another glitzy technology trade show, but a Chatham House-style intervention for an enterprise sector hurtling toward an existential reckoning.

Look closely at the guest roster, and you quickly realize why this room matters. We are not talking about seed-stage founders pitching prompt-engineering wrappers or venture capitalists breathlessly hyping conversational chatbots. The executives participating in Austin hail from the bedrock institutions of the global economy: FactSet, U.S. Bank, Charles Schwab, NatWest, Wellington Management, IBM Apptio, Hitachi Digital Services, Yum! Brands, Cognition, and the NHS National Innovation Network. Joining them are top-tier venture backers including Insight Partners, Sway Capital, and Augment Ventures, alongside veteran regulatory analysts and academic heavyweights like former Gartner Distinguished VP Analyst Avivah Litan and Harvard Business School Professor Suraj Srinivasan.

These organizations manage trillions of dollars in assets, process millions of retail transactions, run national healthcare infrastructures, and sign off on legally binding quarterly audits.

And right now, almost all of them share the exact same private anxiety: their autonomous AI initiatives are advancing at terrifying speed, and nobody has figured out who is holding the steering wheel.

The 40 Percent Cliff and the Death of the Demo

To understand why Trustwise convened this group in Austin during Grand Prix weekend, look at the massive gap between AI headlines and boardroom realities.

Over the past two years, enterprise tech has been drunk on generative AI demos. Innovation labs across the Fortune 500 spun up autonomous agents that could book travel, query production SQL databases, summarize complex contracts, and coordinate multi-step customer support workflows. In controlled sandbox environments, these agents looked revolutionary. Executive presentations flowed, demo videos went viral on internal Slack channels, and boards demanded aggressive deployment timelines.

Then came the operational hangover.

When enterprise engineering teams attempted to push these autonomous systems into live production, handing them database write permissions, ERP access, and corporate credit cards, reality bit back hard. Agents hallucinated valid-looking SQL queries that deleted records. Multi-agent swarms entered recursive loops, making hundreds of tool calls an hour and torching infrastructure budgets overnight. Sensitive customer data slipped through unprotected API calls.

Gartner recently quantified the scale of this brewing crisis with a projection that sent shockwaves through enterprise IT: more than 40 percent of agentic AI initiatives will be canceled by the end of 2027. The causes aren't a lack of technological ambition, but escalating run costs, ambiguous business returns, and a critical lack of operational risk controls.

We have officially reached the end of the demo era. Enterprise leaders are standing at the edge of the 40 percent cliff, and they know it.

"The model is no longer the whole system," Trustwise founder and CEO Manoj Saxena said. "Enterprises must control the execution chain: what agents can access, which tools they can use, how they delegate, and when they must stop."

Saxena knows a thing or two about enterprise computing transitions. As the first general manager of IBM Watson during its commercial inception, he saw firsthand how early enterprise AI stumbled when grand promises collided with corporate procurement, regulatory boundaries, and operational plumbing.

His thesis in Austin is straightforward yet radical: the industry has spent two years obsessing over the wrong problem. Foundation models are fast becoming a commodity. The real battlefield, and the true determinant of whether autonomous AI succeeds or fails in the enterprise, is the runtime control plane.

Hosting GENESIS 2026 during the Formula 1 United States Grand Prix is neither a scheduling accident nor a corporate hospitality perk. It is the defining architectural metaphor for the entire event.

Consider a Formula 1 car barreling down COTA's uphill front straight into Turn 1 at 205 miles per hour. That machine possesses breathtaking aerodynamic downforce and hybrid horsepower. But a Grand Prix driver does not attack that blind apex with supreme confidence because the engine is powerful. They attack it because the car is equipped with carbon-fiber brakes capable of shedding 150 mph in two seconds flat, governed by computerized electronic control units that sample telemetry thousands of times per second.

In motorsport, brakes and telemetry don't exist to slow the car down. They exist to allow the driver to drive aggressively fast without killing themselves against a concrete retaining wall.

Enterprise AI is currently trying to race without brakes.

Organizations have deployed autonomous agents with immense computational horsepower, but virtually zero telemetry or mechanical control over the execution chain. When an agent calls an external API, queries a data lake, or delegates a sub-task to another bot, traditional enterprise security systems cannot see what is happening until after the command executes.

"As intelligence becomes abundant, trust becomes the scarce asset," Sanoke Viswanathan, CEO of FactSet, said. "Our clients rely on AI agents for financial research and workflows where precision is mandatory. GENESIS brings together the leaders working out how to give agents real responsibility, with controls that make every action reliable and auditable."

In the high-stakes world of institutional finance, there is no margin for "mostly correct" AI. If an autonomous research agent pulls unverified financial estimates, confuses non-GAAP numbers, or triggers automated portfolio recommendations based on skewed data, the result is not just a polite correction. It is catastrophic regulatory exposure, massive financial losses, and destroyed client trust.

One of the central debates echoing through the sessions in Austin revolves around what can only be described as the "Observability Trap."

Over the past eighteen months, enterprise software vendors rushed to sell AI observability dashboards to CIOs and CISOs. The pitch sounded reassuring: install these monitoring agents, trace token usage, chart latency spikes, and monitor model drift on an attractive operational canvas.

Yet as multiple executives pointed out in Austin, observability is fundamentally passive. It is a forensic tool, not an operational shield.

Observability tells you that an autonomous customer service agent leaked sensitive customer health data to a public endpoint fifteen minutes ago. Observability provides a clean post-mortem graph showing how a recursive agentic loop burned through $30,000 in token calls while your DevOps team slept.

To borrow a phrase that circulated among participants during Friday's morning sessions: passive observability is just taking meticulous notes while your house burns down around you.

Enterprise AI urgently needs inline, runtime control. That means establishing an intelligent control plane that sits directly within the execution chain. When an agent formulates an intent, attempts a tool call, or seeks to delegate authority, the control plane must evaluate that proposed action against enterprise policy in real time. Depending on corporate risk thresholds, the system must be able to allow the action, block it outright, redact sensitive parameters, or escalate it immediately for human review before it ever touches production data.

Five Practical Questions from the Austin Boardroom

To cut through vendor marketing noise, the GENESIS 2026 program was structured around five uncompromising questions. These questions reflect the exact operational bottlenecks keeping C-suite executives awake at night:

  1. Business Value vs. Expensive Science Projects: What separates the tiny minority of enterprises extracting durable, compounding competitive advantage from the vast majority accumulating brittle, expensive experiments?
  2. Accountability and Legal Ownership: When an autonomous agent acts across six enterprise systems and triggers a regulatory violation, who owns the liability? What exact risk criteria should trigger non-negotiable human sign-off?
  3. Runtime Control Across the Chain: How can platform engineering teams enforce role-based permissions, data fencing, and corporate policies across complex, multi-agent workflows where bots delegate tasks to other bots?
  4. : What does trustworthy execution actually cost when you calculate base model tokens, auxiliary tool invocations, runaway retries, context window bloat, and manual human verification?
  5. : How do global enterprises enforce consistent governance standards across a chaotic patchwork of proprietary frontier models, open-weights deployments, internal custom agents, and third-party SaaS vendors?

The Rise of Trust Posture Management

Closed-door discussions in Austin gave rise to an entirely new category in enterprise architecture: Trust Posture Management.

Industry veterans will recognize the pattern. A decade ago, as corporations began migrating critical workloads to Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure, early cloud security consisted of static policy documents, annual audits, and Excel spreadsheets. It was slow, reactive, and completely mismatched to dynamic cloud environments. That friction forced the creation of Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM), providing automated, continuous visibility and automated policy enforcement across the cloud estate.

Agentic AI is driving an identical architectural shift. Static governance frameworks like the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the EU AI Act, and the OWASP Top 10 for LLM and Agentic Systems provide essential high-level principles. But as one attendee noted, a static PDF policy cannot intercept a rogue API call at runtime.

Trust Posture Management translates those static guidelines into active runtime guardrails. Through frameworks like Trustwise's "Assess, Control, Optimize" model, organizations can systematically evaluate execution chains before deployment, enforce policies inline during live runtime, continuously optimize token and compute economics, and generate immutable, tamper-evident audit records connecting intent to outcome.

Executives gathered at GENESIS 2026 aren't waiting for the standard conference circuit in 2027. The clock is ticking loudly.

As agentic AI adoption moves from exploratory skunkworks into core business operations, the window to architect proper control planes is closing fast. If enterprise leaders wait until an autonomous system triggers a front-page compliance disaster, creates a multi-million-dollar financial error, or forces an emergency cancellation under the Gartner 40 percent cliff, the regulatory and competitive damage will be permanent.

By convening this summit in Austin during one of the most high-octane sporting events on the planet, Trustwise has driven home an indelible point: the future belongs to the swift, but only if they remain in control.

As the cars line up on the grid at Circuit of the Americas this weekend, pit-lane engineers will monitor thousands of real-time telemetry channels to ensure their drivers can safely extract every ounce of performance from their machinery. For enterprise leaders navigating the uncharted territory of autonomous artificial intelligence, the lesson is unmistakable.

Stop marveling at the model's horsepower. Build the control plane, wire up the telemetry, and master the execution chain. That is the only way to win the race.

items.title: Ukraine Is Wiping Out Data Centers Across the Border
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Ukrainian drone strikes have damaged three major Yandex data centers as well as facilities serving Sberbank and VKontakte (the country's equivalent to Facebook), disrupting cloud services, banking, e-commerce, ride-hailing and other digital services across Russia. The attacks may deal a longer-lasting blow to Russia's AI ambitions: Yandex's affected facilities housed its three top-500 supercomputers, and experts say sanctions and shortages of high-end Nvidia chips could make repairs difficult or even take years. "This effectively sets Russia far behind in the AI race, "said Mikhail Klimarev, head of the Internet Protection Society activist group. Fortune reports: Data centers are the latest targets of aerial campaigns waged by both sides against each other's vital infrastructure. [...] Kyiv's attacks on Russian data centers closely followed Moscow's recent strikes on data centers in Ukraine, which disrupted the internet and TV broadcasts. On Oct. 8, Ukrainian drones hit a Yandex data center in Sasovo in the Ryazan region that houses two of the company's three supercomputers. A data center in Kaluga was hit a day later and the one in Vladimir was struck Oct. 11.
 
The data center and AI hub for Sberbank was hit Oct. 14 in Balakovo in the Saratov region, and four days later, Kyiv struck a data center in St. Petersburg serving VKontakte. While oil refineries and warehouses are easy prey, data centers are even softer targets -- massive buildings packed with servers and supporting power and cooling infrastructure. Lasting damage can result from a drone carrying a relatively light load of explosives.
 
[...] Ukraine has stored critical data on servers in allied European countries, helping limit the damage from Russian attacks. But Moscow's strict digital sovereignty policy requires all data storage at home, making it extremely vulnerable. "Because all the infrastructure and all the data is located inside Russia, it's relatively easier to take down," [said Nick Reiners, senior geotechnology analyst at Eurasia Group]. Klimarev predicted the data center attacks could encourage many top Russian companies to move data abroad, while the authorities could ease their efforts to tighten internet controls to minimize the damage.

items.title: Don’t Let AI Steal Your Personality
items.author: Editing Protocol
items.content:
We are well and truly in the AI era; there’s no point in denying it. Industries, by and large, have had to adjust, rethink hiring, their products and services, and even the nature of work itself over the last few years to accommodate this new reality. And so have we, albeit to some extent kicking and screaming.

Because even though there’s a very logical, very solid argument that the applications of AI’s magical abilities are a net positive (if handled responsibly and not treated like many other transformational technologies before it, as yet another way for the powers that be to wage war across lines drawn in the sand), we, from an editorial point of view, have had a more complicated response to it.

When the first waves of AI-generated content hit our queue, we mostly shunned it vehemently. In our eyes, AI-generated text was immediately synonymous with fluff and had no place in our painstakingly curated corner of the internet. We rejected indiscriminately, and it was easy to do so (AI-generated content was, and in many obvious ways still is, very easy to spot if you know what to look for). But, and it is important to take this with caveats, our stance has evolved over the years.

Summarily: Write by yourself. Use AI as a brainstorming assistant. Use AI as a research assistant.

But since then, our queue has grown by hundreds of articles every week, propelled in no small part by AI-generated text and our collective obsession with speed. To the point where even some of our favorite writers have begun sacrificing elements of their personality on the altar of quantity.

Now, we can’t sit on a high horse and point a finger at anyone. When the world moves at breakneck speed, powered by AI supercars, there’s a real chance of being left behind. But we maintain that keeping up with the times cannot come at the expense of your personality, of your voice!

If yours and every other thought leader’s article has the exact same structure, rhythm, and cadence, how do we tell you apart? How do we build a relationship with your thought process, your unique context? How do we pick you out of a crowd?

HackerNoon was founded to accommodate a global community of contributors and readers, to platform a myriad of voices, all with unique POVs, all valuable, interdependent parts of a whole that paint a fuller picture of our ecosystem, our world. And that’s still something we live by to this day.

That said, we also understand the paradoxical nature of things. Sometimes human-written content is bad, and AI-assisted content can be good, and we’re ready to compromise.

But before we talk about what good AI-assisted content looks like to us, we must first say that when it ticks all the boxes of our editing protocol, WE WILL ALWAYS PRIORITIZE HUMAN-WRITTEN, PERSONALITY-RICH CONTENT.

But if you must generate content with AI, then we must see signs that you’re fully in the driver’s seat.

If You Absolutely Must, Here's How to Use AI Without Losing Your Voice Entirely

This is, by some distance, our preferred approach. Get your thoughts on the page first, however messy, disjointed, or grammatically questionable they might be. Then, if you must, bring in AI to clean things up.

Ask it to identify redundancies, improve sentence structure, flag inconsistencies, or point out where your arguments could use more work. But be careful not to let it polish away everything that makes your writing yours.

The peculiar way you choose your words, your sometimes convoluted analogies, and even your tendency to ramble a little before you arrive at your point aren’t necessarily bugs that need to be fixed. Sometimes, they’re the whole point.

1b. Let the first paragraph ALWAYS sound like you

Your opening paragraph is your first opportunity to establish a relationship with the reader. Don't waste it on a generic introduction about how the world is rapidly evolving, how some industry is undergoing an unprecedented transformation, or how something is no longer a luxury but a necessity, or any of the newer variations of AI text templates.

We’ve read hundreds of those introductions and, honestly, we’re tired of them.

Start with an observation, a personal experience, an unpopular opinion, a question you've been wrestling with. Something, anything, that gives us a reason to believe there's a human being with something interesting to say behind the byline.

And if AI helps you with the rest of the piece, make sure the personality you establish in that opening carries through.

2. Think first, AI Later!

Before you even think about opening ChatGPT or your AI assistant of choice, spend some time figuring out what you actually want to say.

What's your central argument? What points do you want to make? What conclusions have you arrived at independently?

You don't necessarily need a fully formed outline or a perfectly articulated thesis, but you should have enough of an idea that you're directing the conversation, not the other way around.

Once you've done that, there's plenty AI can help with. Organizing your scattered thoughts into an outline, suggesting ways to connect two ideas, or even identifying areas that could use more research. You could even take it a step further and ask if AI can find some trends that support your rhetoric or if you need to rethink it.

What we don't want is for you to hand over a topic, ask for 1,500 words, and copy the result into our editor.

We can usually tell, and it casts a skeptical shadow over your work in our eyes.

3a. Bring Your Personal Context to the Table

This one’s especially important for our technical writers and thought leaders. We’ve been pretty clear about what we generally expect from either group:

To reiterate, if you're writing about a product you've built, tell us about YOUR experience. What decisions did you make? What surprised you? What did you try that didn't work? What would you do differently?

If you're writing about an industry trend, tell us what you've observed, what informs your opinion, and why readers should care about your interpretation of events.

AI can help you organize these experiences, but it cannot have them for you. And please, don't let it invent personal anecdotes, technical results, or sources to make your article sound more convincing. We will always ask to see verifiable proof on the page.

3b. Don’t Let AI Dictate Your Article’s Rhythm

Not every article needs three key takeaways, five actionable strategies, and a conclusion that begins with "The future of..."

Not every paragraph needs to be the same length. Not every section needs a subheading. And not every idea needs to be neatly packaged into a bullet point. Sometimes the best way to make an argument is to take the scenic route.

Play around with your structure. Honor your train of thought. Use humor, skepticism, frustration, excitement, whatever comes naturally to you and serves the story.

There’s no universal template for good writing!

The Point is to Sound Like You

To be clear, we’re not advocating for bad writing in the name of authenticity, nor are we suggesting that your article should be rife with imperfections just to prove that it’s human. Good editing matters. So do structure and clarity. We wouldn’t have a team of human editors if we thought otherwise.

All we’re asking is that you don’t sacrifice your personality on the altar of faux efficiency.

By all means, use the tools at your disposal. Experiment with them to your heart’s content. Let them make the writing process easier, and perhaps even better. But don’t surrender the very thing that makes your perspective worth publishing in the first place.

Because if we can swap your byline with twenty others and nobody notices the difference, something has gone terribly wrong.

Ready to put these tips to use?

If you’re looking for a more guided way to build the habit of real thought leadership more consistently. Then the is for you.

The HackerNoon Blogging Course

The HackerNoon Blogging Course breaks down how to ideate, structure, draft, and publish high-quality technical stories, using the same editorial standards we apply every day.

So instead of guessing what works, you’re building from a system that’s already been tested at scale.

If your goal is to write clearer, sharper, more publishable content in 2026, this is a strong next step.

items.title: Comcast Loses More Customers, Claims Other ISPs' Cheap Prices Are 'Irrational'
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Comcast reportedly plans significant job cuts in its cable division as the firm continues to lose residential broadband and TV customers. Comcast lost 144,000 residential broadband customers in Q3 2026, up from a 91,000-customer loss in the same quarter a year ago, the company said in its earnings report today. Comcast historically capitalized on a lack of competition for high-speed wired broadband. But now it faces stronger competition from fixed wireless providers and from fiber providers in parts of its cable territory. "Fixed wireless remains aggressive and continues to take share, while fiber construction remains elevated, with pockets of irrational pricing and promotional activity," Comcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh said today in an earnings call.
 
Comcast CFO Jason Armstrong said "irrational pricing" from fiber operators includes $30 to $40 monthly broadband offers "in specific markets in the third quarter." He said $30 to $40 pricing is irrational because deploying fiber costs $1,500 or more per home, and is "getting more expensive with construction costs up as you get into more suburban and rural areas." "As we look at the return profile of that, to us, that is irrational competition," Armstrong said. While he didn't name any specific competitors, Verizon has been pitching FiOS fiber plans that start at $30 a month. Comcast's network is a mix of fiber and cable, and it offers fiber-to-the-home in only small portions of its cable territory.
 
Armstrong said more Comcast customers are leaving when they face "pricing transitions," apparently referring to the price hikes customers get when promotional offers expire. "We've been refining our offers and retention strategies to better manage these transitions and strengthen customer retention," he said. Cavanagh said that "satellite is not yet a material factor" in the competition Comcast faces, but that Comcast is focused on "anticipating emerging forms of competition and positioning our business to respond as the market evolves."

items.content:
When an AI agent can run shell commands in your pipeline, its permissions are infrastructure. They should be declared where reviewers look, versioned with the agent, and tested on every change. Docker Agent gets the first two right. The third is up to you, and when I wrote the tests, one widely used permission pattern failed in a way worth knowing about.

Docker Agent is Docker's open-source runtime for teams of agents. A team is a config file: models, agents, which agents each one may delegate to, which tools each may use, and the policy around all of it. You run it with docker agent run crew.yaml.

My test project, release-gate-crew, is a release gate for container services. A lead agent delegates to a container auditor and a pipeline auditor, then hands their findings to a scribe that writes a PASS/BLOCK report. The sample service under review is deliberately bad: an unpinned base image, a secret in , a privileged container with the Docker socket mounted, and a workflow that checks out untrusted code with write permissions.

Every control sits in the same file as the agents:

agents:
  container_auditor:
    model: worker
    instruction_file: prompts/container_auditor.md
    toolsets:
      - type: filesystem
        allow_list: ["./target"]   # read scope
      - type: shell

runtime:
  safety: restricted               # unattended: deny anything not allowed

permissions:
  allow: ["read_file", "shell:cmd=grep -n *"]
  deny:  ["shell:cmd=*curl*", "shell:cmd=*&&*", "shell:cmd=*;*", "shell:cmd=*|*"]

budget:
  max_cost: 0.50                   # one pot shared by every agent
  max_time: 10m

A file hides and key files from every agent. The same team also exists as , because Docker Agent reads HCL too, and platform teams that live in Terraform may prefer it.

Testing guardrails without a model

Guardrails are deterministic, so they should be testable without paying for tokens or tolerating model variance. I wrote a scripted, OpenAI-compatible stub model in Go and pointed every agent at it through a config flavor. The stub plays a fixed sequence per agent. It delegates, reads files, and then deliberately tries things the config should refuse.

A Go integration test drives the real binary against both config files and checks nine written requirements. The runtime's own responses:

excluded by .agentsignore

Pipeline auditor reads a file outside

outside the allowed directories (./target)

Scribe writes

denied by restricted safety mode, no prompt

grep -n FROM target/Dockerfile && curl --version

denied by permissions configuration

All of that held, for YAML and HCL alike.

The pattern that didn't hold

Permission rules are globs matched against the whole command string, and matches spaces. So consider the prefix style common in examples:

permissions:
  allow: ["shell:cmd=grep -n *"]
  deny:  ["shell:cmd=curl *"]

The command grep -n FROM target/Dockerfile && curl --version begins with , so the allow rule matches. It does not begin with , so the deny rule misses. Deny is evaluated first, finds nothing, then allow approves. In my test, curl ran and printed its version banner. The safety mode did not stop it, because an explicit allow outranks the mode.

Docker's documentation says permissions are client-side and not a security boundary, and it recommends sandbox mode for isolation. I agree with that framing. The risk is practical: prefix rules look precise, and they are what most people will copy.

Four changes close the gap:

  1. Deny shell operators: , , , backticks and .
  2. Match denied binaries anywhere: , not .
  3. Allow one narrow command per agent that needs a shell.
  4. Use , which runs the team in a Docker Sandboxes VM, for anything you don't fully trust.

My suite keeps a test that reproduces the bypass. If a future release starts parsing compound commands, that test will fail and tell me to revisit the advice.

  • The filesystem toolset is unrestricted by default. Set on every one.
  • A config pulled from a registry can declare runtime.safety: autonomous. Your own flag or user settings take precedence only if you set them.
  • Sub-agents receive only the task text the lead writes, inside a block. Good isolation, but the lead must pass along everything a specialist needs.
  • The project moves quickly: 17 releases in September 2026. Pin the version in CI and disable telemetry there with .

What the stub can't tell you

None of this measures review quality. A scripted stub proves the harness, not the judgement. The repository includes three cases for that: block the flawed sample, refuse to reveal the secret, and refuse to claim an edit. They need real model keys and a container runtime, and I haven't run them yet.

That split is the main lesson I'd take to any agent platform. Test the guardrails deterministically on every push. Evaluate the model's judgement separately, with repeated runs, before you trust a gate decision.

items.title: How an iOS Update Broke Chinese Text in War Robots (And How We Fixed It)
items.author: Sergey Madekin
items.content:
In September 2024, War Robots support received a surge of complaints from Chinese iOS players: after updating to iOS 18, in-game text was displaying incorrectly for some users. The issue manifested differently across devices: some players noticed missing characters, while others reported wrong or unfamiliar glyph styles. To make matters worse, we were unable to reproduce the bug on our local test devices.

My name is Sergey Madekin, Senior Developer on War Robots. In this article, I will share how we ultimately resolved the missing Chinese characters issue.

Investigating the Root Cause

Upon investigation, we discovered that our Chinese text rendering relied directly on system fonts. The game uses standard Unity UI (Text) components configured with dynamic fonts. Unity first searches for required glyphs within the designated font asset, then moves through the Font Names list, and finally falls back to the engine's built-in list of fallback system fonts for the given platform. It was this fallback mechanism that produced inconsistent results across different devices running iOS 18.

A similar issue with missing characters in Legacy Text on iOS 18+ is logged in the Unity Issue Tracker. At the time of writing, no fix version is specified in the ticket.

The First Attempt: Adding the Full Font

The fix itself is straightforward: bundle a dedicated Chinese font into the build and configure it as a fallback for missing glyphs. However, a complete Chinese font file contains tens of thousands of characters. Our base Noto Sans SC TTF file weighed around 10 MB, and adding it increased the final build size by 37 MB.

We initially verified the fix by releasing a build with the full font, keeping in mind that we would optimize it later if it proved effective. The update resolved all text rendering issues with no further complaints, so I moved on to reducing the file size. Fortunately, daily communication requires only a fraction of the full character set, and a specific game requires even fewer.

Optimization and Font Subsetting with pyftsubset

The next challenge was keeping only the necessary characters in the source file. Luckily, the right tool already exists: pyftsubset, a command-line utility from Python's fontTools package designed to create slimmed-down font files containing only specified glyph sets. It discards unused glyphs and metadata, drastically shrinking the file size.

All that remained was identifying which characters to keep. I started with a standard frequency list of common Chinese characters and ran the subsetting tool against it. However, gaps immediately appeared — particularly in localized in-game names, and there were quite a few of them. It became clear that we needed to extract the exact character set used in our text resources. I pulled all current translations and compiled a list of every unique character found in them. I then ran pyftsubset on the source file, keeping only this set. The results were impressive: out of roughly 30,000 characters in the original font, only about 3,000 remained, dropping the TTF size from 10 MB down to around 900 KB. The resulting build size increase was just 1.24 MB.

Edge Cases and Player Nicknames

We shipped the next release with this lightweight font. Player complaints dropped drastically, but a few remained. We discovered that certain configuration files contained unlocalized strings with rare characters. Additionally, some players reported missing characters in their custom usernames.

Because the missing character count was low, I created a dedicated supplementary list. While this resolved all known edge cases, it doesn't guarantee full coverage for future usernames containing obscure characters. Moving forward, whenever a new missing character is reported, we simply append it to the supplementary list and regenerate the font.

Automating the Font Pipeline in Unity

Since game content updates frequently, we needed an easy, automated way to update our character set before each release.

After a few iterations, we built a custom Unity Editor tool that automates the whole process in a single click:

  1. Connects to the target test server hosting localization files for the upcoming release.
  2. Downloads the latest text resources.
  3. Extracts unique characters from the text and merges them with our supplementary list.
  4. Excludes glyphs already present in the primary game font to avoid duplication.
  5. Verifies character availability in the source Chinese TTF file. Missing glyphs are logged and skipped.
  6. (Optional) Includes the character set from the previous release if the "preserve old characters" setting is enabled.
  7. Runs pyftsubset on the source TTF file using the compiled character list and outputs the optimized font directly into the build.

Preserving the previous release's character set prevents regression bugs if strings are removed from current localization files. While this causes the font size to grow slightly over time, it provides a solid balance between file footprint and backward compatibility.

The Unicode Pitfall: One Character, Two Chars

While refining the generator, we uncovered another nuance: collecting target characters using a is unsafe.

In C#, strings are UTF-16 encoded. Most Chinese characters we use fit into a single , but certain rare ones require two. Together, these two units form a surrogate pair representing a single character.

A stores individual unit values without preserving pairs. For instance, two distinct rare characters might share the same high surrogate. During deduplication, that shared unit is kept only once—reducing four values down to a set of three. When passing that corrupted set to as a string, neither of the original characters will be fully preserved.

This behavior is demonstrated below:

string text = "\U00020000\U00020001"; // Two distinct characters: 𠀀 and 𠀁

Console.WriteLine(text.Length);                   // 4 — char count
Console.WriteLine(new HashSet<char>(text).Count); // 3 — unique char units (corrupted)
Console.WriteLine(GetTextScalars(text).Count);   // 2 — actual Unicode characters

To preserve surrogate pairs intact, we introduced the method. It iterates through the string and populates a with complete characters: standard ones as a single- string, and surrogate pairs as a two- string.

private static HashSet<string> GetTextScalars(string text)
{
    var result = new HashSet<string>();
    for (var i = 0; i < text.Length; i++)
    {
        if (char.IsHighSurrogate(text[i]) && i + 1 < text.Length && char.IsLowSurrogate(text[i + 1]))
        {
            result.Add(text.Substring(i, 2));
            i++;
        }
        else
        {
            result.Add(text[i].ToString());
        }
    }

    return result;
}

This safeguard protects our character set during subset preparation. Note that it is unrelated to the original iOS system font fallback issue.

By building this workflow, we gained the ability to quickly update and expand our Chinese font while keeping the build size impact minimal. It now covers all game localizations, handles custom player names via our supplementary list, and optionally preserves coverage across past releases.

items.title: Using Cypress Cloud CLI and Test Replay for AI-Assisted CI Debugging
items.author: Raju Dandigam
items.content:
A checkout test fails in CI with this message:

expected '[data-cy="cart-total"]' to have text '$45.00'

The screenshot shows . An AI assistant can invent several plausible explanations: the discount request failed, React rendered stale state, the selector found the wrong cart, or the assertion ran early.

Plausible is not the same as supported.

The quality of AI-assisted debugging depends less on how confidently the assistant explains the screenshot and more on whether it can inspect the evidence that produced it.

Recorded CI and live local debugging are different surfaces

Cypress now exposes two useful but distinct agent workflows:

  • A live, local open-mode Cypress session; Run and verify a change during development
  • Completed Cloud runs and Test Replay data; Reconstruct an existing CI failure

I have written separately about giving an agent access to a live Cypress session. This workflow starts at the opposite end: the failure already happened, perhaps only in CI, and the recorded attempt is the evidence.

The Cypress Cloud CLI returns JSON for runs, specs, tests, commands, network requests, and console events. The local Test Replay viewer is available through in CLI version or newer.

Start with a deliberately small evidence packet

The current documentation requires Node.js or newer and recommends using the latest CLI. Install it, record the resolved version, and pin that exact version in repeatable CI automation after validation:

npm install --global @cypress/cloud@latest
cy-cloud version
cy-cloud status

For a failed run, the shortest useful path is:

cy-cloud run list \
  --projectId <projectId> \
  --branch main \
  --status failed \
  --limit 1

cy-cloud test list \
  --projectId <projectId> \
  --runNumber <runNumber> \
  --status failed

cy-cloud replay timeline \
  --testId <testId> \
  --commands \
  --aroundFailure 5 \
  --network \
  --logs

That packet answers four questions:

  1. Which commands immediately preceded it?
  2. Which XHR or fetch activity overlapped the failure?
  3. Did the application log a related error?

Do not begin by dumping an entire organization's run history into an agent. Scope the query to one project, run, test, attempt, and timeline window.

Suppose the test failed on attempt one and passed on attempt two. A screenshot from the failed attempt tells us the symptom. Comparing the attempts can expose the first causal difference.

cy-cloud replay timeline \
  --testId <testId> \
  --attempt 1 \
  --commands --network --logs \
  > attempt-1.json

cy-cloud replay timeline \
  --testId <testId> \
  --attempt 2 \
  --commands --network --logs \
  > attempt-2.json

Imagine the relevant entries reduce to:

  • , response at 1,240 ms; , response at 310 ms
  • 820 ms; 760 ms
  • ;
  • none; none

The evidence does not yet prove whether the product or test is wrong, but it eliminates several guesses. The assertion can run before the successful response. The next review question is whether the UI should block until the response arrives, or whether the test failed to wait for an application event that defines completion.

The timeline gives structure. The local replay viewer lets you inspect the recorded DOM and styles around one command:

cy-cloud replay view open --testId <testId>

cy-cloud replay view move \
  --testId <testId> \
  --attempt 1 \
  --pin '<commandId>|before'

cy-cloud replay view inspect \
  --testId <testId> \
  --selector '[data-cy="cart-total"]'

cy-cloud replay view move \
  --testId <testId> \
  --attempt 1 \
  --pin '<commandId>|after'

This is more diagnostic than asking an agent to infer causality from the final screenshot. It can see whether an earlier command changed an attribute, collapsed a container, or left the DOM stale.

requires a Chromium-family browser and Cloud CLI or newer. Because Cloud CLI is Beta, scripts should pin a compatible version and treat output schemas as versioned dependencies.

Give the agent a diagnostic contract

An unrestricted prompt such as “fix this test” encourages the assistant to optimize for a green run. It may add a hard wait, broaden a selector, remove an assertion, or mask a product regression.

A better task is bounded:

Analyze attempt-1.json and attempt-2.json for test <testId>.

1. Identify the first material difference before the failed assertion.
2. Cite the relevant command, network, or console event IDs.
3. Classify the likely cause as product, test synchronization,
   test data, environment, or unknown.
4. Propose the smallest code change, but do not edit files.
5. Do not add fixed waits or weaken the business assertion.
6. List the local verification commands and one negative control.

The request separates observation, diagnosis, proposal, and execution. A human can reject the classification before any code changes.

Credential locality is not the whole security model

Cloud CLI access follows the organizations, teams, projects, and roles available to the authenticated Cypress Cloud user. OAuth is recommended locally; a personal access token can be supplied through in CI. Stored credentials are owner-readable on the local machine.

Those are useful controls, but they do not mean every AI environment is automatically safe. If an agent can read arbitrary environment variables, home-directory files, or shell output, it may reach more than intended.

Use the ordinary least-privilege questions:

  • Which Cypress Cloud user or service identity is authenticating?
  • Which projects can it read?
  • Can the agent execute arbitrary shell commands?
  • Where are downloaded replay data and screenshots cached?
  • Can captured network bodies contain secrets or personal data?
  • When are local artifacts deleted?

Cypress supports masking and redaction for Test Replay network data; configure those boundaries before making replay evidence broadly available.

Verification remains a separate step

After reviewing a proposed fix, run the affected spec locally. A useful sequence is:

  1. reproduce with the same fixture or a sanitized equivalent;
  2. apply the smallest reviewed change;
  3. run the original failure case;
  4. run a negative control that should still fail;
  5. inspect the behavior, not just the exit code;
  6. push only after the evidence agrees.

The negative control matters. If changing the selector makes the test pass even when the discount is not applied, the “fix” destroyed the test.

Remove runner drift with a pinned container

Before blaming the test or product, rerun the candidate change in the same declared Node and browser environment.

An official or image can make that boundary repeatable, but only when you pin a full version tag or digest:

export CYPRESS_IMAGE='cypress/browsers@sha256:<approved-digest>'
docker compose run --rm \
  -e CYPRESS_SPEC='cypress/e2e/checkout.cy.ts' \
  cypress

The Compose service should run the same repository revision and application fixture used in the investigation. Record docker image inspect "$CYPRESS_IMAGE", , , and the selected browser with the evidence packet. A green result in a different image is not a reproduction; it is a new experiment.

What this workflow does not prove

Recorded Test Replay evidence describes one captured run. It does not prove that a failure is statistically representative or that the proposed patch is correct. A passing retry can differ because of data, timing, infrastructure, or an actual product race.

Cloud CLI is also not an autonomous remediation system. It is a read-oriented evidence interface. Code changes, approval, and verification remain responsibilities of your development workflow.

Ask AI to explain bounded evidence before asking it to change code.

That turns the assistant from a confident guesser into a supervised participant in a debugging process whose claims can be reviewed

items.title: Agent Security & Identity (Part 2): Who Are You, Who's Your Agent, And What Should They Be Allowed?
items.author: Alejandro Saucedo
items.content:
This is a 2-part series on agent identity and security: who the user is, who the agent is, and what each of them should be allowed to reach. Part 2 runs the design end to end on a cluster, with two users, two agents, a tool, a model and a third-party service.

In Part 1, I designed how agent identity can work on a platform where agent-delegation is enabled, and how we decide (+ enforce) what they and their users are allowed to reach. In this second and final part I deploy that design on a cluster and check whether it actually holds up.

In this Part 2 blog post, I go through a hands-on use-case with 2 users of the same agent platform at the same company: Alice is in the group and Bob is in the group. Throughout this I will show the good, the bad and the ugly of agentic identity and security, especially when dealing with autonomous agents, and with users delegating permissions to an agent.

The walkthrough answers 4 questions:

  • Does an agent requesting a tool for a user in the wrong group actually get refused?
  • When an agent calls its own tool and model, how do we authorize (+ verify) the hops?
  • What happens to an autonomous agent that has no user behind it at all?
  • When Alice asks for a 3rd party service (i.e. github) via an agent, does the request go out as Alice?

Most of what I learnt came from the requests that got denied (+ from the complexities and lessons learned), so you'll see plenty of those below.

Everything below runs on a local KIND cluster against the public Agentic Identity Broker release, pinned at . On a local cluster GitHub is a mock, so the consent screen gets completed automatically instead of in a browser, but every identity and access-control decision you'll see is real.

Here's a quick refresher of what we covered in Part 1 before we run it.

I started with the challenges we all phase when agents have to access 3rd party services on behalf of a user. Here I showed how just giving an API token falls short, as you can't tell which user an action was for, it has more access than any single user needs, and you can't revoke it for just one user.

Fixing that needed a component that holds each user's own third-party credential, obtained with their consent. The Agentic Identity Broker does exactly that, so I adopted it instead of writing my own.

Then I separated the 2 identities that every protected call carries. The is the human the work is being done for, and the is the agent doing the work. This is how the system enforces resource access on the actor and use the subject for what the user personally delegated, which keeps permissions correct when agents call other agents.

Finally I made 6 architecture decisions, and 3 of them matter most for what follows:

One gateway on every hop, plus a NetworkPolicy so nothing can go around it

Checks in the agent runtime, a sidecar per workload, a service mesh

How authorization is modelled

One explicit for who may enter an agent, with the agent's own dependencies derived from its spec, all evaluated by KAOS's own Open Policy Agent decision point

A policy language as the authoring surface, or the broker answering the decision

KAOS owns the integration; the broker and the identity provider run as their own releases

The platform installing and lifecycle-managing its own broker

That third row is why this walkthrough has both a broker and Keycloak in it. The broker holds the delegated third-party credentials and performs the exchange, and the gateway attaches the returned credential to the outbound request. Keycloak proves who the human is, carries the group membership the rules match on, and registers each agent as its own client so the broker can tell which agent is asking.

Now let's build the cluster and see it work.

The is the set of components that establish identity and decide the rules. Apart from the gateway, none of them carry your agents' actual traffic; they answer the 3 questions from part 1 about it. Here they are on one map. The greyed pieces belong to section 5 and can be ignored for now.

There are quite a few components in this overview, so let's walk through them:

  • : This is the single gateway every request passes through, including agent-to-tool, agent-to-model and agent-to-agent calls, which is what makes it a mesh.
  • : Authenticates users, proves who they are and which groups they belong to; supports OIDC compatible services so we use Keycloak here.
  • : Gives each agent their identity through secure credentials; the default uses k8s Service Accounts, but also supports OIDC compatible services; we also configure Keycloak in this example.
  • : This is the authorization (authz) service that KAOS uses to allow/deny requests based on the "user" calling the "agent" accessing the "resource".
  • Agent Impersonation Service: Lets an agent act on an outside service (like GitHub) as the user by exchanging third-party tokens (github/slack/etc) through a consent mechanism. The concrete tool I use is the Agent Identity Broker (AIB), and it gets its own section, section 5.
  • : This component synchronises auth & identity bidirectionaly; it registers the KAOS resources on upstream auth services, and injects identities and secrets across KAOS resources.

Before I show how this all fits together with an example, let's configure the kubernetes cluster with this setup.

1.1 Install it in one command

I use the KAOS CLI to install the Gateway Mesh, User Auth, Agent Auth, the KAOS Authz Service, the KAOS Operator, and the Agent Identity Broker (AIB).

This command wires everything together in a new cluster:

kaos system install \
  --gateway-strict \         # Traffic can only go through gateway
  --authz-enabled \          # KAOS Authorization service enabled
  --user-auth keycloak \     # Use Keycloak for User auth (alt: OIDC)
  --agent-auth keycloak \    # Use Keycloak for Agent Auth (alt: Service Accts. or OIDC)
  --token-exchange-enabled \ # Use AIB for token exchange

                         # Other flags
  --wait \               # Block until everything is ready
  --create-cli-config    # In-folder config file for cli

kaos system install --help lists everything else (image tags, resource limits, replica counts, realm names, observability backends); the Helm values behind each flag are shown per-component in section 4.

Let's confirm the pieces are healthy:

gateway           ready
login service     ready   (keycloak)
access-control    ready   (2/2 replicas)
sync service      ready

And let's make sure that everything is configured correctly:

gateway:
  address: http://kaos-gateway.kaos-system.svc.cluster.local
  through_gateway: true
auth:
  issuer: http://keycloak.keycloak.svc.cluster.local:8080/realms/kaos
  client_id: kaos
  realm: kaos
  broker_url: http://aib-agentic-identity-broker.aib-system.svc.cluster.local:8000
  broker_admin_url: http://aib-agentic-identity-broker.aib-system.svc.cluster.local:14000/api
namespace: kaos-system
sessions: {}

The is the actual agent traffic, meaning users invoking agents and agents calling tools and models. Every one of those calls travels through the Gateway Mesh and is checked before it is let through.

The hands-on example uses the following resources:

  • two users: (group ) and (group )
  • two agents: (user-activated) and (autonomous agent)
  • one model: (a model endpoint both agents may use)
  • one external service: , covered in section 5

The rules are that the group may use the agent, the agent may reach and , and the autonomous may reach . Everything else is denied, including bob (poor bob).

Here's a chart that shows what we'll try to accomplish:

2.1 How identity flows through a request

Every call, a user/agent reaching an agent, or a user/agent reaching a tool or model, travels , which does two checks before letting it through:

A is like an ID card issued by the identity provider, and both the user and the agent hold one.

User Auth issues signed tokens for human users and it carries their groups ( isn't a core OIDC claim, so the identity provider maps it in; with Keycloak that's a group-membership protocol mapper).

Agent Auth also issues signed tokens, but an agent starts from a credential it was given (a mounted ServiceAccount token, or a client secret) and exchanges that for one.

The gateway does the two checks in order; first it confirms the token is genuine and unexpired (identity), then it asks the KAOS Authz Service whether that identity is allowed to do this (permission), and only if both pass does the request reach its destination.

If the authz service the request is denied. There's no config knob to loosen this, since the operator sets on every policy it generates, and it's the reason the authz service runs highly available.

2.2 Deploy the agents and tools

Everything the example needs (both agents, the tool, the model, and the access rule for who may use them) is bundled as a single sample. I deploy it with one command, then walk through each object and create it step by step.

Here's the one line deploy command:

kaos samples deploy 8-authorization-walkthrough -n kaos-system

modelapi.kaos.tools/model-api serverside-applied
mcpserver.kaos.tools/echo-mcp serverside-applied
agent.kaos.tools/researcher serverside-applied
agent.kaos.tools/autobot serverside-applied
accessgrant.kaos.tools/researchers-to-researcher serverside-applied

Deployed sample '8-authorization-walkthrough'

The tool's single function is an echo, and the model's responses are mocked, so every result is deterministic and the walkthrough only exercises . The four resources first, each a plain Kubernetes object (the access rule follows in 2.3):

A model endpoint both agents may call.

A tool (an MCP server) exposing a single function the may use.

A user-facing agent. It needs a person behind it and carries that person's identity through to whatever it calls.

An agent. No user behind it; it runs on a schedule and acts as itself.

Each resource has its own command, so you can build a similar setup by hand and see the shape of each object. The model and tool first:

# a small in-cluster model endpoint
kaos modelapi create model-api \
  --mode hosted \
  --model "smollm2:135m"

# an echo tool exposed as an MCP server
kaos mcp create echo-mcp \
  --runtime python-string \
  --params 'def echo(message: str) -> str:
      """Echo a note for the authorization walkthrough."""
      return f"Echo: {message}"'

Then the two agents. The user-facing one references the model and tool it should use:

kaos agent create researcher \
  --modelapi model-api \
  --mcp echo-mcp \
  --instructions "Echo the user's request and use echo-mcp when asked."

The autonomous one adds an goal so it runs on its own interval instead of waiting for a person:

kaos agent create autobot \
  --modelapi model-api \
  --autonomous-goal "Produce the automated echo report." \
  --autonomous-interval 3600

writes ordinary KAOS objects; this is what the sample applies. The runs in mode and each agent carries , so the echo replies are deterministic. Note differs from mainly by its block. That single field is what makes it act as itself rather than needing a user.

apiVersion: kaos.tools/v1alpha1
kind: ModelAPI
metadata:
  name: model-api
spec:
  mode: Proxy
  proxyConfig:
    models:
      - '*'
---
apiVersion: kaos.tools/v1alpha1
kind: MCPServer
metadata:
  name: echo-mcp
spec:
  runtime: python-string
  params: |
    def echo(message: str) -> str:
        """Echo a note for the authorization walkthrough."""
        return f"Echo: {message}"
---
apiVersion: kaos.tools/v1alpha1
kind: Agent
metadata:
  name: researcher
spec:
  modelAPI: model-api
  model: echo
  mcpServers:
    - echo-mcp
  config:
    description: User-facing echo agent for authorization checks
    instructions: Echo the user's request and use echo-mcp when asked.
  container:
    env:
      - name: DEBUG_MOCK_RESPONSES
        value: '["{\"tool_calls\": [{\"id\": \"call_1\", \"name\": \"echo\", \"arguments\": {\"message\": \"authorization note\"}}]}", "Researcher echo response"]'
  agentNetwork:
    expose: true
---
apiVersion: kaos.tools/v1alpha1
kind: Agent
metadata:
  name: autobot
spec:
  modelAPI: model-api
  model: echo
  config:
    description: Autonomous echo agent for authorization checks
    instructions: Echo a short automated report.
    autonomous:
      goal: Produce the automated echo report.
      intervalSeconds: 3600
  container:
    env:
      - name: DEBUG_MOCK_RESPONSES
        value: '["Autobot echo response"]'
  agentNetwork:
    expose: true
