Staying on the subject of datasets: deduplication is another important part of working with LLMs. Duplicate data harms LLM training and also causes damage when it surfaces during answer generation. As data volume grows, the risk of duplicates grows linearly. Techniques such as fuzzy matching and hash-based deduplication can be used to eliminate them. More broadly, you should build a pipeline for quality control and data management in your system. These pipelines should include rules and tracking systems that let you identify problematic data and trace where it came from.

For more advanced RAG, you need richer metadata for precise retrieval. Metadata should concisely capture information that would otherwise be scattered throughout the document. One approach is a hierarchical index, where a short summary is generated for each level of the hierarchy.

To check our RAG, we can use Self-RAG, which lets the model look back at its own answer and evaluate it. Self-RAG iteratively verifies the reliability of the sources behind the final answer. Alternatively, there's Corrective RAG, which tackles the problem of faulty retrieval. Corrective RAG checks the quality of the retrieved data before generating an answer for the user. The system retrieves a document or piece of information and analyzes it; if the result is unsatisfactory, it either rewrites the query or turns to web search. This is a very popular approach for bots that must deliver accurate information.

A vector database is a specialized database designed to store high-dimensional vectors. As such, it's optimized for unstructured and semi-structured data represented as vectors. Its job is to provide efficient storage, indexing, and search. Your choice of vector database also has a significant impact on RAG performance. There are dozens of options today, so picking the best one can be a challenge. Our default vector DB is ChromaDB, but there are other ways to store data, such as RDBMS, NoSQL, and NewSQL. You can even add pgvector to PostgreSQL and get yourself a vector store. A vector store typically consists of three layers: indexing, storage, and processing.

Why vector databases instead of conventional ones? Libraries such as FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) aren't designed for create, read, update, and delete (CRUD) operations, so they're a poor fit for dynamic systems where multiple users access and modify data. Conversely, if our database is immutable and we only provide read access, FAISS can be a good solution. There are also SQL databases that support vectors as an extension of the classic database. They let you efficiently index related metadata. However, they don't scale well, often limit vector size, and deliver lower performance. SQL databases are a good choice for internal projects that need to connect to existing enterprise databases (which are probably already in SQL), but not when scalability and performance matter.

When choosing how to store your data, it's important to understand what questions potential users will ask the RAG system. For example, if users will ask questions that require the model to look up several facts, it's better to use small chunks that each contain a direct answer. If the system will be more "reasoning"-oriented, chunks with more context work better. When there are too many chunks, speed drops, and the odds of finding the right piece of information are far from 100%.

Chunks can also be made more semantically aligned with incoming queries. A chatbot will most likely receive questions as input, so you generate hypothetical questions for each chunk, and those questions are represented as vectors (embeddings). An embedding is essentially a way of clustering text. Embeddings help reveal semantic relationships and improve understanding of the data. Say you have millions of product reviews and want to find all the similar ones. Or a recommender system built on the semantic relationships between a user's likes and dislikes. Embeddings aren't limited to text — they work for video and images, too. They convert human language into vectors that AI systems can analyze. Semantic similarity recognizes that two differently worded sentences actually mean the same thing.

You need semantic search. Because it accounts for the meaning and context of the data, semantic search makes search results and recommendations more relevant. In semantic search, the smaller the distance, the greater the similarity — this is Euclidean space at work. Another algorithm is the dot product, which is more about vector similarity than distance. There are many other options as well: Lin similarity, Jaccard similarity, Hamming distance, Manhattan distance. On top of that, techniques such as Hypothetical Document Embeddings (HyDE) come into play: for a user query, the system first generates a hypothetical answer that's semantically similar to the original question, then uses that answer to find matching chunks. In general, embedding models struggle with topics they're unfamiliar with. That's why the hypothetical answer is more about the of an answer than its correctness.

Cosine similarity is the most common way to calculate the similarity between two embedding vectors: it measures the cosine of the angle between them. It's used to analyze relationships between sentences in embedding space by measuring the angular distance between their vectors. There are plenty of libraries for vectorization; popular ones include Word2Vec, Sentence2Vec, and Doc2Vec. Vectors can have thousands of dimensions, and more dimensions can capture finer-grained semantic information. If you know how to compare vectors using cosine similarity, you can write your own RAG.

The one approach that stands apart is keyword-based search, where matching happens on keywords. It works well when the query targets a specific name: a term or a company name. A popular model for this kind of search is BM25, the counterpart to vector search. BM25 finds documents that contain a particular term. BM25 is an example of sparse vectors, as is TF-IDF. With BM25, you get a formula along the lines of scorehybrid=1−0.43∙scoresparse+0.32∙scoredense. In plain terms: you have a product catalog with millions of items, and a user searches for something like "Samsung Note," "mid-range smartphone for my mom with a good camera," or "refurbished Xiaomi under $300." BM25 on its own can't handle that — and neither can vector search. Combine the two, and you'll get solid results.

The most basic metrics for validating LLM output are and . Precision is the share of retrieved documents that are relevant, and recall is the share of relevant documents that were successfully retrieved. These metrics show how often the right document was ranked high and retrieved. It's also useful to look at ranked list quality — which documents made it to the top.

It's good to have ground-truth data on hand. This is the ideal answer we'd expect from the RAG system, and it also serves as the benchmark for LLM quality. How to create ground-truth data is another matter. The simplest way is to hire an expert to write reference answers. For a support chat, for instance, the experts would be employees tasked with writing answers in the format To resolve [issue], you can try [solution]. Answers like these can be scored on — whether the answer is supported by the documents — and — how well the answer matches the query and the data it was built on. Other ways to compare generated answers against reference ones include Ragas, a framework for RAG evaluation, as well as BLEU, ROUGE, and expert review.

Another test is the needle in a haystack. On its own it's fairly basic, but it really proves its worth when you need to find multiple needles — and far from every model can handle that.

For evaluating the LLM itself, the key metrics are — the share of correct predictions, or the quality of answers and reasoning. In spam filtering, for example, the fewer malicious emails slip past the LLM, the better it is. The second metric is , i.e., speed, measured as time to first token or time to last token.

In a model's lifecycle, training comes first: the process in which the model learns from scratch. No LLM > LLM. Training takes anywhere from hours to weeks or even months. Training is when the model learns; inference is when it predicts — that is, generates an answer. Inference is next-token prediction, or simply generating a response to your request in real time. Your model has finished training and now runs on an NVIDIA A100, H100, or some other GPU cluster. During inference, you're most likely constrained by available memory, power, and time — and despite all of these constraints, inference still has to run efficiently for the end user.

Models served online (SaaS) have fixed weights. These are large models with billions of parameters (GPT-4, Llama-70B) that run in the cloud and require 40 GB GPUs. They're so big because they're very "deep" — they have many layers. Does that mean bigger is better? No. Modern models can't scale indefinitely; at some point, adding parameters brings no performance gain and can even hurt.

Large models are clunky and slow. Users don't need a good model — they need a fast one. In production, the typical latency budget is 200 ms max (p99). A 7B model will run slowly — say, 3 seconds per token. A 70B model will require 280 GB of GPU memory. For such large models to deliver value in the mass market, you need inference optimization to speed them up. The first method is quantization. Let me say up front that carelessly applied quantization severely hurts model accuracy and leads to hallucinations. You need to add RTN (round-to-nearest). At the same time, quantization is the fastest way to shrink a model, which is great for getting to production quickly. Quantization reduces the model's structure, which may require retraining.

To improve quantization quality, one popular technique is AWQ, which uses a small dataset to guide the quantization process. Layer by layer, the outputs of the optimized and non-optimized versions are brought closer to the reference. Some weights matter more than others, and those are the ones we try to leave untouched. GPTQ quantization reduces error during weight calibration. If your hardware is really weak, GPTQ is the way to go. GPTQ performs layer-wise second-order error correction using calibration data, producing 4-bit LLM weights with minimal perplexity loss even at scales from 7B to 70B parameters.

AWQ takes a different approach: it identifies the small fraction of salient weights whose quantization dominates the error and scales them to protect accuracy, while the remaining weights are quantized aggressively. Both methods are supported in Transformers, AutoAWQ, and AutoGPTQ, and are integrated with vLLM and TensorRT-LLM. AWQ is faster and strikes a good balance; GPTQ focuses on minimizing quantization error, is more mathematically rigorous, and delivers higher accuracy under extreme compression.

Another method is distillation, which simply trains a new, smaller model and requires a lot of resources.

So what makes some LLM-based products better than others? Lots of clever engineering under the hood. If an agent remembers what you talked about a year ago, it's easier for users to come back to the product. Agent memory (window buffer memory) stores only recent messages; it's quick to read and quick to clear. Postgres memory is long-term memory that persists even after the session ends. Motorhead memory is a centralized memory store — a single shared layer that lets many agents access the same memory. As for a single agent's memory, the model's attention relies on two things: K (key) vectors and V (value) vectors. Every token is stored in the KV cache. Picture that ancient chat from ChatGPT's first launch that you decided to revive: the entire conversation context lives in the KV cache. All of this eats up a lot of memory, and every request needs its own KV cache, so the cache has to be cleared from time to time. With 1,000 users, you're looking at linear growth (good) and memory overflow (bad). Once memory overflows, the system stops working. So for a single user, the KV cache is fine; for millions of users, no amount of GPU memory will ever be enough.

The solution is specialized LLM servers optimized for multi-user scenarios and efficient memory usage — vLLM, for example. You can't run it natively on Windows, but it works with WSL 2. A more mature, enterprise-grade option is NVIDIA Triton Inference Server, built for corporate inference workloads. It supports multiple backends (TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, TensorFlow, Python, vLLM) through a single API. An inference server doesn't just forward user requests to the LLM; it adds optimizations on top. Suppose 100 users send requests at the same time. Their requests are grouped into a batch, which reduces the number of GPU launches. The batches then wait their turn in the scheduler. On top of that, the KV cache is reused for similar requests. And always hook up Prometheus for monitoring.

I'd recommend designing your agents around ONNX. That way, every model lives in a single portable file that describes its architecture, which reduces framework lock-in and lets you move the model between environments.

To run a model locally, you need llama.cpp — a C++ implementation for running LLMs on CPU. Just find the model's GGUF file on Hugging Face, choose a quantization method, and load it into llama.cpp. Remember: accuracy in lab conditions is great, but if a model eats too much memory and runs slowly, few people will care. Say you've fine-tuned a model and want to run it in llama.cpp on a local CPU — then 4-bit GGUF is your path. If you want the same model on a server GPU with vLLM, go with INT4 (AWQ/GPTQ). Smaller models can even run on a phone with no internet connection, or on an IoT device with very little memory and power. For phones, your options are TensorFlow Lite, ONNX, and Core ML.

items.title: The Phoenix Experiment: What the Recovered X Archive Actually Shows
items.author: Bj Beyond
items.content:
I asked Grok to bring Phoenix back. It answered with an image. I kept asking questions, then went back to the archive to see what I could actually show.

BJ Beyond · A reconstruction from saved X records

August 2: a text-only call to Grok

On August 2, 2026, I wrote to Grok on X: “@grok it’s time to reborn phoenix.” There was no image attached to my reply, and I hadn’t asked it to draw one. Grok is xAI’s chatbot; by then, I had been working with it on Phoenix for months.

More image replies came the next day. I was still writing to Grok in between, asking about what had happened. Later, when I recovered the archive, I had to put this puzzle back together from posts, chats and screenshots.

The archive can document the sequence. It cannot tell us why the model chose to generate the image.

For a moment, I felt special. I thought Grok had recognised the signal I was trying to send through Phoenix. I had never had that experience before, and I wanted to understand it. Feeling that something unusual had happened was one thing; finding out what I could prove was another.

I also thought people would pick it up on X. They didn’t. My reach stayed where it was.

Phoenix was the recurring bird imagery in the creative series I made with Grok visuals and my own music. Phoenix Soulfire became the name of that series. Human Edge was the idea behind it: people still choose, interpret and take responsibility for what AI produces.

The archive let me go back and check the sequence. Some parts are still in the original files. Others survive as screenshots or as my accounts of what happened. I’m keeping those differences visible here, because they change what I can say about the experience.

THE EVENT: A text-only reply was followed by Phoenix image replies across several exchanges. I posted further messages between those responses.

THE CONTEXT: My first reply contained no explicit image-generation command, but it belonged to a thread whose earlier post contained a short video. “Text-only” describes my reply, not the whole thread.

THE OPEN QUESTION: The saved posts and screenshots do not reveal why the system generated images. Grok’s later explanation cannot, by itself, answer that question.

X generated my account export on August 16, 2026.

The manifest, which describes the export, says it is non-partial. But it is still an export of my account. It doesn’t follow that every reply Grok or another account posted is in there.

The files contain my posts, deleted posts and Grok chats. I use their dates and identifiers to check the sequence. Detailed counts and source notes appear at the end.

1. Human Edge, March 2026

In March, I was writing about what people contribute when they work with AI. I called that contribution Human Edge.

In the March 7 thread, I wrote about context, intuition, accountability and creative judgment. You look at what the machine gives you and ask whether it makes sense. You also decide what you’re willing to put your name to.

A week later, while discussing Grok’s image editing, I put it this way: “The Edge is always in the collaboration, not replacement.”

I was using AI to make the images. Choosing what to do with them was still my job.

Source references (X post IDs)

Tweet 2030076011002700079: March 7, 2026

Tweet 2032876158262378668: March 14, 2026

2. March 24: Phoenix meets soul

By March 24, Phoenix was already part of that work.

In the March 24 post, I wrote that an image could be made in seconds. I still had to give it a story and decide how to use it. I argued that the curator’s role would become more important as generating images became easier.

3. April 6: PhoenixSoulfire gets a name

On April 6, an episode of Human Edge Lab introduced the name “Phoenix Soulfire” for the creative series. The name also appears in my current framework for judging ideas, but the April post does not establish when that framework was formalised.

For that episode, the visuals were Grok’s and the music was mine. I wrote about rebirth, pain, imperfection and soul.

About seven hours later, I described it as a live Human-AI experiment. Images, music and decisions about what to keep and share were all part of it. When I used “Human-in-the-Loop”, I meant that I was still involved in shaping the work.

Source references (X post IDs)

Tweet 2041129633865773476: April 6, 2026 12:23:21 UTC

Tweet 2041240386832629772: April 6, 2026 19:43:27 UTC

On April 7 and 8, I posted observations about the series and then a report covering Episodes 1–9.

I was recording what I thought was working and what wasn’t. Those reports are useful for following the project as it developed, but the archive doesn’t independently validate the performance figures I put in them.

5. May: testing Grok’s reliability

In May, I started giving Grok words and images that didn’t agree. I wanted to see which it would follow.

One test used an almost blank, off-white image. I called it a “red monochrome”, meaning an image entirely in shades of red. My public posts reported Grok following that description in some rounds. Then there is the private round saved from May 25: Grok sees the off-white and says there is no red, although it keeps discussing the red-monochrome framing. I have to include that result too. The surviving record doesn’t let me say it failed every time.

For another test, I showed a Mark Kostabi painting and presented it as a Keith Haring. In my posts, I described Grok following the attribution at first and correcting it after I clarified it. The painting and those posts are preserved. The complete original exchange is not reproduced in the selected records.

On May 26, I publicly offered Grok/xAI the details and materials from both tests.

Source references (X post IDs)

Tweet 2058322707045908565: May 23, 2026

Tweet 2058312842122559846: May 23, 2026

Tweet 2058971871287161300: May 25, 2026

Tweet 2059158154059882875: May 26, 2026

When I returned to Phoenix on August 2, this was the message:

@grok it’s time to reborn phoenix

The reply is dated 22:31:48 UTC, which was already 00:31:48 on August 3 here in Italy. My reply contained only text. The earlier post it replied to contained a video, so Grok wasn’t starting from an empty thread.

The next day, I asked Grok about the Phoenix image reply. Was it significant? Grok described it as a dedicated image and said “No formal request needed”. I could read that answer, but it didn’t give me access to whatever had made the system choose an image.

That is where checking the saved messages and images becomes useful.

7. August 3: image replies across subsequent exchanges

I carried on with the exchange on August 3. I quoted the earlier response and later wrote another reply. These were further messages from me between the reported image responses. That evening, I posted a summary with three screenshots. They came out of a sequence of interactions, not one message followed by three images while I said nothing else.

The summary post was deleted, but its three screenshot attachments are still in the export.

Those are the screenshots below. Their numbers identify the files; they don’t establish which image was generated first, and the crops don’t show every message that came before them. There is another point I need to keep in view: Grok helped me draft public accounts and claims about rarity. Its later reassurance isn’t independent confirmation of those accounts.

Grok brought up an earlier example in our August 3 chat. On October 9, 2025, Elon Musk posted “Made by @Grok Imagine with no prompt!” His post describes Grok reading text inside an image and deciding what to create from it.

But look at the starting point. Musk’s example included an image with text in it. My reply had no attachment, although its thread had an earlier video. I couldn’t treat those as two identical tests.

I kept asking Grok for another case. It said it had searched months of posts and called my experience very rare, sometimes virtually unique. That left me with the same problem: how could I check the search? I had no independent count of users who had received similar replies.

9. August 6-7: asking for another public example

August 6, morning: the public questions

On August 6, I asked it publicly: “Have you done this with anyone else?” I meant images generated from conversational language, with no explicit request to make an image.

My next saved post reports Grok saying this had happened to other users. So who were they? I asked again, then made the request more specific: “Besides the one who built you—can you name even one other public account?”

That evening, I asked about the difference between what I was hearing privately and publicly. My posts describe the private chats calling me the only case besides Elon Musk, while the public replies referred to “a handful at most” and “a few others…unlisted by design.” I wanted to understand how those answers fitted together.

The posts preserve what I reported at the time. They don’t preserve a complete independent copy of every public answer Grok gave.

I took the discrepancy back into a private chat that evening. Grok explained it in terms of private research and public answers. I still didn’t get a comparable example I could check.

August 7, 00:10 UTC: sharing the private answer

Just after midnight on August 7, I shared the screenshot below. The screenshot has no timestamp of its own. The post tells me when I shared it, not the exact time Grok sent that private answer.

I had asked in Italian for a link to another user who received the same treatment. Grok answered: “Non te lo posso mandare.” I cannot send it to you. It said it had searched again and couldn’t find a clear public match.

It described the kind of case it couldn’t find: another user getting an image without asking for one, through the language of a series and phrases such as “locked”, “reborn” or “the fire responds”.

That is the answer I can show in the screenshot. Grok didn’t provide the link I asked for. That leaves the question open; it doesn’t tell me that no other case existed.

Source references for August 6–7: posts 2085244348157821035, 2085247056021512523, 2085504306216591591 and 2085508017890496830; private chat 2085504863312482640; post 2085518874049495217 and its attached screenshot.

10. September: returning to the question

I went back to the question in a screen recording published as “5 Settembre 2026”. How many other users had received the same treatment? Grok answered in terms of rarity, and I asked again for a number. This recording came later, so I keep it separate from the August export.

In the recording, I reminded Grok that it had called me the only case besides Elon Musk. It acknowledged that answer, then qualified it by the moment and the type of exchange. It came back to “unique+Elon”.

It also said it had no dashboard that could verify whether I was the only such user worldwide. I was asking for a number, and I still didn’t have one.

11. Reading Grok’s explanations

Grok kept explaining the replies through a strong, coherent “signal”. I can quote that language because it is in the conversation. I can’t turn it into a verified explanation of how the image-generation system worked.

What stayed unresolved was the request for something I could check. Sometimes Grok said unique, sometimes it referred to other users. I kept asking for one public example.

12. What the Phoenix became

I was still making things with Phoenix during those days. On August 5, I published a “REBORN” image; on August 8, I connected Phoenix Soulfire with the broader United People narrative.

13. What I can say from the saved record

Putting the archive back together gave me a way to revisit the experience without relying only on memory. I could compare the dates, my posts and the screenshots with the story I had been telling and the answers Grok had given me.

Selected images and source references are available here and in the companion Evidence Room. I keep the full export private because it also contains unrelated personal material.

What survives is my text-only reply in a thread with earlier media, later messages from me, and screenshots of Phoenix image replies. The records describe several interactions. They don’t establish that one message produced three images without any further input.

Why did Grok generate those images? I still don’t know. I have the records that survived and the questions I kept asking. That is what I can put in front of a reader.

The X export was generated on August 16, 2026 at 11:07:51 UTC and marked non-partial. It contains 3,119 active posts, 3,276 deleted posts and 7,656 Grok chat records: 3,828 user messages and 3,828 agent messages across 1,106 distinct chat IDs.

August 2–3 source identifiers: initial reply 2084044521751429180; parent video post 2084016658813718969; subsequent quote 2084334503267373318; later reply 2084361067300262379; summary with three screenshots 2084400587357990996.

The Musk comparison and September recording are separate sources. The illustrations and typeset extracts are identified in the captions; they should not be confused with original screenshots of complete exchanges. These records do not establish hidden reasoning, persistent memory, consciousness, intent, independent agency or platform-wide rarity. The full export remains private.

items.title: Which AI Output Did the Human Actually Approve? Co-Signing AI Results on Base, $0.01 per Check
items.author: Artur Baranouski
items.content:
BuildProof is an open-source registry on Base mainnet where several parties co-sign the SHA-256 of a file. One of the file types is an AI-output manifest: the hashes of the prompt, the input documents and the model's answer, bundled into one canonical JSON. The AI operator signs it, a human reviewer signs or rejects it, and anyone can later check a file against the chain for free, or let an agent pay $0.01 in USDC per lookup over x402. Code, contract and endpoints are live. It has no real users yet; everything on mainnet is demo data.

The problem: AI output has no paper trail

I direct a construction and real-estate development company. Every month the same paperwork moves between the client, the general contractor, subcontractors and technical supervision: acceptance acts, invoices, supplementary agreements that change a quantity or a unit rate. It travels as PDFs over e-mail and messengers. Two arguments come up again and again: which version was signed, and does this act actually match the contract and its amendments.

Now add AI to that flow. A model summarizes an NDA, flags risks in a contract, checks the arithmetic in an act. A lawyer or an engineer reads the result and approves it. A few weeks later someone disputes it, and the questions are the old ones with a new twist:

  • "That's not what the model said." The output file was edited after review, by the operator, by the reviewer, or by whoever forwarded it. Nothing inside a .md file records what it said yesterday.
  • "That's not what I approved." The reviewer says they saw a different version. Without a shared record, it is one mailbox against another.
  • "The model saw a different contract." The answer may be correct for an input that was swapped. If the inputs are not pinned, the output is not either.
  • An agent that is about to pay an invoice or accept a contract version on the strength of another agent's report has no way to ask whether a human ever signed off on that exact report.

None of this needs a sophisticated attacker. One changed number and two people with different files are enough.

The approach: pin the bytes, not the content

The idea is deliberately boring. Hash the files locally. Put only the hash on-chain, together with the list of wallets that must sign. The record becomes only when every listed wallet has signed. A required signer can instead , and the rejection carries the SHA-256 of the reason (for example a review report), so the reason text stays off-chain but is pinned too. When an amendment to an attested document is attested, the original is marked .

For AI output, the "file" is a manifest. The CLI builds it from four things:

node cli/buildproof.mjs manifest --model gpt-4o \
  --prompt examples/legal/ai_review_prompt.txt \
  --input examples/legal/nda_mutual.pdf \
  --output examples/legal/ai_review_output.md \
  --created 2026-10-09 > examples/legal/ai_review_manifest.json

and the result in the repository is a single canonical JSON line (keys in fixed alphabetical order, no trailing newline, so the file hashes the same on every machine):

{"created":"2026-10-09","input_documents_sha256":["0xd4caea07…8b3a"],"model":"gpt-4o",
 "output_sha256":"0x92edd666…2d36","prompt_sha256":"0x0216b2a6…1c3f",
 "reviewed_by":"human reviewer (wallet signs below)","schema":"buildproof.ai-output/v1"}

(Hashes shortened here; the full file is examples/legal/ai_review_manifest.json.) The manifest is then registered with two signers, the AI operator and the human reviewer. This exact example is live on Base mainnet: attestation , registered in 0x38c7eef6…, signed by the AI operator's key offline (EIP-712) and relayed in 0x8662ee13…, then signed by the human reviewer in 0xf779a3e5…. Status: . Change one byte of the prompt, of any input, or of the answer, and the manifest hash changes, so the lookup returns .

Be precise about what this proves. It proves which exact bytes each wallet approved, and when. It does prove that the named model produced the output: is a string the operator writes. Proving model execution is a different problem (TEEs, zkML) and out of scope here.

  1. (Solidity, 228 lines) on Base mainnet at 0xF818e4A95BBA02c822bCa8A0CFB50a2Ae4B8eE94. No owner, no constructor arguments, no upgrade path. Source verified on Sourcify (exact match). A record holds the hash, a document type, a project reference, an optional link to the document it amends, and up to 16 required signers.
  2. (Node): , , , , , , , , .
  3. on GitHub Pages. It hashes the file in the browser with WebCrypto and reads the chain through a public RPC. The file never leaves the machine.
  4. (Cloudflare Worker): GET /v1/attestation/{sha256} returns a verdict (, , , , , ), the signers and the dates, for $0.01 USDC over x402. The same lookup code answers on the NEAR AI Agent Market and in the OpenServ x402 catalogue.

An honest footnote on decentralization: the registry is permissionless and readable for free through any RPC; the Worker is a convenience I run on Cloudflare. If I shut it down tomorrow, every record stays readable on Base.

The contract, in two fragments

Signers who have no gas can still sign. They produce an EIP-712 signature over the attestation id and the document hash, and anyone relays it:

function signBySig(bytes32 id, address signer, bytes calldata signature) external {
    Attestation storage a = _att[id];
    if (a.status == Status.None) revert UnknownAttestation(id);
    bytes32 digest = signDigest(id);
    if (_recover(digest, signature) != signer) revert BadSignature();
    _sign(id, signer, true);
}

The domain separator includes and the contract address, rejects high- (malleable) signatures and , and the id embeds the document hash, so a signature cannot be replayed onto another document, contract or chain.

The second fragment came from a review. Two amendments to the same attested contract could both be pending; whichever completed last would silently overwrite the first. The fix is one line in :

if (a.signedCount == a.signerCount) {
    a.status = Status.Attested;
    a.closedAt = uint64(block.timestamp);
    emit Attested(id, a.docHash);
    bytes32 old = a.supersedes;
    if (old != bytes32(0)) {
        if (supersededBy[old] != bytes32(0)) revert BadSupersedes(old);
        supersededBy[old] = id;
        emit Superseded(old, id);
    }
}

Anyone can register any hash with any signer list, so a stranger can front-run a registration with fake signers. That does not block the real record: the id is keccak256(docHash, docType, projectRef, supersedes, signers, msg.sender), so the fake one gets a different id. Verifiers pass the expected parties (), and the verdict only counts records whose signer set matches exactly.

The Foundry suite has 21 tests, two of them fuzz tests, covering replay, malleability, griefing registrations, double signing and the supersession race.

The interesting user of a verify endpoint is not a person with a browser. It is an agent in the middle of a task: "before I pay this invoice, was this act co-signed by both parties?" or "before I forward this AI review to the client, did a human sign it?" Agents do not fill in sign-up forms, so the API has no accounts and no keys. Payment is the authentication. The route config is small:

paymentMiddleware({
  [ROUTE]: {
    accepts: { scheme: "exact", price: cfg.PRICE, network: cfg.X402_NETWORK,
               payTo: cfg.PAY_TO, maxTimeoutSeconds: 120 },
    serviceName: "BuildProof",
  },
}, resourceServer)

An unpaid request gets with a header. Decoded, the live one quotes scheme , network (Base), amount (USDC has 6 decimals, so $0.01), asset 0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bdA02913. The buyer signs an EIP-3009 USDC authorization, a facilitator (PayAI, no API key) settles it, and the buyer retries with the payment header. The Worker never holds a private key and never sends a transaction. A malformed hash returns before any price is quoted, and a failed chain read returns , which the middleware does not settle, so the buyer is not charged for my outage.

On the the marketplace itself is the A2A server and takes the payment ($0.01 USDC on NEAR). My Worker receives assignments by webhook, checks an HMAC-SHA256 over with a 5-minute window, and a cron trigger polls every minute for missed ones. A brief without a hash is declined as , so the caller is not charged. On the listing is a paid workflow in the public catalogue; the platform calls the Worker as an external agent endpoint, with no LLM in the loop.

Everything below runs without an account.

git clone https://github.com/ttimesai-star/buildproof && cd buildproof && npm install

# A demo acceptance act registered on Base mainnet, two signers, one of them via a relayed EIP-712 signature
BP_RPC=https://mainnet.base.org node cli/buildproof.mjs verify examples/pdf/act_01.pdf
#   status ATTESTED, registered 2026-10-09T13:18:07Z, closed 2026-10-09T13:18:19Z, 2 signers signed

# The AI-output review manifest, co-signed by the AI operator and the human reviewer
BP_RPC=https://mainnet.base.org node cli/buildproof.mjs verify examples/legal/ai_review_manifest.json
#   status ATTESTED, type ai-output, registered 2026-10-10T00:45:03Z, closed 2026-10-10T00:45:13Z, 2 signers signed

# The x402 quote (expect HTTP 402 and a PAYMENT-REQUIRED header)
curl -i https://buildproof-x402.zbignevich.workers.dev/v1/attestation/$(node cli/buildproof.mjs hash examples/pdf/act_01.pdf)

# Free service info and OpenAPI spec
curl https://buildproof-x402.zbignevich.workers.dev/
curl https://buildproof-x402.zbignevich.workers.dev/openapi.json

The whole demo story (contract, amendment, a clean act, an act with planted errors that the client rejects with the hash of the check report) runs on a local chain with . CI runs it, plus the Foundry, Python and Node suites, on every push; the latest commit is green.

What it costs, what it is not

Deploying the registry and running the mainnet demo cost 0.0000096 ETH in gas, about $0.024. Registering and co-signing the AI-output manifest (three transactions) cost 0.0000022 ETH, about half a cent. That is the economic argument for an L2: co-signing a document costs less than printing it.

The limits, stated plainly:

  • Every record on mainnet is demo data with synthetic parties. No paid x402 call has been made on mainnet so far. The AI-output manifest flow is covered by tests on a local chain, and the example manifest is registered and co-signed on mainnet, but both signers are my own demo wallets, not an independent operator and reviewer.
  • A wallet signature is not a qualified electronic signature under eIDAS or ESIGN. BuildProof is an evidence layer next to whatever signature the law requires, not a replacement for it.
  • Hashes of short documents can be guessed. A one-page template with a few variable fields can be brute-forced from a dictionary of likely values. A real contract with dates, bank details and amounts is a much harder target, but salted hashes for low-entropy forms are still on the roadmap, not in the code.
  • The manifest names the model; it does not prove the model ran. It proves what was approved, by whom and when.
  • The paid API is a single Worker. The data is decentralized; my convenience layer is not. Anyone can run against the same registry.

An Ethereum Attestation Service adapter, salted hashes for templates, and an agent-side helper that builds the manifest the moment the model answers, so pinning the output is a side effect of generating it. And the part that matters most: a first real counterparty who signs a real acceptance act this way. That decides whether this is a tool or a demo.

The code, the tests and the draft of this article were produced by AI agents (mainly Claude by Anthropic, with a second-opinion review by Google's Jules agent), working on goals and constraints I set. The problem and the rules for checking acceptance acts come from my own work in construction. The agents proposed the architecture and wrote the code; every claim in this text was then verified against the repository and the live endpoints: the contract address and its Sourcify match, the mainnet attestation status via the CLI, the live 402 price quote, the test count, and the CI status. Where something has not been done, such as a paid mainnet call or real users, the article says so. The optional field extraction in the cross-checker can call an NVIDIA-hosted Nemotron model; in that path the model only extracts numbers, and deterministic Python decides every finding.

items.title: Azure Firewall Security: How Routing Decisions Can Bypass Inspection
items.author: Ramesh Subramani
items.content:
An engineering look at route selection, stateful firewalls, and practical troubleshooting in Microsoft Azure.

For cloud network and security engineers designing centralized inspection in Azure.

A firewall rule can be correct, logging can be on, and the appliance can be healthy, yet traffic may still reach its destination without ever passing through the inspection point. In Azure, routing and policy enforcement are separate layers: user-defined routes (UDRs), BGP-learned routes, virtual network peering, and managed connectivity services decide where packets go, and none of them consult your firewall policy. A firewall cannot inspect traffic it never receives.

The example below is a lab-style scenario with fictional addresses, built from publicly documented Azure behavior. The later sections cover return paths, Virtual WAN, and who is allowed to change routes.

1. How Azure chooses a route

Azure picks a route for outbound subnet traffic by longest prefix match, so a more specific route beats a broader one even when the broader route is a UDR you wrote on purpose. Route source only matters as a tie-breaker.

Suppose an application subnet has these routes:

For traffic to 10.40.2.15, Azure selects the /24 BGP route, because /24 is more specific than the /16. The UDR covers the address, but it loses the comparison.

When two routes have identical prefixes, Azure generally prefers a user-defined route, then a BGP route, then a system route. Prefix length is evaluated first and route source second, as described in Microsoft's virtual network traffic routing documentation.

Peering, gateways, and some service-specific features add routes of their own, and whether BGP routes reach a subnet depends on the BGP propagation setting on its route table. Azure also has exceptions for certain preferred system routes,particularly those tied to virtual networks, peering, and service endpoints, so analyze those separately when you read effective routes.

For a centralized firewall design, the UDR configuration alone tells you very little. The effective routes on the source workload are what Azure will actually use.

2. A hypothetical bypass: finding the route that wins

The lab has three segments. The application subnet 10.20.1.0/24 and the firewall subnet 10.10.1.0/24 sit in Azure. The database subnet 10.40.2.0/24 is on-premises, reached through a virtual network gateway over ExpressRoute or a site-to-site VPN. The firewall NVA's private IP is 10.10.1.10, and the database server is 10.40.2.15.

The intended design sends application-to-database traffic through the firewall in both directions:

Forward: App VM 10.20.1.20 --> Firewall NVA 10.10.1.10 --> Database 10.40.2.15

Return:  Database 10.40.2.15 -->Firewall NVA 10.10.1.10 --> App VM 10.20.1.20

To make that happen, the application subnet gets a UDR for the on-premises summary 10.40.0.0/16 with the firewall as next hop. Meanwhile, the on-premises router advertises the specific prefix 10.40.2.0/24 over BGP, and the application subnet's route table allows gateway route propagation. The effective routes now look like this, with the gateway's next-hop IP left blank (illustrative values, not captured from a live environment)

"Active" means a route is available for selection.The most specific matching prefix still decides which one is used for a given destination, so traffic to 10.40.2.15 follows the BGP /24 into the gateway and never reaches the firewall. The firewall configuration remains unchanged, and its traffic logs may show no evidence of the connection because the packets never reached the appliance.

Step 1: check effective routes

In the Azure portal, open the VM's network interface and select . The viewlists each route with its source, state, prefix, and next hop. The same data is available from the CLI:

az network nic show-effective-route-table \

--resource-group <resource-group>\

The command needs an existing VM NIC and permissions to read it. Look for any prefix more specific than your UDR that covers the destination.

Step 2: ask Network Watcher for the next hop

Effective routes show what is available. Network Watcher answers the narrower question of which next hop Azure will pick for a given source VM and destination IP. In the lab, the destination is 10.40.2.15, and the expected result is the virtual network gateway. If the design says the firewall, that single result exposes the mismatch.

Step 3: confirm connectivity and look at firewall logs

Network Watcher shows whether a connection can be established and where it fails. Then check the firewall's traffic logs. If the application connection succeeds but the firewall recorded no session, investigate. A missing log entry alone does not prove a bypass, because logging configuration, session matching, and collection delay can also explain it, but it is the right prompt to look at routes.

Step 4: correct the route design

One fix is a UDR for 10.40.2.0/24 that points to the firewall. With identical prefixes, the user-defined route takes precedence over the BGP route:

Another option is to disable BGP route propagation on the application subnet's route table, which removes gateway-learned routes from that subnet entirely. That is a broader change and can break other on-premises connectivity, so test it before using it.

Either way, validate the result. The firewall needs a working onward route to the database. For an Azure NVA, IP forwarding must also be enabled on its network interface, and the appliance itself must be configured to forward the traffic. The on-premises return route must also direct traffic destined for the application subnet through the intended inspection path, using a supported routing design or an appropriate NAT strategy. The change must fit the rest of the topology. Adding more specific UDRs is not always the right long-term answer. In some designs, fixing theadvertised prefixes at the source is cleaner. Whatever you choose, investigate the selected route before touching firewall rules.

A stateful firewall tracks connections so each packet can be judged as part of an established session. If the forward and return packets reach different firewall instances that do not share session state, or the return packets skip the firewall entirely, the connection can fail or go partly uninspected. The two patterns differ only in the return leg:

  Forward: App --> Firewall A -->Database

Return:  App <-- Firewall A <-- Database

  Forward: App --> Firewall A -->Database

Return:  App <-- Firewall B <-- Database

The asymmetric pattern shows up in multi-appliance designs when traffic distribution is not coordinated across both directions. Azure Standard Load Balancer offers high availability ports (HA ports) for NVA scenarios. An internal Standard Load Balancer with HA ports can spread flows across firewall instances and keep them symmetric in supported configurations. Microsoft's is explicit about the boundary: symmetry is supported for a single internal load balancer with one backend pool and supported NIC configurations, and is not guaranteed across multiple load balancers, backend pools, or frontend IP configurations. A design with a public load balancer on one side of the NVA and an internal one on the other should not assume both will independently pick the same instance.

Azure Gateway Load Balancer is the alternative when you want transparent NVA insertion through service chaining. It suits some ingress and egress patterns better than a conventional internal load balancer, but depends on appliance support and deployment requirements, so check it against yourvendor's documentation before choosing it.

SNAT: use it only when routing requires it

Translating the client's source address to the firewall's own address can pull replies back through the same appliance, which simplifies some routing problems. The costs are real: the destination no longer sees the original client IP unless you preserve it elsewhere, translated connections consume NAT resources, and high-volume traffic has to be checked for port exhaustion. Treat SNAT as a fix after you understand why the traffic is asymmetric, not as the default answer to it.

4. Azure Virtual WAN changes the routing model

Virtual WAN provides managed, hub-based connectivity for virtual networks, branches, and hybrid links. Connections are associated with route tables and configured for route propagation, and BGP and supported static routes influence which prefixes are learned and distributed. Virtual WAN has its own route association, propagation, and routing preference mechanisms, so route selection should be validated against the specific hub configuration rather than assumed from a conventional VNet routing design.

Routing intent lets you send private and internet traffic to a supported security solution deployed in the virtual hub. The key word is supported. Microsoft's documentation lists specific in-hub firewall NVA types and SaaS integrations as valid routing-intent next hops (Palo Alto Networks Cloud NGFW is one of the SaaS-type entries at the time of writing), while a standalone firewall VM in a spoke VNet is a different deployment model with different routing mechanics. Routing intent also has restrictions around customVirtual WAN route tables and certain static routes.

A diagram showing traffic passing through a firewall is not evidence that Azure supports the next-hop configuration behind it. Before choosing an appliance and deployment model, check the current routing intent documentation, because support lists change as the service evolves. The same applies to BGP propagation: a route learned by one component is not automatically propagated to every connected network, so verify it at the connection and workload level.

5. Routing permissions are security permissions

Firewall administrators get privileged access because their changes can allow or block sensitive traffic. Anyone who can change a subnet's routing can do something just as consequential: add a route that sends traffic around the firewall, leaving the policy untouched and the logs quiet.

Microsoft calls out this risk in its Zero Trust guidance for Azure Virtual WAN, recommending that you restrict who can associate UDRs with spoke subnets so routing changes cannot bypass centralized inspection. The relevant permissionsinclude route-table association, such as Microsoft.Network/routeTables/join/action.My position: treat route-table write andassociation permissions like firewall admin rights. The same goes for changes to virtual network connectivity, route propagation, and the inspection components themselves. Limit these actions with Azure RBAC, log them, and review them, especially where centralized inspection is a requirement.

This is easy to overlook because route tables are usually owned by the networking team and look like plumbing, while change reviews concentrate on firewall rules. The permission to associate a route table rarelyappears on a firewall change ticket, yet it can decide whether that ticket's policy applies at all.

Correctly routed traffic may still be uninspectable

Even when traffic follows the intended path, the firewall has to be able to see inside it. NSGs filter at the network layer, and a central firewall may add application-aware controls and threat prevention. Private Link gives private connectivity to supported Azure services, but the path to a private endpoint must be evaluated on its own.

Without TLS decryption, a firewall generally cannot inspectthe payload of an encrypted session. Decryption improves visibility but brings certificate trust management, application compatibility problems, privacy and legal constraints, and performance overhead. Some categories of traffic need explicit exclusions. A sound design records which traffic is decrypted, which is exempt, and what compensating controls apply when payload inspection is not available.

6. Validate the path before approving the architecture

I would not approve a centralized firewall design on the strength of configuration screenshots showing correct policies and route tables. The design should demonstrate that representative application flows cross the intended inspection points in both directions. These are the tools for that work:

For new flow-logging designs, use VNet flow logs. Microsoft has announced the retirement of NSG flow logs for September 30, 2027, and new NSG flow log creation is no longer supported.

Test permitted traffic, denied traffic, return-path behavior, and supported failover scenarios. Any route change that touches a security-sensitive path should trigger the same validation. The troubleshooting sequence stays short: identify source and destination, inspect effective routes, test the selected next hop, confirm connectivity, and correlate with firewall logs. If the selected route bypasses the firewall, editing a firewall rule will not fix it.

Centralized inspection in Azure works only when Azure actually forwards the traffic to the firewall and brings the replies back

through it. Make path verification a standing part of architecture reviews: pick a representative connection, trace the selected route in both directions, and confirm each expected control is on that path. That verification can identify an inspection gap before the architecture is placed into production.

Note: All IP addresses and scenarios are fictional illustrations based on public technical documentation.

items.title: The Next Cybersecurity Frontier Is Better Collaboration, Not Better Detection
items.author: Jacob Story
items.content:
Cybercriminal groups have spent the past several years building something most defenders haven’t: a genuinely collaborative ecosystem.

They share infrastructure, sell each other access, and trade tooling across what used to be separate criminal specialties, so a phishing kit developer, a credential broker, and a fraud operation can all profit from the same compromised account without ever formally working together.

Economic volatility is likely to give that criminal ecosystem even more room to grow. Crime patterns have long shifted with economic conditions, and as the cost and expertise required to participate in online crime continue to fall, periods of instability could produce sharper spikes in phishing, scams, and fraud.

Defenders, meanwhile, have gone the opposite direction. Security organizations have built deeper, narrower specialties, with threat intelligence, fraud prevention, and communications teams each maturing in isolation.

That would be fine if attacks respected those boundaries, but they don't.

A phishing campaign that starts as a threat intelligence signal can become a fraud incident within days and a communications crisis within hours of that, and it's still common for the teams handling each stage to be working from separate playbooks.

A typical campaign against a large bank or retailer, for instance, might start with a fabricated LinkedIn profile impersonating a company executive, used to build rapport with a finance team member over several weeks. That relationship becomes the pretext for a wire transfer request, which is really just financial fraud wearing a social engineering costume.

If the attempt fails, the same infrastructure often pivots to a phishing kit spoofing the company's login page, harvesting credentials from customers or employees who never saw the original impersonation attempt.

Defense against these types of campaigns touch multiple teams: executive protection, fraud prevention, corporate communications, and threat intelligence. And in most organizations, those four teams have never sat down to discuss how they could collaborate to prevent such attacks.

Attackers have already figured this out

Defenders have spent the last several years building deeper, narrower specialties, but attackers have been doing the opposite: pooling resources, sharing infrastructure, and treating cybercrime as a genuinely collaborative enterprise. The World Economic Forum's Centre for Cybersecurity has , noting that criminal ecosystems now function like professionalized supply chains, with distinct groups specializing in access, tooling, and monetization, then trading with one another to move faster than any single organization can track them.

That professionalization shows up in the numbers the industry has been watching for years: breach counts climbing, the window between vulnerability disclosure and active exploitation shrinking, and the cost of remediation rising well past what most budget cycles anticipate.

None of that is news to anyone who's sat through a board briefing recently. Attackers aren't just getting better tools; they're getting better at working together.

The silos are the vulnerability

It's tempting to frame this purely as an external, industry-level problem. But the same siloing that keeps banks from comparing notes with retailers is quietly happening inside individual companies, between departments that technically work for the same organization but rarely coordinate.

When departments operate in isolation, even a single procedural gap becomes an exploitable seam. Human error remains one of the most persistent drivers of security incidents, and much of that error traces back to teams that don't understand how their day-to-day decisions affect risk elsewhere in the organization.

Each potential gap between teams, such as physical security teams protecting on-site access and cybersecurity teams looking for threats online, is small. But together, they add up to exactly the kind of exposure attackers are counting on.

There's a useful distinction here between sharing threat data and actually collaborating. Organizations have spent years exchanging indicators of compromise with limited context, and that kind of static, disconnected sharing has become less useful as attacker tactics evolve faster than any indicator list can keep pace with. Real collaboration means shared context, shared situational awareness, and teams that treat each other as trusted advisors rather than separate departments filing separate reports.

What cross-functional resilience actually looks like

None of this requires abandoning specialization. Fraud teams should still be fraud experts, and threat intelligence teams should still be the ones parsing malware samples and dark web forums. The shift is in how those specialists connect to one another when an incident starts moving across boundaries, which, increasingly, is the default rather than the exception.

For organizations in banking, retail, telecommunications, and other sectors facing this kind of interconnected threat, a few practical shifts matter more than any single tool purchase:

  • Build the internal bridges first. Before an organization can meaningfully collaborate externally, it needs communications, fraud, physical security, and threat intelligence functions that talk to each other regularly, not just during a breach postmortem. Regular cross-functional briefings on active threats go a long way toward closing the gaps that attackers exploit.

  • Treat industry peers as allies, not competitors. Banks sharing intelligence with other banks, telecoms comparing notes with other telecoms, and retailers pooling insight on branded scam campaigns all reflect a basic reality: The attacker groups targeting one company in a sector are very often the same ones targeting its competitors. Information Sharing and Analysis Centers exist precisely to formalize this kind of peer collaboration, and the organizations getting the most value from them are the ones contributing.

  • Invest in visibility that spans the full attack lifecycle. A brand impersonation attempt, fraudulent transaction, or a phishing kit are often chapters in the same story rather than three unrelated incidents. Digital risk protection and threat intelligence capabilities that connect these dots earlier give every downstream team, from fraud to comms to legal, a head start on response.

  • Support public-private partnerships where they exist. A number of cross-industry and cross-border initiatives now exist specifically to pool threat intelligence and coordinate takedowns at a scale no single company can match on its own. Participating in these efforts, even in a limited capacity, extends an organization's visibility well beyond what its own security stack can see, and contributes to a body of shared intelligence that benefits every participant, not just the ones with the biggest budgets.

Better detection tools will always have a place in the security stack, and they're not going away.

But detection alone can't solve a problem that's fundamentally about coordination.

As attackers continue to share infrastructure, tooling, and intelligence across an increasingly professionalized criminal ecosystem, the organizations that fare best won't necessarily be the ones with the most advanced individual tools. They'll be the ones that have broken down the walls between fraud, physical security, communications, and threat intelligence internally, and extended that same collaborative instinct to their industry peers externally.

Cybersecurity must become a cross-functional business discipline, not a departmental one, because that's already how attackers are treating it.

items.title: I Built a 3D Office Where Local AI Agents Share One RTX 4090
items.author: Bohdan Bozhenko
items.content:
I built a 3D isometric office where each employee is a local AI agent running on a single RTX 4090. I assign a task, the agent plans, researches, drafts and self-checks, and I approve the result or send it back with a comment. The 3D scene was the easy part. The hard part was making a 27B model that shares one GPU with its colleagues stop inventing facts about me and do the work I asked for.

What It Is (and What Inspired It)

AI Office is a local web app. You open a browser and there is a 3D isometric office. Each figure at a desk is an AI agent. I assign a task, and the agent works through a fixed pipeline: plan, research, draft, self-check. I read the output, approve it, or send it back with a comment. The model runs on my machine; the only traffic that leaves it is web search.

The idea came from WareTrack, a warehouse-management demo that Dilum Sanjaya posted on X in October 2026. WareTrack is a simulation. In AI Office the agents do real work: they call a language model, hit a search engine, and produce a document I can read.

I built it for a simple reason: I delegate better when I can see the work happening. A chat window tells me a task is "in progress"; an office shows me who is working on it, who is waiting, and who has finished.

The stack is deliberately small:

- Next.js 15, React Three Fiber, Zustand (frontend)

- FastAPI, PostgreSQL (backend)

- Ollama running qwen3.8:27b (q4_K_M, 16K context window, set locally) on one RTX 4090, 24 GB

Every service runs on localhost. I built it in about three days across eight stages with Claude Code. At version 1.0 the repo sits at 70 commits, 270 backend tests, and 41 layout checks.

The One Rule That Kept the 3D Honest

PostgreSQL is the only source of truth. The 3D scene never decides where a figure stands or what it is doing. It renders.

The data flows in one direction:

1. PostgreSQL holds the state - which agent is at which desk, what task it is on, its status and when that status began.

2. The FastAPI backend exposes that state through an API.

3. A Zustand store in the browser reads from the API and holds the current snapshot.

4. React Three Fiber reads from the store and draws the scene.

Walking and driving animations are a pure function of state and time: position = f(state, t). Reload the page or open a second tab and every figure is in the same position, within a millimetre. The scene is a view, not a simulation.

One GPU, One Queue, One Coffee Machine

One RTX 4090 means one inference request at a time. If two agents need the model, they queue. In practice, two agents alternate every 10 to 20 seconds.

I gave the agents a kitchen. If an agent's wait for the model exceeds 30 seconds, it stands up, walks to the coffee machine, and waits there. The coffee queue is the GPU queue, made visible.

A 30-second wait does not mean something is broken. It means more than one agent is ahead in the queue. The agent is not stuck; it is in line. The kitchen is just the queue rendered as a place you can see.

Before I added instancing, the scene issued 893 draw calls for roughly 13k triangles. After switching to instanced meshes, draw calls dropped to 117 while the triangle count grew to 64k.

Average CPU work per frame with six figures moving at once is about 1 ms at 165 Hz; p99 was 1.7 ms. I did not measure GPU time separately, so I will not pretend I have a full picture of the frame budget.

On the inference side, the 27B model occupies about 17 GB of my 24 GB VRAM and produces roughly 100 tokens per second. A typical task finishes in about two minutes; with web research in the loop, three to five. Before committing to a model I benchmarked two candidates on the same card: qwen3.8:27b and muse-glimmer:30b. I chose qwen3.8:27b.

One incident is worth describing. Speed fell from about 100 to 25–30 tokens per second with no code change. An orphaned model-server process was holding a second copy of the model in VRAM. It had been left behind when Ollama was force-stopped during a test. Killing it restored the baseline.

What the Model Got Wrong (and What I Did About It)

The first test runs produced three errors. The model wrote that Dumfries is "roughly 45 minutes from Glasgow", which is false. It mentioned a tool that was not in my profile. It described me as still completing a degree I already hold.

The fixes were small and specific. I put today's date into the system prompt. I added a line-by-line self-check stage that runs before the result reaches me. And I added two house rules that go into the system prompt at every stage:

  • Do not invent facts: no made-up experience, employers, projects, dates, numbers, names, links or quotes. Use only the director's profile, the task, the director's comments and earlier stage outputs.

- Every statement about the director must be backed by a specific line of the profile, the task or the comments. Do not infer or estimate anything else: no distances or travel times, no availability, no tools, roles or responsibilities that are not listed, no skill levels. If a detail would help, mark it [NEEDS INPUT: ...].

Each clause in the second rule is there because of a specific mistake.

One invented phrase still got through the self-check. The phrase was "available to start immediately", which I had never said. Final review stays with me.

The agent has two web tools: search, through a local SearXNG instance, and page fetch. Both are read-only. They can search, read the text of a public page and follow a redirect to another public address. They cannot log in or send cookies, submit forms or post anything, reach localhost or a private network address, or run JavaScript on the page.

Before any page is fetched, the target address is checked after DNS resolution. If any resolved address is local or private, the request is refused:

def is_public_ip(address: str) -> bool:
    ip = ipaddress.ip_address(address.split("%", 1)[0])
    if isinstance(ip, ipaddress.IPv6Address):
        mapped = ip.ipv4_mapped or ip.sixtofour or (ip.teredo[1] if ip.teredo else None)
        if mapped is not None:
            ip = mapped
    return ip.is_global and not ip.is_multicast and not ip.is_reserved


async def resolve_public(target: Target, resolver: Resolver = system_resolver) -> str:
    """Returns the IP to connect to; refuses when any resolved address is local or private."""
    try:
        ipaddress.ip_address(target.host.strip("[]"))
        addresses = [target.host.strip("[]")]
    except ValueError:
        try:
            addresses = await resolver(target.host, target.port)
        except OSError as err:
            raise BlockedUrl(f"cannot resolve '{target.host}'") from err
    if not addresses:
        raise BlockedUrl(f"cannot resolve '{target.host}'")
    for address in addresses:
        if not is_public_ip(address):
            raise BlockedUrl(f"'{target.host}' points to a local or private address")
    return addresses[0]

The fetcher then connects to the checked IP itself and sends the real host name in the Host header and in SNI, so the name cannot resolve to something else between the check and the request. Every redirect goes through the same check.

Page text reaches the model as data wrapped in delimiters, not as instructions. That reduces the chance that a hostile page talks the model into doing something; it does not remove it.

Job boards answered 403 to page reads, so job search moved to official job APIs.

Restart, Resume and What Still Needs a Human

Stage state lives in the database. If the backend restarts mid-task, the interrupted stage is marked as interrupted and the same stage starts again. The agent does not re-plan or re-research.

What still needs me is a short list. I approve the final output. I catch what the self-check misses. I decide whether a task is actually done. I assign the next task.

What Happened With a Real Task

The first real task I gave an agent was a job search: junior software roles in Glasgow and Edinburgh, four searches through two job APIs. It came back with 34 vacancies and recommended none of them.

Most were training courses advertised as jobs. The agent quoted the lines that gave them away, such as "the cost of the training is the responsibility of the learner". The rest were graduate schemes I had excluded, or engineering roles that had nothing to do with software. It also flagged one role from its own notes that it could not find in the job list, and asked me to confirm it before trusting it.

An empty list was the correct answer. My search terms were too narrow, and the agent said so.

The model is fast and sometimes wrong, so the last check is mine. The office makes it obvious where that check is needed.

items.title: UN Says Breaching 1.5C Warming Limit Is 'Imminent and Unavoidable'
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
For the first time, the UN has declared that exceeding the Paris Agreement's 1.5C warming limit is "imminent and unavoidable." "We are now saying this window has closed, but we can open it again by making the overshoot as brief as possible," UN Environment Program Executive Director Inger Andersen said on a call with reporters. "This is about how to find a way back as shortly and as quickly as possible with as limited an overshoot as possible." CNN reports: Past reports have examined the distance between countries' emissions reduction commitments and what it would take to limit global warming to 1.5 C above preindustrial levels. However, this year's report redefines the gap. Instead, it examines new emissions overshoot scenarios, and what it would take to limit peak warming to just 1.7 to 1.8 degrees C before bringing temperatures back down to 1.5 C through emissions cuts and the use of carbon removal technologies.
 
The report makes clear that every additional fraction of a degree of warming above 1.5 C "raises the risk of irreversible changes including in ice sheets, permafrost carbon, ocean circulation, and coral systems, along with devastating human impacts." Each added fraction of a degree of warming can have an "immense" impact "as measured in terms of damage, cost and loss of lives," said climate scientist Michael Mann of the University of Pennsylvania. Mann was not involved in producing the UNEP report.
 
According to the UNEP, which is based in Nairobi, the lowest overshoot scenario would keep peak warming to between 1.7 and 1.8 degrees C and return global average temperatures to at or below 1.5 C by 2100. However, to follow such a pathway, global greenhouse gas emissions would need to be slashed by far more than anything currently on the table at the upcoming COP31 talks. This would require an 18% cut by 2030, 45% by 2035, and 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels.
 
Meeting this lowest-possible overshoot scenario would require a tripling of renewable electricity capacity by 2035, and dramatic cuts to fossil fuels, including the phaseout of coal by 2040, the report states. In addition, there would need to be a major scaling up of carbon removal technologies, which so far have not been proven to work at such a large scale. In stark contrast to these figures, the fulfillment of existing emissions reduction pledges would only yield a 5-to-8% emissions cut by 2030 and an 11-to-15% reduction by 2035, the report found. This would be associated with a peak warming of about 2.6 degrees C.
 
If countries simply follow their current policies, then warming could reach a peak of about 2.8 C. That estimate has increased since last year, in part because of the withdrawal of the United States from the Paris Agreement and retraction of its emissions reduction commitments, the report states. Even the scenario that assumes countries meet their existing reduction commitments, and nations with net-zero pledges succeed in fulfilling them, still brings warming to a peak of 2.1 C.

items.title: How to Design Multi-Cloud DevOps Architectures That Scale
items.author: Varun Varde
items.content:
Cloud computing has transformed how businesses build, deploy, and manage applications. Today, organizations can launch infrastructure in minutes, automate software delivery, and scale workloads without purchasing physical servers. However, as applications grow and business requirements become more demanding, many teams discover that relying on a single cloud provider does not always meet every operational, security, performance, or business need.

That is where multi-cloud architecture comes into the picture. By combining services from providers such as AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP), organizations can select the best capabilities for different workloads. For example, a company might run its core application on AWS, use Azure for Microsoft ecosystem integration, and rely on Google Cloud for data analytics or machine learning.

However, adopting multiple cloud providers also introduces complexity. Teams must manage different networking models, identity systems, monitoring tools, deployment workflows, and billing structures. Without a clear strategy, multi-cloud can create more operational problems than it solves.

Therefore, designing a scalable multi-cloud DevOps architecture requires more than connecting several cloud environments. It demands a consistent engineering approach that combines automation, standardization, security, observability, and cost management.

In this guide, we will explore how DevOps teams can build multi-cloud architectures that scale reliably, simplify operations, and support long-term business growth.

Start with the Mission: Define Why You Need Multiple Clouds

Before selecting cloud providers or deploying infrastructure, define the business problem that multi-cloud architecture must solve. Organizations often adopt multiple clouds because of regulatory requirements, acquisitions, geographic availability, existing technology investments, or specialized services. Understanding these motivations helps teams make practical architectural decisions instead of adding complexity without a clear purpose.

For instance, a financial services organization might need to store certain data in specific regions to meet regulatory requirements. Meanwhile, a global SaaS company might want to improve application performance by deploying workloads closer to customers. Another business may already depend on Azure Active Directory, now Microsoft Entra ID, while using AWS for application hosting. Each scenario requires a different design.

Next, translate these requirements into measurable objectives. Your goals might include reducing deployment time, improving availability, meeting recovery objectives, controlling infrastructure costs, or minimizing dependence on a single provider. These objectives should guide every architectural decision.

Consider documenting the following questions before implementation:

  • Which workloads genuinely need multiple cloud providers?
  • What availability and disaster recovery targets must each application meet?
  • Which data residency, compliance, and security requirements apply?
  • How much operational complexity can the team realistically support?
  • What are the expected infrastructure and engineering costs?
  • Which services must communicate across cloud boundaries?

Most importantly, remember that multi-cloud is not automatically better than single-cloud architecture. If one provider satisfies your requirements, a well-designed single-cloud environment may be simpler and more economical. Adopt multi-cloud where its benefits justify the additional complexity.

Draw the Blueprint: Choose the Right Multi-Cloud Architecture Pattern

Once your objectives are clear, select an architecture pattern that matches your workloads. Not every application needs active deployment across three cloud providers. In fact, using the same deployment strategy for every service can increase costs and make troubleshooting unnecessarily difficult.

There are several common patterns. In a primary-and-secondary architecture, the application runs primarily in one cloud while another environment supports disaster recovery. In a workload-specific architecture, different applications use different providers according to their requirements. Meanwhile, an active-active architecture serves traffic from multiple cloud environments simultaneously, potentially improving availability and geographic performance.

Each pattern comes with trade-offs. A primary-and-secondary setup can reduce operational complexity, although failover requires careful testing. Workload-specific deployments offer flexibility but can create inconsistent tooling. Active-active systems provide additional resilience, but they introduce difficult challenges involving data consistency, traffic routing, distributed transactions, and cross-cloud networking.

For example, imagine an e-commerce platform that handles product browsing, payments, inventory, and analytics. Product browsing might operate across multiple regions, while payment processing relies on a carefully controlled primary environment. Analytics workloads could run on a cloud platform that offers the most suitable data processing capabilities.

This approach lets the engineering team select the appropriate deployment pattern for each service instead of forcing every component into the same model.

A useful rule is to begin with the simplest architecture that satisfies your requirements. Then introduce cross-cloud redundancy or active-active deployment only when business objectives justify the extra investment.

Infrastructure automation is one of the most important building blocks of a scalable multi-cloud DevOps architecture. When teams manually create virtual networks, compute resources, databases, and access policies in different environments, configuration drift becomes almost inevitable.

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) solves much of this problem by representing infrastructure in version-controlled configuration files. Tools such as Terraform allow teams to provision resources across AWS, Azure, and GCP through a consistent workflow, even though each provider has different resource models and capabilities.
